metadata.concept: Decide which of two identifiers wins arbitration by comparing bits from the most significant end

payload.concept: Decide which of two identifiers wins arbitration by comparing bits from the most significant end
payload.explanation: CAN is wired so that a dominant bit (0) overrides a recessive bit (1). Nodes send the identifier most significant bit first and a node that sends a 1 but reads a 0 drops out. So the numerically lowest identifier wins. Two nodes must never send the same identifier at the same time. The loop compares bit 10 down to bit 0 and the first difference decides.
payload.misconception: The frame with the larger identifier has higher priority.

payload.document:
Embedded C · STM32_HAL · can bus · exercise · explain-why · Intermediate
Prompt: Why does the CAN frame with the lowest identifier win arbitration without any data being lost?

payload.answer: The bus is wired so that a dominant 0 overrides a recessive 1. Each sender transmits its identifier most significant bit first and reads the bus at the same time. A sender that transmits a 1 but reads a 0 knows another node has a lower identifier, stops sending and retries later. The node with the lowest identifier never sees a mismatch, so its frame continues unchanged and is not corrupted or delayed.
payload.prompt: Why does the CAN frame with the lowest identifier win arbitration without any data being lost?

metadata.concept: Accept a frame when the masked identifier equals the masked filter value

payload.concept: Accept a frame when the masked identifier equals the masked filter value
payload.explanation: In mask mode a filter has an id value and a mask. A 1 in the mask means that bit must match and a 0 means do not care. The test is (id & mask) == (value & mask). If the value is not masked too, any bit set in the value outside the mask makes the match fail for every frame, and the node silently receives nothing.
payload.misconception: A mask filter compares the identifier directly with the filter value.

metadata.concept: Build the identifier field of the transmit mailbox for standard and extended frames

payload.concept: Build the identifier field of the transmit mailbox for standard and extended frames
payload.explanation: In the bxCAN transmit identifier register TIR a standard 11-bit identifier occupies bits 31 to 21. An extended 29-bit identifier occupies bits 31 to 3 and the IDE bit (bit 2) must be set. The RTR bit is bit 1 and the TXRQ request bit is bit 0. Using the standard shift for an extended frame cuts off the top 8 identifier bits and leaves IDE clear, so the frame goes out as a different, standard frame.
payload.misconception: The identifier sits in the same bits for standard and extended frames.

payload.bad_label: undefined behaviour reported by the sanitizer: left shift
payload.concept: Read a 32-bit little-endian value from the data bytes of a frame without signed overflow
payload.explanation: A uint8_t is promoted to int before it is shifted, so d[3] << 24 is a signed shift. For a byte of 0x80 or more the result does not fit in a 32-bit int, which is undefined behaviour even though the value is then stored in an unsigned variable. Cast to uint32_t before shifting. The data bytes of a frame are an array, so the order (little- or big-endian) is a protocol choice and not a property of the CPU.
payload.misconception: A byte shifted left by 24 is safe because the result is stored in an unsigned variable.

A frame carries an 11-bit or 29-bit identifier that names the message and sets its priority, up to eight data bytes, a CRC and an acknowledge slot. Nodes arbitrate bit by bit while sending the identifier, so there is no bus master and the lowest identifier always wins.

metadata.concept: Derive the bit timing register value from the peripheral clock, baud rate and segment lengths

payload.concept: Derive the bit timing register value from the peripheral clock, baud rate and segment lengths
payload.explanation: A CAN bit is split into time quanta: one synchronisation quantum, then segment BS1, then segment BS2. The baud rate is pclk / (prescaler x (1 + BS1 + BS2)). The sample point is at (1 + BS1) / (1 + BS1 + BS2) of the bit, commonly 75 to 87 percent. In the bxCAN BTR register every field is stored minus one (prescaler, BS1, BS2, SJW), so writing the plain values makes every segment one quantum too long and the bus speed wrong. Return zero when the prescaler does not divide evenly.
payload.misconception: The bit timing register stores the segment lengths exactly as you choose them.

payload.concept: Add to a shared value with a compare-and-swap loop that retries when another context changed it
payload.explanation: An atomic store alone does not help when the new value depends on the old one. The loop load, compute, compare-exchange succeeds only if the value is still the one the computation used; otherwise it reloads and tries again. On Cortex-M3 and above this compiles to load-exclusive and store-exclusive. Cortex-M0 has no exclusive instructions, so there the compiler needs a library or a short interrupt-off section.
payload.misconception: Reading a shared value, adding to it and writing it back is safe if the write is atomic.

payload.concept: Save the interrupt mask on entry and restore it on exit so critical sections can nest
payload.example_bad:
void enterBad(void) { __disable_irq(); }
void exitBad(void) { __enable_irq(); }
payload.explanation: If code that is already inside a critical section calls a function that has its own, the inner exit enables interrupts too early and the rest of the outer section runs unprotected. Read PRIMASK on entry, disable interrupts, and write the saved value back on exit. The inner section then restores the already-disabled state.

metadata.concept: Protect a read-modify-write of a shared counter so an interrupt cannot make an update disappear

payload.concept: Protect a read-modify-write of a shared counter so an interrupt cannot make an update disappear
payload.explanation: count++ is a load, an add and a store. If an interrupt that also increments the counter runs between the load and the store, the store overwrites its increment with a stale value and one update is lost. Wrap the read-modify-write in a critical section, or use an atomic operation, so the interrupt waits until it is complete.
payload.misconception: The statement count++ is a single operation and cannot be interrupted.

payload.document:
Embedded C · STM32_HAL · volatile and race conditions · exercise · explain-why · Advanced
Prompt: Why is volatile not enough to make count++ safe against an interrupt that also increments count?

payload.answer: volatile only ensures that each access in the source happens. count++ still consists of a load, an add and a store, and an interrupt can run between the load and the store. When the main code then stores its stale result it overwrites the interrupt update. The operation must be made indivisible, with a critical section or an atomic read-modify-write.

metadata.concept: Read a 64-bit counter updated by an interrupt by reading the high word before and after the low word

payload.concept: Read a 64-bit counter updated by an interrupt by reading the high word before and after the low word
payload.explanation: A Cortex-M core loads 32 bits at a time, so reading a 64-bit tick counter takes two loads, and an interrupt between them can carry from the low word into the high word. The result is a value that never existed, off by 2^32. Read the high word, then the low word, then the high word again, and retry when the two high words differ; no interrupt masking is needed.
payload.misconception: A 64-bit counter can be read as two 32-bit loads at any time.

metadata.concept: Mark a variable shared with an interrupt volatile so each read really happens

payload.concept: Mark a variable shared with an interrupt volatile so each read really happens
payload.explanation: The compiler optimises the main loop as if nothing else could change a variable. A flag set by an interrupt must be volatile, otherwise the compiler may read it once and keep the value in a register, and the loop never ends. In the compiled Cortex-M code the difference shows as a second load instruction. volatile does not make a multi-step operation atomic; it only keeps each access.
payload.misconception: A variable that an interrupt handler sets can be read normally in the main loop.

Prompt: Why can a main loop that waits for a flag set in an interrupt run forever when the flag is not declared volatile?

payload.answer: The compiler assumes no other code changes the flag while the loop runs, because the loop never changes it. It is then free to read the flag once before the loop and test the copy kept in a register, so the interrupt writes the real variable but the loop never looks at it. volatile forces a fresh read of the variable on each test.

metadata.concept: Derive the timer input clock from the bus clock, which is doubled when the APB prescaler is not 1

payload.concept: Derive the timer input clock from the bus clock, which is doubled when the APB prescaler is not 1
payload.explanation: The timers on an APB bus run at twice the bus clock whenever the APB prescaler is greater than 1, and at the bus clock when it is 1. With a 168 MHz core, APB1 divided by 4 gives 42 MHz and its timers run at 84 MHz; APB2 divided by 2 gives 84 MHz and its timers at 168 MHz. Using the bus clock gives a timer frequency that is half the real one.
payload.misconception: A timer runs at the APB clock of its bus.

payload.concept: Encode M, N, P and Q into PLLCFGR with P as a two-bit code and the HSE source bit set
payload.explanation: PLLCFGR holds M in bits 5:0, N in bits 14:6, the P code in bits 17:16, the source select in bit 22 (1 for HSE) and Q in bits 27:24. The P field is a code, not a divider: 0 means 2, 1 means 4, 2 means 6 and 3 means 8, so P = (divider / 2) - 1. Writing the divider itself selects the wrong value.
payload.misconception: The P field holds the divider value directly.

payload.concept: Pick the flash wait states for a core clock, rounding down at exact multiples of the step
payload.explanation: At 2.7 to 3.6 V the STM32F4 flash needs one more wait state for each 30 MHz step of the core clock: 0 wait states up to and including 30 MHz, 1 up to 60 MHz, and so on. The count is (hclk - 1) / 30 MHz; plain division gives one too many at exactly 30, 60, 90, 120, 150 and 180 MHz. The latency must be set before the clock is raised.
payload.misconception: The number of wait states is the clock divided by 30 MHz.

metadata.concept: Compute the system clock from the PLL settings and reject values outside the VCO limits

payload.concept: Compute the system clock from the PLL settings and reject values outside the VCO limits
payload.explanation: On the STM32F4 the PLL first divides the oscillator by M to get the VCO input (1 to 2 MHz, 2 MHz preferred), multiplies by N to get the VCO output (192 to 432 MHz), and divides by P (2, 4, 6 or 8) to get the system clock. With an 8 MHz crystal, M = 8, N = 336 and P = 2 give 1 MHz, 336 MHz and 168 MHz. Leaving out the division by M gives a number eight times too high, and values outside the limits must be refused.
payload.misconception: The system clock is the oscillator frequency times N divided by P.

metadata.concept: Switch to the PLL clock in a safe order: oscillator, PLL, flash latency, then the switch

payload.concept: Switch to the PLL clock in a safe order: oscillator, PLL, flash latency, then the switch
payload.explanation: Raising the clock before the flash has the right number of wait states makes the CPU read instructions that the flash cannot deliver in time. The safe order is: start the oscillator and wait for it, start the PLL and wait for it, set the flash latency (and bus prescalers), switch the clock source, and wait until the status confirms the switch. Each wait needs a timeout so a missing crystal does not hang start-up.
payload.misconception: The system clock can be switched as soon as the PLL is ready; the flash settings can follow.

payload.document:
Embedded C · STM32_HAL · clock tree · exercise · explain-why · Intermediate
Prompt: Why must the flash wait states be set before the system clock is raised?

payload.answer: The flash can only deliver an instruction in a fixed time, so a faster clock needs more wait states. If the clock rises first, the CPU fetches instructions faster than the flash can supply them and gets wrong data or faults. Setting the latency first makes it correct for the faster clock; when lowering the clock the order is reversed.

metadata.concept: Compute CRC-16/CCITT-FALSE with polynomial 0x1021 and initial value 0xFFFF

payload.concept: Compute CRC-16/CCITT-FALSE with polynomial 0x1021 and initial value 0xFFFF
payload.explanation: The initial value matters for interoperability: CRC-16/CCITT-FALSE starts at 0xFFFF and gives 0x29B1 for 123456789, while CRC-16/XMODEM uses the same polynomial 0x1021 but starts at 0 and gives 0x31C3. A zero start also cannot detect leading zero bytes. Always name the full parameter set (width, polynomial, initial value, reflection, final XOR) when you specify a protocol.
payload.misconception: The initial value of a CRC does not matter as long as sender and receiver agree.

payload.document:
Embedded C · STM32_HAL · crc calculation · exercise · explain-why · Intermediate
Prompt: Why does the initial value of a CRC matter even though the receiver recomputes the same CRC?

payload.answer: Both ends must use the same initial value or the checks never agree, so it is part of the protocol. A start value of zero also makes the CRC blind to leading zero bytes: a message and the same message with extra zero bytes in front have the same CRC. A non-zero start such as 0xFFFF makes the register change for leading zeros and so catches that kind of error.

metadata.concept: Compute the reflected CRC-32 used by Ethernet and zip with initial and final XOR

payload.concept: Compute the reflected CRC-32 used by Ethernet and zip with initial and final XOR
payload.explanation: The common CRC-32 is reflected: it processes the low bit first with the reversed polynomial 0xEDB88320, starts the register at 0xFFFFFFFF and XORs the result with 0xFFFFFFFF at the end. The check value for 123456789 is 0xCBF43926. Skipping the initial value or the final XOR gives a valid-looking number that no other implementation will match.
payload.misconception: CRC-32 starts at zero and ends with the raw register value.

metadata.concept: Compute an MSB-first CRC-8 by testing the top bit before each shift

payload.concept: Compute an MSB-first CRC-8 by testing the top bit before each shift
payload.explanation: A CRC is the remainder of the message polynomial divided by a generator polynomial. For the common MSB-first form, each byte is XORed into the top of the register, then for each of 8 steps the register is shifted left and the polynomial is XORed in when the bit shifted out was 1. CRC-8 with polynomial 0x07 and initial value 0 gives 0xF4 for the ASCII text 123456789. Testing the low bit and shifting right is the reflected variant and needs a different polynomial constant.
payload.misconception: A bitwise CRC tests the lowest bit and shifts right.

metadata.concept: Match the STM32 hardware CRC unit with CRC-32/MPEG-2 (polynomial 0x04C11DB7, no reflection)

payload.concept: Match the STM32 hardware CRC unit with CRC-32/MPEG-2 (polynomial 0x04C11DB7, no reflection)
payload.explanation: The default STM32 CRC unit uses polynomial 0x04C11DB7, initial value 0xFFFFFFFF, no input or output reflection and no final XOR; that is CRC-32/MPEG-2, whose check value for 123456789 is 0x0376E6E7. It differs from the zip CRC-32 (0xCBF43926). To reproduce it in software, process bits most significant first. Hardware consumes 32-bit words, so a byte stream must be fed in the same grouping on both sides.
payload.misconception: The STM32 hardware CRC gives the same value as the zip CRC-32.

Context: platform: STM32_HAL
Embedded C · STM32_HAL · CRC calculation · Overview
A cyclic redundancy check treats a message as a long binary number and divides it by a fixed generator polynomial; the remainder is sent along with the message. It detects all burst errors up to its width and most random errors, and is cheap in hardware and software. Different standards fix a width, polynomial, initial value, bit order and final XOR, and all of them must match.

metadata.concept: Replace the inner bit loop with a 256-entry lookup table built once

payload.concept: Replace the inner bit loop with a 256-entry lookup table built once
payload.explanation: The table holds the result of 8 shift steps for every possible byte, so one table lookup replaces the bit loop. It does not depend on the message length. Build it once at start-up (or at compile time and store it in flash) and use crc = (crc >> 8) ^ table[(crc ^ byte) & 0xFF] for the reflected CRC-32. Check that table[1] is 0x77073096 and that the result matches the bitwise version.
payload.misconception: A table-driven CRC needs a different table for every message length.

metadata.concept: Compute Fletcher-16 with two running sums modulo 255 so that byte order matters

payload.concept: Compute Fletcher-16 with two running sums modulo 255 so that byte order matters
payload.explanation: Fletcher-16 keeps two sums: sum1 adds each byte and sum2 adds sum1 after every byte, each modulo 255. The second sum depends on position, so swapping two bytes changes the result, which a plain sum cannot see. The check value for abcde is 0xC8F0. Reducing modulo 256 instead of 255 makes the result different from the standard and weakens error detection.
payload.misconception: Fletcher-16 reduces both sums modulo 256.

payload.document:
Embedded C · STM32_HAL · checksum · exercise · explain-why · Intermediate
Prompt: Why can Fletcher-16 detect two swapped bytes when a plain 8-bit sum cannot?

payload.answer: A plain sum is the same for any order of the bytes. Fletcher keeps a second sum that adds the first sum after each byte, so each byte is counted once for every byte that follows it. Moving a byte therefore changes the second sum, and the result changes, while the first sum alone stays the same.
payload.prompt: Why can Fletcher-16 detect two swapped bytes when a plain 8-bit sum cannot?

metadata.concept: Keep the running sums in a state object so a checksum can be updated as bytes arrive

payload.concept: Keep the running sums in a state object so a checksum can be updated as bytes arrive
payload.explanation: In a UART receiver the bytes arrive one at a time from an interrupt. Keep the running sums in a small state structure, update it per byte, and read the result when the frame ends. Resetting the state at the start of each call, as a one-shot function does, discards the earlier bytes.
payload.misconception: A checksum must be computed over the complete buffer in one call.

metadata.concept: Create a two-complement sum checksum so that all bytes of the record add up to zero

payload.concept: Create a two-complement sum checksum so that all bytes of the record add up to zero
payload.explanation: Intel HEX and many bootloaders use a two-complement checksum: the checksum byte is the value that makes the 8-bit sum of all bytes of the record, checksum included, equal to zero. That is (0 - sum) & 0xFF, which is the inverse plus one. Using only the inverse is off by one, and the receiver check sum == 0 always fails.
payload.misconception: The checksum byte is the bitwise inverse of the sum.

metadata.concept: Verify a received frame by summing all bytes including the checksum byte

payload.concept: Verify a received frame by summing all bytes including the checksum byte
payload.explanation: With a two-complement checksum the receiver sums every byte of the frame including the checksum, and a good frame gives zero. A common mistake is to include the checksum byte in the calculation and then compare against it, which only matches by accident. Also check the length first, because an empty frame has no checksum byte to read.

metadata.concept: Compute an NMEA 0183 checksum as the XOR of the characters between the dollar sign and the asterisk

payload.concept: Compute an NMEA 0183 checksum as the XOR of the characters between the dollar sign and the asterisk
payload.explanation: An NMEA sentence looks like $GPGLL,...*31. The two hex digits after the asterisk are the XOR of all characters between the $ and the *, exclusive of both. XOR is cheap and catches any single-bit error, but it cannot detect two errors in the same bit position and it ignores byte order. Include the $ in the loop and every checksum is wrong.
payload.misconception: The NMEA checksum covers every character of the sentence.

Prompt: Why does a button need debouncing, and how does the stable-for-20-ms rule remove false presses?

payload.answer: A mechanical contact does not close cleanly: for a few milliseconds the contacts make and break, so the pin flips between levels several times. Code that reacts to each change sees several presses. The rule remembers when the raw level last changed and accepts it as the new stable level only after it has stayed unchanged for the debounce time, so the short flips are ignored.

metadata.concept: Report a press once, on the stable falling edge, not on every loop while held

payload.concept: Report a press once, on the stable falling edge, not on every loop while held
payload.explanation: loop() runs thousands of times per second, so a level test fires on every pass while the button is held. A press event is a transition: the stable level was HIGH on the previous pass and is LOW now. Keep the previous stable level and compare. The same idea gives a release event with the opposite change.
payload.misconception: Acting whenever the button is pressed gives one action per press.

payload.concept: Tell a short press from a long press by comparing the hold time at release
payload.explanation: delay() freezes everything else for a second. Record the time at the press event and decide at the release event: a hold shorter than the long-press time is a short press, otherwise a long press. payload.concept: Wire a button to ground, use INPUT_PULLUP and treat LOW as pressed

payload.misconception: A pressed button reads HIGH.

metadata.concept: Compare elapsed time with unsigned subtraction so millis() rollover is harmless

payload.concept: Compare elapsed time with unsigned subtraction so millis() rollover is harmless
payload.explanation: millis() is an unsigned 32-bit counter that wraps to 0 after about 49.7 days. start + interval can wrap while now has not, so the addition form fires immediately or never. Unsigned subtraction wraps the same way as the counter, so (uint32_t)(now - start) is the correct elapsed time across the wrap as long as the interval is shorter than half the range.
payload.misconception: now >= start + interval is the same as now - start >= interval.

metadata.concept: Compute how many unread bytes lie between the read index and the DMA write index with wrap-around

payload.concept: Compute how many unread bytes lie between the read index and the DMA write index with wrap-around
payload.explanation: When DMA has wrapped past the end of the buffer, head is numerically smaller than tail and head - tail is negative; with unsigned types it becomes a huge number. Add the buffer size before taking the remainder: (head + size - tail) % size. This gives 0 for an empty buffer, so a completely full buffer cannot be told apart from an empty one and the reader must run often enough to stay behind a full lap.
payload.misconception: The number of unread bytes is head minus tail.

Prompt: Why can a circular DMA buffer not tell a completely full buffer from an empty one using head and tail alone?

payload.answer: When the write index has advanced a full lap and caught up with the read index, head equals tail, which is exactly the state of an empty buffer. The two states are indistinguishable from the indices. The reader must therefore run often enough that DMA never gains a full lap, for example by using the half-transfer and transfer-complete interrupts, or the design must keep a separate count.

metadata.concept: Give DMA the transfer count in items of the configured width, not in bytes

payload.concept: Give DMA the transfer count in items of the configured width, not in bytes
payload.explanation: NDTR counts data items of the width configured for the transfer (8, 16 or 32 bits), not bytes. For a 32-bit transfer of 64 bytes the count is 16. Writing 64 makes the controller move four times as much memory and overwrites whatever follows the buffer. Also check that the buffer address is a multiple of the item width.
payload.misconception: The transfer count register is always in bytes.

metadata.concept: Drain the circular buffer from tail to head, wrapping at the end of the buffer

payload.concept: Drain the circular buffer from tail to head, wrapping at the end of the buffer
payload.explanation: If head is below tail the new data is in two pieces: from tail to the end of the buffer and from the start to head. Loop with an index that wraps (i = (i + 1) % size) until it reaches head, and store the new tail. A loop that only runs while i < head skips the first piece after a wrap.
payload.misconception: A drain loop that copies from tail up to head works for every position.

metadata.concept: Convert the DMA remaining-count register NDTR into the next write index of a circular receive buffer

payload.concept: Convert the DMA remaining-count register NDTR into the next write index of a circular receive buffer
payload.explanation: NDTR counts the transfers that are still to be done, and in circular mode it counts down from the buffer size and then reloads. The write position is therefore size - NDTR, and when NDTR has just reloaded to the full size that means index 0. Using NDTR directly as the index mirrors the buffer: the first received byte appears to be at the end.
payload.misconception: The NDTR register holds the index where DMA will write next.

metadata.concept: Acknowledge an EXTI line by writing a 1 to its PR bit with plain assignment

payload.concept: Acknowledge an EXTI line by writing a 1 to its PR bit with plain assignment
payload.explanation: A pending bit in EXTI->PR is cleared by writing 1 to it; writing 0 changes nothing. The read-modify-write form reads PR, ORs in the bit and writes everything back, so every other line that was pending in the copy is written as 1 and is cleared too, even if its handler has not run. Assigning only the bit you handled writes 0 to all the others. If the handler forgets to clear PR at all it runs again immediately.
payload.misconception: EXTI->PR |= bit acknowledges the interrupt.

payload.answer: Pending bits are cleared by writing 1. The |= form reads the whole register, so every line that is pending at that moment is 1 in the copy, and the write-back writes 1 to all of them, clearing them without their handlers running. Assigning EXTI->PR = bit writes 1 only to the handled line and 0 to the rest, and writing 0 has no effect.

metadata.concept: Handle every pending line in a shared handler such as EXTI9_5 with a loop over the PR bits

payload.concept: Handle every pending line in a shared handler such as EXTI9_5 with a loop over the PR bits
payload.explanation: Lines 5 to 9 share one vector. If two pins trigger before the handler runs, an else-if chain handles only the first and the second pending bit makes the handler run again later, at the cost of latency and, if it was cleared by the wrong write, loss. Read PR once, loop over lines 5 to 9, call the handler for each set bit and acknowledge that bit.
payload.misconception: EXTI9_5_IRQHandler can check the lines in an else-if chain.

metadata.concept: Encode with COBS so the packet contains no zero bytes and zero can be the delimiter

payload.concept: Encode with COBS so the packet contains no zero bytes and zero can be the delimiter
payload.explanation: COBS replaces each zero by a count of the bytes up to the next zero. The encoder reserves a slot for the count, copies non-zero bytes, and when it meets a zero (or has copied 254 bytes) writes the count into the slot and reserves a new one. The final count must be written after the loop, otherwise the last block header is left unset. For {11 22 00 33} the output is 03 11 22 02 33.
payload.misconception: COBS output can be written in one pass without going back.

Concept: Size the output buffer for the worst case before encoding
Misconception: The encoded packet is never more than one byte longer than the input.
Explanation: COBS adds one byte per 254 input bytes plus one, so 254 non-zero bytes become 256 bytes; the formula is n + n / 254 + 1. SLIP can double the size, since every byte may be escaped, plus the two END bytes: 2 n + 2. Allocating n + 1 for COBS overflows for long non-zero runs.
Incorrect:
size_t cobsMaxBad(size_t n) { return n + 1; }
Correct:
size_t cobsMax(size_t n) { return n + n / 254 + 1; }
size_t slipMax(size_t n) { return 2 * n + 2; }
Complexity: O(1)

payload.example_good:
size_t cobsMax(size_t n) { return n + n / 254 + 1; }
size_t slipMax(size_t n) { return 2 * n + 2; }
payload.explanation: COBS adds one byte per 254 input bytes plus one, so 254 non-zero bytes become 256 bytes; the formula is n + n / 254 + 1. SLIP can double the size, since every byte may be escaped, plus the two END bytes: 2 n + 2. Allocating n + 1 for COBS overflows for long non-zero runs.
payload.misconception: The encoded packet is never more than one byte longer than the input.

metadata.concept: Encode a packet with SLIP by escaping the END and ESC bytes

payload.concept: Encode a packet with SLIP by escaping the END and ESC bytes
payload.explanation: SLIP marks the end of a packet with the byte 0xC0 (END). If the data contains 0xC0 it is sent as 0xDB 0xDC, and because 0xDB (ESC) now has a special meaning it too must be escaped, as 0xDB 0xDD. Skipping the ESC rule makes the decoder misread any data byte 0xDB. Check the output capacity before every write.
payload.misconception: Only the END byte 0xC0 has to be escaped.

payload.document:
Embedded C · STM32_HAL · serial framing · exercise · explain-why · Intermediate
Prompt: Why must a SLIP encoder escape the ESC byte as well as the END byte?

payload.answer: The escape sequences themselves start with ESC. If a data byte equal to ESC were sent unchanged, the decoder would take it as the start of an escape sequence and read the following byte as 0xDC or 0xDD. So ESC in the data must be sent as ESC followed by 0xDD, which keeps every ESC on the wire unambiguous.
payload.prompt: Why must a SLIP encoder escape the ESC byte as well as the END byte?

metadata.concept: Decode SLIP one byte at a time with an escape flag

payload.concept: Decode SLIP one byte at a time with an escape flag
payload.explanation: A byte-at-a-time decoder keeps a flag that says the previous byte was ESC. After ESC, 0xDC means 0xC0 and 0xDD means 0xDB. END with at least one data byte ends a packet; an empty packet (two END bytes in a row) is ignored. Treating the byte after ESC as itself turns 0xDB 0xDC into two data bytes.
payload.misconception: The decoder can treat every byte after 0xDB as data.

metadata.concept: Select an alternate function through AFR[pin / 8] using four bits per pin

payload.concept: Select an alternate function through AFR[pin / 8] using four bits per pin
payload.explanation: Each pin needs a 4-bit alternate-function number (AF0 to AF15), so a 32-bit register holds only 8 pins. The 16 pins are split over AFR[0] (pins 0 to 7) and AFR[1] (pins 8 to 15). The index is pin >> 3 and the shift is (pin & 7) * 4. Shifting by pin * 4 for pin 8 or higher shifts a 32-bit value by 32 or more, which is undefined behaviour in C. The pin must also be in alternate-function mode (MODER = 10).
payload.misconception: One 32-bit AFR word holds the alternate function of all 16 pins.

metadata.concept: Change one output pin atomically by writing BSRR instead of read-modify-write on ODR

payload.concept: Change one output pin atomically by writing BSRR instead of read-modify-write on ODR
payload.explanation: ODR |= mask is three steps: read ODR, OR, write ODR. If an interrupt changes another pin of the same port between the read and the write, the write puts back the old value and that change is lost. BSRR is write-only: bits 0..15 set pins, bits 16..31 reset pins, and zero bits do nothing, so one store changes exactly the pins you name.
payload.misconception: ODR |= mask is a single safe operation.

Prompt: Why is writing BSRR safer than ODR |= mask when an interrupt handler also changes pins of the same port?

payload.answer: ODR |= mask reads the port, modifies a copy and writes the whole register back. If an interrupt changes another pin between the read and the write, the write restores that pin to its old value and the interrupt's change is lost. BSRR is a write-only register where each set or reset bit affects only its own pin and zero bits do nothing, so a single store changes exactly the named pins and cannot overwrite changes made elsewhere.

metadata.concept: Set a pin mode with a two-bit field in MODER: clear the field, then write the mode

payload.concept: Set a pin mode with a two-bit field in MODER: clear the field, then write the mode
payload.explanation: Each pin owns two bits in MODER: 00 input, 01 general-purpose output, 10 alternate function, 11 analog. Pin n sits at bit 2n. OR-ing 1 << n sets the wrong field (bit 5 belongs to pin 2) and can never clear an old mode. Clear the two bits with a mask, then OR in the new mode shifted to 2n. PUPDR and OSPEEDR use the same two-bit layout.
payload.misconception: MODER has one bit per pin, so setting bit n makes pin n an output.

metadata.concept: Choose open-drain with OTYPER for shared lines: the pin only pulls low, a resistor pulls high

payload.concept: Choose open-drain with OTYPER for shared lines: the pin only pulls low, a resistor pulls high
payload.explanation: OTYPER bit n = 1 selects open-drain: writing 0 to ODR pulls the line to ground, writing 1 releases it and an external (or internal) pull-up brings it high. Several open-drain outputs on one wire form a wired-AND: the line is high only if every device releases it. I2C relies on this. Push-pull (bit = 0) drives both levels, so two push-pull outputs fighting on one wire short each other.
payload.misconception: An open-drain output can drive the pin high.

payload.concept: Give an input a pull-up in PUPDR and read a pressed button as 0
payload.explanation: An input with no driver and no pull resistor floats and can read either level. PUPDR (two bits per pin: 00 none, 01 pull-up, 10 pull-down) ties the pin to a defined level through an internal resistor. A button wired to ground then reads 1 when idle and 0 when pressed, so the code must treat the pin as active low. The level is read from IDR, bit n.

payload.concept: Pass through coast when reversing so the bridge never changes direction in one step
payload.explanation: Reversing a spinning motor at once makes it act as a generator and drives a large current back through the bridge and the supply, and with discrete switches it can turn two switches of one leg on together. Prompt: Why should a motor driver pass through coast before reversing?

payload.answer: A motor spinning in one direction keeps turning and behaves as a generator when the drive is reversed abruptly, so a large current flows through the bridge, and with discrete transistors a short pause is needed so that the two switches of one leg are never on together. A coast step lets the current decay and the bridge settle before the new direction is applied.

metadata.concept: Turn a signed speed into the two input duties of an H-bridge channel

payload.concept: Turn a signed speed into the two input duties of an H-bridge channel
payload.explanation: A dual-input driver such as the DRV8833 turns forward when only IN1 is driven and reverse when only IN2 is driven. A signed speed therefore becomes: positive gives IN1 = duty and IN2 = 0, negative gives IN1 = 0 and IN2 = duty, zero gives both low (coast). The duty is the absolute value, limited to the PWM range. Writing a negative number to an unsigned compare register wraps it to a large positive duty.
payload.misconception: A negative speed can be written straight to the PWM compare register.

metadata.concept: Convert a shunt amplifier reading into motor current in milliamps, including the amplifier gain

payload.concept: Convert a shunt amplifier reading into motor current in milliamps, including the amplifier gain
payload.explanation: The shunt voltage is small, so a current-sense amplifier multiplies it by a fixed gain before the ADC. The ADC voltage is code x Vref / 4095, and the current is that voltage divided by the gain and the shunt resistance. With 100 milliohm, a gain of 20 and a reading of 1000 on a 3.3 V reference, the voltage is 805 mV and the current is 402 mA. Leaving out the gain gives a value 20 times too high and trips the current limit.
payload.misconception: The motor current is the ADC voltage divided by the shunt resistance.

metadata.concept: Convert a 7-bit I2C address to the left-shifted form the STM32 HAL expects

payload.concept: Convert a 7-bit I2C address to the left-shifted form the STM32 HAL expects
payload.explanation: Datasheets print a 7-bit I2C address such as 0x48. On the wire the address is followed by the read/write bit, so the first byte is (address << 1) | R/W. The STM32 HAL functions take the address already shifted left by one and set the R/W bit themselves. Passing the raw 7-bit value addresses a different device, so the transfer fails or reaches the wrong chip. Keep the address as 7 bits in your own code and shift it in one helper.
payload.misconception: The HAL takes the same 7-bit address that the datasheet prints.

metadata.concept: Compute the largest pull-up resistor that meets the rise time for a given bus capacitance

payload.concept: Compute the largest pull-up resistor that meets the rise time for a given bus capacitance
payload.explanation: The open-drain bus rises through the pull-up resistor Rp, so the 30 to 70 percent rise time is about 0.8473 x Rp x Cb. For a rise-time limit tr (1000 ns in standard mode, 300 ns in fast mode) the largest resistor is Rp = tr / (0.8473 x Cb). In integer arithmetic the numerator tr_ns x 10^7 reaches 10^10, which does not fit in 32 bits and silently wraps for unsigned values; use a 64-bit intermediate. Treat the result as an upper bound and check the lower bound from the sink current.
payload.misconception: A 32-bit multiply is wide enough for the pull-up formula.

metadata.concept: Free a bus held low by a slave with up to nine clock pulses followed by a STOP

payload.concept: Free a bus held low by a slave with up to nine clock pulses followed by a STOP
payload.explanation: If the microcontroller resets in the middle of a transfer, a slave may still be driving SDA low while it waits for the rest of a byte. The master cannot issue a START until SDA is released. Pulse SCL until SDA goes high, at most nine times (eight data bits and the acknowledge), and then create a STOP condition by pulling SDA low and releasing it while SCL is high. Give up and report an error after nine pulses.
payload.misconception: One clock pulse is enough to release a stuck bus.

payload.document:
Embedded C · STM32_HAL · i2c master · exercise · explain-why · Intermediate
Prompt: Why is a bus recovery limited to nine clock pulses?

payload.answer: A stuck slave is partway through shifting a byte, and a byte on the I2C bus is eight data bits followed by an acknowledge bit, so at most nine clocks complete whatever the slave was doing. After that the slave releases SDA. If SDA is still low after nine pulses the cause is something other than a half-finished byte, such as a short or a hung device, and more pulses will not help, so the function should report failure.

Context: platform: STM32_HAL
Embedded C · STM32_HAL · I2C master · Overview
I2C is a two-wire, open-drain bus with a clock line SCL and a data line SDA shared by one or more masters and many slaves. Every transfer starts with a START condition and a 7-bit address plus a read/write bit, each byte is answered by an acknowledge bit, and the transfer ends with a STOP. Pull-up resistors, not the chips, create the high level, so the resistor value and bus capacitance set the maximum speed.

metadata.concept: Read a sensor register and report failure instead of returning stale data

payload.concept: Read a sensor register and report failure instead of returning stale data
payload.explanation: HAL_I2C_Mem_Read returns a status. When the device does not acknowledge, the buffer is left as it was, so a function that ignores the status hands the caller whatever the buffer held, which looks like a real reading. Check the status, write the result through an output pointer only on success, and return an error code the caller can test.
payload.misconception: A register read always produces a valid byte.

payload.concept: Scan the usable address range 0x08 to 0x77 and collect the devices that acknowledge
payload.explanation: I2C reserves addresses 0x00 to 0x07 (general call, START byte, CBUS, high-speed master code and others) and 0x78 to 0x7F (10-bit addressing and reserved). A scan probes only 0x08 to 0x77, which is 112 addresses. Use HAL_I2C_IsDeviceReady with one trial and a short timeout and store each address that answers.
payload.misconception: A bus scan should probe every address from 0 to 127.

metadata.concept: Take an ISR event flag with an atomic test-and-clear, and clear it before processing

payload.concept: Take an ISR event flag with an atomic test-and-clear, and clear it before processing
payload.explanation: If the ISR sets the flag again while the main loop is still processing the previous event, clearing the flag afterwards erases the new event. Read and clear the flag in one step with interrupts off, then process; a new event that arrives during processing sets the flag again and is handled on the next pass. The flag must be volatile because the compiler cannot see the interrupt write it.
payload.misconception: Clearing the flag after processing the event is the same as clearing it before.

Prompt: Why must the main loop clear an ISR event flag before it processes the event, and why must the flag be volatile?

payload.answer: If the flag is cleared after processing, an interrupt that arrives during processing sets the flag again and the clear that follows erases that new event, so it is lost. Clearing first (together with the test, with interrupts off) keeps the new event for the next pass. The flag must be volatile because the interrupt changes it outside the normal flow of the main loop; without volatile the compiler may read it once and never see the update.

metadata.concept: Count dropped bytes in the receive ISR instead of waiting for space

payload.concept: Count dropped bytes in the receive ISR instead of waiting for space
payload.explanation: An ISR that waits for the main loop to free a slot never returns, because the main loop cannot run while the ISR is executing. The ISR must finish quickly: when the buffer is full it drops the byte and increments a counter. The main code can report or react to the counter. Ignoring the return value of the push loses data without any sign.
payload.misconception: If the buffer is full the ISR should wait until the main loop makes room.

payload.concept: Find which pins caused a pin-change interrupt by XOR-ing the new port value with the old one
payload.explanation: One pin-change interrupt vector serves a whole group of pins (eight on PORTB of the ATmega328P) and does not say which one changed. Keep the previous port value in a variable, XOR it with the current value to get the changed bits, and AND the changed bits with the current value to get the rising ones; changed AND NOT current gives the falling ones.
payload.misconception: The pin-change vector tells you which pin changed.

metadata.concept: Pass bytes from an ISR to main code with a power-of-two ring buffer that keeps one slot free

payload.concept: Pass bytes from an ISR to main code with a power-of-two ring buffer that keeps one slot free
payload.explanation: With only a head and a tail index, head == tail must mean empty, so full has to be detected earlier: the buffer is full when advancing head would make it equal to tail. That wastes one slot, so 8 slots hold 7 bytes. With a power-of-two size the wrap is a mask instead of a division, which is cheap on an 8-bit CPU. The ISR writes only head and main code writes only tail, so the two never write the same variable.
payload.misconception: A ring buffer of 8 slots can hold 8 bytes.

metadata.concept: Compute the RFC 1071 Internet checksum with end-around carry and an odd trailing byte

payload.concept: Compute the RFC 1071 Internet checksum with end-around carry and an odd trailing byte
payload.explanation: The Internet checksum, used by IPv4, ICMP, UDP and TCP, is the one's complement of the one's complement sum of the data taken as 16-bit big-endian words. Carries out of bit 15 must be added back (end-around carry), so accumulate in 32 bits and fold. A trailing odd byte is padded with a zero byte on the right. The RFC 1071 example bytes 00 01 F2 03 F4 F5 F6 F7 give 220D; a 16-bit accumulator drops the carry and gives 220F. A packet that includes its correct checksum sums to zero.
payload.misconception: Summing the 16-bit words in a 16-bit variable gives the checksum.

metadata.concept: Pack an IPv4 address and test whether two addresses share a subnet under a prefix length

payload.concept: Pack an IPv4 address and test whether two addresses share a subnet under a prefix length
payload.example_bad: int netBad(uint32_t x, uint32_t y, uint32_t m) { return (x & m) == y; }
payload.explanation: An IPv4 address is a 32-bit value; the first octet goes in the top byte, so 192.168.1.10 is 0xC0A8010A. Two hosts are on the same subnet when their addresses agree after masking, so the mask must be applied to both. A /24 mask is 0xFFFFFF00. Computing a mask as all ones shifted left by (32 - bits) is undefined for bits = 0, because the shift count is 32, so handle that case separately.

metadata.concept: Copy a packet out of a chain of pbufs, crossing segment boundaries and respecting the destination size

payload.concept: Copy a packet out of a chain of pbufs, crossing segment boundaries and respecting the destination size
payload.explanation: lwIP stores a packet as a linked chain of pbufs: each has its own payload and len, and the head also holds tot_len for the whole chain. A received frame can be split across several pbufs, for example when it spans memory pool blocks. Reading only p->payload gets the first segment and silently loses the rest. Walk the chain, copy at most the remaining room of the destination at each step, and stop at the end of the chain.
payload.misconception: The first pbuf of a chain holds the whole packet.

metadata.concept: Send a whole buffer through a socket-style call that may accept only part of it

payload.concept: Send a whole buffer through a socket-style call that may accept only part of it
payload.example_bad:
typedef int (*SendFn)(const uint8_t *, size_t);
int sendBad(SendFn f, const uint8_t *p, size_t n) { return f(p, n); }
payload.explanation: On a TCP socket, send or lwip_write can return fewer bytes than requested when the send buffer is nearly full. The return value is the number of bytes accepted, and the caller must send the rest. Loop until all bytes are accepted, advance the pointer by the returned count, and treat a result of zero or less as an error so a closed connection cannot make the loop spin forever.
payload.misconception: A successful send call has accepted all of the bytes.

Prompt: Why can a send call accept fewer bytes than requested, and what must the caller do?

payload.answer: The call copies data into the connection send buffer, whose free space is limited by the window and by memory. When there is less room than requested, only part is accepted and the call returns that count. The caller must keep the rest and send it again, advancing by the returned count, until everything is accepted, and treat zero or a negative result as an error or a closed connection.

metadata.concept: Compare TCP sequence numbers with modular arithmetic so that the wrap at 2^32 is handled

payload.concept: Compare TCP sequence numbers with modular arithmetic so that the wrap at 2^32 is handled
payload.example_bad: int seqLtBad(uint32_t a, uint32_t b) { return a < b; }
payload.explanation: TCP sequence numbers are 32-bit and wrap around. The ordering is defined modulo 2^32: a is before b when the signed 32-bit difference a - b is negative, which is the TCP_SEQ_LT macro in lwIP. A plain a < b says that 0xFFFFFFF0 comes after 5, although 5 is only 21 bytes later in the stream. A window test uses the same idea: seq is inside the window when the unsigned distance from the window start is less than its length.
payload.misconception: Sequence number a comes before b when a < b.

metadata.concept: Compute the bit-band alias address of a peripheral bit on Cortex-M3 and Cortex-M4

payload.concept: Compute the bit-band alias address of a peripheral bit on Cortex-M3 and Cortex-M4
payload.explanation: Cortex-M3 and Cortex-M4 map each bit of the peripheral region 0x40000000 and the SRAM region 0x20000000 to one word in an alias region, so that a single store sets or clears one bit atomically. The alias address is alias_base + (byte_offset x 32) + (bit x 4). Cortex-M0, M0+ (which includes the RP2040) and M7 have no bit-band region, so portable code uses the set and clear registers of the peripheral instead.
payload.misconception: Bit-banding is available on every Cortex-M core.

payload.example_bad:
typedef struct { volatile uint32_t SR, DR, CR1; } DevBad;
size_t crOffBad(void) { return offsetof(DevBad, CR1); }
payload.explanation: A struct laid over the peripheral base address works only if every register sits at the right offset, so unused and reserved registers must still be represented. Leaving out a reserved gap moves every later register. Assert the offsets with _Static_assert and offsetof so a mistake stops the build. metadata.concept: Write unlock keys in the order the reference manual gives

payload.concept: Write unlock keys in the order the reference manual gives
payload.explanation: Flash and some other registers are protected by a key sequence: write KEY1 (0x45670123) and then KEY2 (0xCDEF89AB) to the key register. A wrong or reversed key typically locks the register until the next reset, and the next write then fails or causes a bus error. Write the keys in manual order and confirm the lock bit before starting an erase or program.
payload.misconception: The two flash unlock keys can be written in any order.

metadata.concept: Declare register pointers volatile so every read and write reaches the bus

payload.concept: Declare register pointers volatile so every read and write reaches the bus
payload.explanation: A register can change without the program writing it, and a read can have side effects such as clearing a flag. volatile tells the compiler that every access in the source must happen, in order. Without it the optimiser may combine two reads of the same address into one or move a read out of a loop. On Cortex-M the generated code shows it: two reads through a volatile pointer give two load instructions, through a plain pointer only one.
payload.misconception: The compiler always performs each read of a register that the source code contains.

Embedded C · STM32_HAL · memory mapped io · exercise · explain-why · Intermediate
Prompt: Why must a status register pointer be volatile even though the program never writes to the register in the loop that polls it?

payload.answer: The hardware changes the value, not the program. If the pointer is not volatile the compiler may assume that nothing else modifies the location, read it once, and keep the value in a CPU register for the whole loop, so the loop never sees the flag change. volatile forces a fresh bus read at every access in the source.

metadata.concept: Poll a status register with a fresh read on every pass and a bounded number of tries

payload.concept: Poll a status register with a fresh read on every pass and a bounded number of tries
payload.explanation: A wait loop must read the register again on each pass, otherwise it tests a stale copy and never sees the flag change. It should also give up after a bounded number of tries and return an error, so a missing clock or a broken peripheral does not hang the program.
payload.misconception: Reading the status register once before the loop is enough.

metadata.concept: Build a CONNECT packet for protocol level 4 with the keep-alive in network byte order

payload.concept: Build a CONNECT packet for protocol level 4 with the keep-alive in network byte order
payload.explanation: All MQTT 16-bit fields, such as the keep-alive and every string length, are big-endian. A CONNECT packet is the byte 0x10, the remaining length, the protocol name "MQTT" with its length 00 04, the level 04, the flags (02 for a clean session), the keep-alive and then the length-prefixed client identifier. Client "a1" with a 60 second keep-alive gives 10 0E 00 04 4D 51 54 54 04 02 00 3C 00 02 61 31. Writing the keep-alive low byte first on a little-endian MCU turns 60 seconds into 15360 seconds.
payload.misconception: Multi-byte fields are written in the byte order of the processor.

payload.concept: Decide when to send PINGREQ with an elapsed-time test that survives the millisecond counter wrapping
payload.explanation: The broker drops a client that is silent for 1.5 times the keep-alive, so the client sends a PINGREQ after half the interval of silence (keep-alive in seconds x 500 milliseconds). The test must use the unsigned difference now - last. Comparing now >= last + interval fails near the wrap of the 32-bit counter: last + interval overflows to a small number and the ping is sent far too early.
payload.misconception: Comparing the current time with the last send time plus the interval works for any counter value.

payload.answer: The broker disconnects a client after 1.5 times the keep-alive without any packet. Network delay, a busy main loop or a retransmission can delay the ping, so sending it after about half the interval leaves margin. Any other packet sent also resets the timer, so only idle connections need a ping.

metadata.concept: Build a QoS 0 PUBLISH whose remaining length counts the 2-byte topic length field

payload.concept: Build a QoS 0 PUBLISH whose remaining length counts the 2-byte topic length field
payload.explanation: In a QoS 0 PUBLISH the remaining length covers everything after the fixed header: the 2-byte topic length, the topic and the payload. Topic "t/a" with payload "hi" gives 2 + 3 + 2 = 7 and the packet 30 07 00 03 74 2F 61 68 69. Leaving out the 2 makes the length too small, so the broker cuts the payload short and parses its tail as a new packet.
payload.misconception: The remaining length is the topic length plus the payload length.

payload.concept: Match a subscription filter with the + and # wildcards against a topic name
payload.example_bad: int topicBad(const char *f, const char *t) { return strcmp(f, t) == 0; }
payload.explanation: A filter is compared level by level, with levels separated by a slash. + matches exactly one level, including an empty one, and # at the end matches the remaining levels; "a/#" also matches "a" itself. So "a/+/c" matches "a/b/c" but "a/+" does not match "a/b/c". An equality test never receives messages published to a more specific topic than the filter.
payload.misconception: A subscription matches a topic when the two strings are equal.

metadata.concept: Encode the MQTT remaining length as a variable-length integer of 7 bits per byte

payload.concept: Encode the MQTT remaining length as a variable-length integer of 7 bits per byte
payload.example_bad: int mqEncBad(uint32_t v, uint8_t *o) { o[0] = (uint8_t)v; return 1; }
payload.explanation: MQTT stores the remaining length in 1 to 4 bytes. Each byte carries 7 bits of the value, least significant group first, and bit 7 means that another byte follows. 127 is 7F, 128 is 80 01 and 321 is C1 02; the largest value, 268435455, takes four bytes. Writing one raw byte truncates any packet of 128 bytes or more, and the broker then reads the following bytes as the next packet.
payload.misconception: The remaining length is a single byte holding the low 8 bits of the size.

metadata.concept: Store a priority in the upper bits of the NVIC byte: priority << (8 - implemented bits)

payload.concept: Store a priority in the upper bits of the NVIC byte: priority << (8 - implemented bits)
payload.explanation: Each interrupt has an 8-bit priority field, but a chip implements only the upper bits (4 on most STM32F4, so values 0 to 15). The value must be shifted left by 8 - 4 = 4. Writing 5 directly stores 0x05, which the hardware reads as priority 0, the highest. A lower number means a higher priority, and an interrupt can preempt only a handler with a numerically larger priority.
payload.misconception: NVIC_IP[n] = priority stores the priority.

payload.concept: Read the enable state of an interrupt from ISER[n / 32] bit n % 32
payload.explanation: The NVIC spreads its enable bits over several 32-bit words: interrupt n lives in ISER[n >> 5] at bit n & 31. USART2 is interrupt 38, so it is bit 6 of ISER[1]. payload.concept: Pull the data/command line low for commands and back high for data around each SPI transfer
payload.explanation: In 4-wire SPI the SSD1306 uses a separate D/C pin to tell commands from display data. A driver that leaves D/C low after a command sends the frame data as commands, and the display shows garbage or reconfigures itself.

payload.explanation: A full frame is 1024 bytes, which takes about a millisecond at 10 MHz, but it is wasted time when only a small area changes. payload.concept: Address a pixel in the page-organised SSD1306 frame buffer
payload.explanation: An SSD1306 128 x 64 display is organised in 8 pages of 8 rows. Each byte is a vertical strip of 8 pixels: the byte index is x + (y / 8) x 128 and the bit is y % 8. A row-major packing, with eight horizontal pixels per byte, puts the bits in the wrong places on the screen. Check the bounds before writing so a stray coordinate cannot overwrite memory.

Prompt: Why does an SSD1306 frame buffer pack eight vertical pixels into each byte?

payload.answer: The controller writes display RAM in pages: each byte covers eight vertically adjacent rows in one column, and the display scans the pages in order. Organising the buffer the same way lets the whole buffer be sent to the controller as a stream without rearranging the bits, and a byte address of x plus 128 times the page number selects the strip.

payload.concept: Parse the frame AA, length, payload, checksum one byte at a time with a state machine and a length limit
payload.explanation: A byte-at-a-time parser keeps its position in a state variable: wait for the sync byte 0xAA, read the length, read that many payload bytes while summing them, then compare the next byte with the sum. The length comes from an untrusted source, so reject zero and anything above the buffer size before storing a byte; without that check a corrupt length writes past the end of the buffer. After the checksum byte the parser always goes back to the sync state.
payload.misconception: The length byte from the wire can be trusted to fit the buffer.

payload.concept: Hand bytes from an interrupt to the parser through a single-producer single-consumer ring buffer
payload.explanation: The interrupt writes at head and the main loop reads at tail. If both positions can be equal when the buffer is empty and when it is full, the two cases are indistinguishable. Give up one slot: the buffer is empty when head == tail and full when advancing head would reach tail. With a power-of-two size the wrap is a mask. Only the interrupt changes head and only the main loop changes tail, so no lock is needed for one producer and one consumer on a single core.
payload.misconception: A ring buffer is full when head equals tail.

Prompt: Why does a ring buffer with head and tail indices keep one slot unused?

payload.answer: If head == tail meant both empty and full, a completely filled buffer would look empty and all its data would be lost. Keeping one slot unused makes the full state (head one behind tail) different from the empty state (head equal to tail), at the cost of one byte of capacity. The alternative is a separate count, which then needs protection from concurrent updates.

metadata.concept: Keep parsing after a bad frame so one corrupt packet does not stop the stream

payload.concept: Keep parsing after a bad frame so one corrupt packet does not stop the stream
payload.explanation: On a noisy line a corrupt frame is normal. The parser returns to the sync state after every frame, good or bad, and the caller simply continues with the next byte. Stopping at the first failure turns one flipped bit into a dead link. Count the good and the bad frames separately so the error rate can be reported.
payload.misconception: On a checksum failure the receiver should stop and report an error.

payload.concept: Drop a half-received frame after a silent gap using wrap-safe time subtraction
payload.explanation: If a byte is lost the parser would wait for the rest of the frame forever, swallowing the start of the next one. Record the time of the last byte and reset the parser when the gap exceeds a limit. Subtract unsigned times (now - last) and compare the difference; the sum last + limit wraps around near the end of the 32-bit millisecond counter and then reports a timeout that has not happened.

Prompt: Why is the compare value computed from ARR + 1 and not from ARR when you want 100 percent duty?

payload.answer: The counter takes ARR + 1 different values (0 to ARR) per period and the output is high while the counter is below CCR. CCR = ARR leaves the counter value ARR where the output is low, so the output drops for one tick every period. CCR = ARR + 1 is above every counter value, so the output stays high for the whole period.
payload.prompt: Why is the compare value computed from ARR + 1 and not from ARR when you want 100 percent duty?

metadata.concept: Compute the auto-reload value as timer clock / ((PSC + 1) * frequency) - 1

payload.concept: Compute the auto-reload value as timer clock / ((PSC + 1) * frequency) - 1
payload.explanation: The counter runs at clock / (PSC + 1) and counts 0 to ARR, which is ARR + 1 steps per period. So frequency = clock / ((PSC + 1) * (ARR + 1)) and ARR = clock / ((PSC + 1) * frequency) - 1. Both registers hold the value minus one: PSC = 0 divides by one and ARR = 0 gives one step. Forgetting the minus one makes every period one tick too long.
payload.misconception: The period register ARR equals timer clock divided by (prescaler times frequency).

payload.explanation: General-purpose timers such as TIM3 have a 16-bit auto-reload register, so ARR + 1 can be at most 65536 (TIM2 is 32 bits wide on many parts, check yours). Divide the clock by the frequency to get the total ticks per period and choose the smallest prescaler that brings that under 65536. A small prescaler gives the most steps and so the finest duty resolution. A value that is silently truncated to 16 bits produces a wrong frequency.
payload.misconception: PSC can stay 0 and ARR can be any 32-bit number.

A timer generates PWM by counting from 0 to ARR and comparing the counter with CCR: the output is high while the counter is below CCR. The frequency is set by the clock, PSC and ARR, and the duty by CCR. Almost all of the work is integer arithmetic with an off-by-one in every formula, plus a few register bits to connect the channel.

metadata.concept: Convert a permille command to a compare value with rounding and clamp it to 100 percent

payload.concept: Convert a permille command to a compare value with rounding and clamp it to 100 percent
payload.explanation: Truncation always rounds down, so a small non-zero command can become 0 and the output never turns on. Add half the divisor before dividing to round to the nearest step. Commands come from control loops and can overshoot, so clamp the input before scaling: a compare value beyond ARR + 1 is harmless in hardware but hides the saturation from the rest of the program.
payload.misconception: Truncating the division is fine and values above 1000 permille cannot happen.

payload.concept: Add hysteresis to a software low-voltage alarm so it does not chatter at the threshold
payload.explanation: The measured supply voltage has noise, so with one threshold the alarm toggles every time the reading wobbles around it. Use two thresholds: enter the low state below the low threshold and leave it only above a higher threshold. In between, keep the previous state.
payload.misconception: A single threshold is enough to decide whether the supply is low.

payload.document:
Embedded C · STM32_HAL · reset and brown-out · exercise · explain-why · Intermediate
Prompt: Why does a voltage alarm use two thresholds?

payload.answer: A measured voltage contains noise, so a reading near a single threshold crosses it back and forth. The alarm would switch on and off repeatedly and could trigger repeated shutdown and restart actions. With a lower threshold to enter the alarm state and a higher one to leave it, the noise has to cover the gap between them to cause a change.

metadata.concept: Pick the newer of two stored records so a power loss during a write cannot destroy the settings

payload.concept: Pick the newer of two stored records so a power loss during a write cannot destroy the settings
payload.explanation: A power failure in the middle of a write can leave a record half-written. Keep two copies, write the older one, and mark each with a sequence number and a check value. At start-up take the valid record with the newer sequence. Compare sequence numbers by subtracting them as unsigned values so the choice stays right after the counter wraps.
payload.misconception: Writing settings to one place in flash is enough.

metadata.concept: Keep a boot counter across soft resets with a magic number that validates the retained data

payload.concept: Keep a boot counter across soft resets with a magic number that validates the retained data
payload.example_bad:
typedef struct { uint32_t magic, count; } Ret;
uint32_t bootBad(Ret *r) { return ++r->count; }
payload.explanation: RAM in a no-init section is not cleared by the start-up code, so it survives a soft reset, but after a power-on it holds random bits. Store a magic number next to the data: if the magic is wrong the contents are garbage and must be initialised; if it is right the data is from the previous run.
payload.misconception: A variable placed in a no-init section always holds the value it had before the reset.

payload.concept: Calculate the supply voltage from an ADC reading of the internal reference
payload.explanation: The internal reference VREFINT is fixed (about 1.2 V), so when the supply drops the ADC code for it rises. The factory stores the code measured at 3.3 V. The supply is therefore 3300 x cal / reading in millivolts. Using reading / cal inverts the ratio and reports the supply rising when it falls.

Context: platform: STM32_HAL
Embedded C · STM32_HAL · Reset and brown-out · Overview
A microcontroller restarts for many reasons: power-on, a supply dip, the reset pin, a watchdog, a software request. The reset flags tell the program why it started, and brown-out detection holds the part in reset while the supply is too low for reliable operation. metadata.concept: Create a queue whose item size is the size of the message struct, not of a pointer

payload.concept: Create a queue whose item size is the size of the message struct, not of a pointer
payload.example_bad:
typedef struct { uint32_t id; uint16_t val; } Msg;
QueueHandle_t newBad(int len) { return xQueueCreate(len, sizeof(uint32_t)); }
payload.example_good:
typedef struct { uint32_t id; uint16_t val; } Msg;
QueueHandle_t newQueue(int len) { return xQueueCreate(len, sizeof(Msg)); }
payload.explanation: A FreeRTOS queue copies items by value and every item has the size fixed at creation. If the queue is created with the size of a 32-bit pointer (4 bytes) but the senders pass a struct, only the first bytes of each struct are copied and the receiver gets a truncated message. Use sizeof of the message type and check the returned handle for NULL.
payload.misconception: A queue stores whatever size of item the sender passes.

int32_t valBad(const Ev *e) { return e->u.i; }

payload.document:
Embedded C · ESP_IDF · rtos queues · exercise · explain-why · Intermediate
Prompt: Why should a producer check the result of xQueueSend even when the queue is large?

payload.answer: A queue is a finite buffer. If the consumer is blocked or slow for long enough, the queue fills and further sends with a zero timeout fail, losing messages. Checking the result lets the producer count drops, retry or report the overload; ignoring it hides data loss that only appears under load.

metadata.concept: Size a queue for a burst from the producer and consumer rates

payload.concept: Size a queue for a burst from the producer and consumer rates
payload.explanation: During a burst of B messages arriving at rate in while the consumer removes messages at rate out, the queue fills at the difference of the rates. The required length is B minus the number the consumer takes during the burst, B x out / in, rounded up. A consumer as fast as the producer needs a length of one. Using B directly wastes RAM and hides a slow consumer.
payload.misconception: A queue only needs to be as long as the burst.

payload.concept: Use a counting semaphore when several events can arrive before the task runs
payload.explanation: A binary semaphore holds at most one token. If an interrupt gives it three times before the task runs, the task takes it once and two events are lost. A counting semaphore keeps the count, so the task takes it three times. Use a binary semaphore for a flag-like signal and a counting semaphore when each event must be handled.
payload.misconception: A binary semaphore remembers every event given to it.

metadata.concept: Raise the owner priority to that of a waiting task so a medium-priority task cannot starve the owner

payload.concept: Raise the owner priority to that of a waiting task so a medium-priority task cannot starve the owner
payload.explanation: If a low-priority task holds a mutex that a high-priority task needs, a medium-priority task can preempt the owner and keep it from releasing the mutex, which delays the high-priority task for as long as the medium task runs: priority inversion. FreeRTOS mutexes use priority inheritance: the owner runs at the priority of the highest waiter until it gives the mutex back.
payload.misconception: A low-priority task holding a mutex cannot delay a high-priority task that waits for it.

payload.document:

Prompt: What is priority inversion and how does priority inheritance stop it?

payload.answer: Priority inversion is when a high-priority task is delayed by a lower-priority one. It happens when a low-priority task holds a mutex that the high-priority task needs and a medium-priority task preempts the owner, so the owner cannot release the mutex. With priority inheritance the owner temporarily takes the priority of the highest waiting task, so the medium task cannot preempt it and the mutex is released quickly.

metadata.concept: Release a mutex on every return path of the function that took it

payload.concept: Release a mutex on every return path of the function that took it
payload.explanation: A mutex taken at the start of a function stays locked until some task gives it back. An early return on an error path that skips the give leaves the mutex locked for good, and the next task that takes it blocks forever. Take the mutex, do the work in one block, give once at a single exit point.
payload.misconception: A function can return as soon as it hits an error while holding the mutex.

payload.explanation: If one task takes A and then B while another takes B and then A, each can hold one and wait forever for the other: a deadlock. Release in the opposite order.

payload.document:
Embedded C · ESP_IDF · rtos tasks · exercise · explain-why · Intermediate
Prompt: Why does vTaskDelayUntil keep a fixed period when vTaskDelay does not?

payload.answer: vTaskDelay measures the time from the moment it is called, so the time spent working is added to the delay and each cycle is longer than the period. vTaskDelayUntil takes the previous wake-up time and computes the next wake-up time from it, which is independent of how long the work took, so the cycles stay on a fixed grid as long as the work finishes within the period.
payload.prompt: Why does vTaskDelayUntil keep a fixed period when vTaskDelay does not?

metadata.concept: Pick the highest-priority ready task and share the time between equal priorities

payload.concept: Pick the highest-priority ready task and share the time between equal priorities
payload.explanation: FreeRTOS runs the ready task with the highest priority. Tasks of equal priority are time-sliced in turn, so one of them cannot starve the others. A pick function that always takes the first of the equal-priority tasks starves the rest. Continue the search after the task that ran last.
payload.misconception: Among ready tasks the scheduler always runs the first one with the highest priority.

metadata.concept: Compute the stack actually used from the high-water mark, which reports the smallest free space

payload.concept: Compute the stack actually used from the high-water mark, which reports the smallest free space
payload.explanation: The high-water mark is the minimum amount of stack that has ever been free, not the amount used. Used stack is the total minus the high-water mark. A task with 2048 bytes total and a high-water mark of 300 has used 1748 bytes and is close to overflow; reading 300 as the usage would suggest a large margin.
payload.misconception: uxTaskGetStackHighWaterMark returns how much stack the task has used.

Embedded C · ESP_IDF · RTOS tasks · Overview
An RTOS runs several tasks, each with its own stack and priority, and switches between them. The scheduler always runs the highest-priority ready task and time-slices tasks of equal priority. A task gives up the CPU by blocking: delaying, waiting on a queue or a semaphore. Time is counted in ticks, and the stack of each task is a fixed allocation.

metadata.concept: Allocate from a bump arena and round each offset up to the requested alignment

payload.concept: Allocate from a bump arena and round each offset up to the requested alignment
payload.explanation: A bump arena moves an offset forward on every allocation and is released all at once by resetting the offset. The next free byte may not be suitably aligned: a uint32_t needs an address that is a multiple of 4, and a misaligned access faults on Cortex-M0. Round the offset up with (off + align - 1) & ~(align - 1) before handing out the block, and fail when the arena is exhausted.
payload.misconception: A bump arena can hand out the next free byte.

payload.document:
Embedded C · STM32_HAL · static allocation · exercise · explain-why · Intermediate
Prompt: Why does an embedded design often prefer static allocation and pools to malloc?

payload.answer: Heap allocation can fail at run time, takes a variable amount of time and fragments memory over weeks of operation, which are all unwelcome in a device that must run for years in small RAM. Static allocation and fixed pools fix the memory use at link time, make failures visible at build time, give constant allocation time and leave no fragmentation.

metadata.concept: Free resources on every exit path of a function by jumping to one cleanup label

payload.concept: Free resources on every exit path of a function by jumping to one cleanup label
payload.explanation: Each early return that follows an allocation must release it, or the memory leaks a little on every failure. A single cleanup label at the end of the function, reached with goto on every error, keeps the release in one place. Counting live allocations in a debug build shows a leak as a number that does not return to zero.
payload.misconception: A function that allocates a buffer is finished when it returns an error code.

metadata.concept: Measure stack high-water mark by painting the stack with a pattern and scanning from the far end

payload.concept: Measure stack high-water mark by painting the stack with a pattern and scanning from the far end
payload.explanation: On Cortex-M, AVR and Xtensa the stack grows toward lower addresses. Fill the whole stack region with a known pattern such as 0xA5 at start-up. Later, scan from the low address upward until the first byte that is not the pattern: everything below that was never touched. The used depth is the region size minus the untouched bytes. Scanning from the wrong end reports the used part as unused.
payload.misconception: The stack grows from the low end of its region, so scan from the high end.

metadata.concept: Build a fixed-size block pool with a free list so allocation never fragments

payload.concept: Build a fixed-size block pool with a free list so allocation never fragments
payload.explanation: A pool hands out equal-sized blocks from a static array. A free list threaded through the free blocks makes allocation and release constant-time and free of fragmentation. Releasing a block that is already free would put it on the list twice and then give the same block to two owners, so the release function should reject a block that is not in use. Keep one flag per block, or search the list, and return an error on a double free.
payload.misconception: Freeing a block twice is harmless.

metadata.concept: Test for a power-of-two buffer size so index wrap can use a mask

payload.concept: Test for a power-of-two buffer size so index wrap can use a mask
payload.explanation: A power of two has exactly one bit set, and x & (x - 1) clears the lowest set bit, so the result is zero only for powers of two. Zero also gives zero, so the test must reject zero explicitly. A static size check like _Static_assert((N & (N - 1)) == 0, ...) stops a wrong buffer size at compile time.
payload.misconception: The test x & (x - 1) == 0 detects powers of two for every x.

metadata.concept: Test whether a task is due with unsigned subtraction so the 32-bit tick counter can wrap

payload.concept: Test whether a task is due with unsigned subtraction so the 32-bit tick counter can wrap
payload.explanation: A free-running 32-bit millisecond counter wraps after about 49.7 days. The test now >= last + period fails near the wrap: the sum wraps to a small number and the task looks due immediately, or the counter wraps and the comparison never succeeds. The difference (uint32_t)(now - last) is correct across the wrap as long as the period is shorter than half the counter range.
payload.misconception: A task is due when the tick counter has reached last plus the period.
