Ruby · Hash · creation · L2
Concept: Hash.new([]) shares one default array and never stores the key; use the block form
Misconception: Hash.new([]) gives every missing key its own empty array.
Explanation: The default value is a single object returned for every missing key. h[:a] << 1 mutates that shared default and stores nothing, so h.keys stays empty and h[:b] also sees the 1. The block form Hash.new { |hash, key| hash[key] = [] } creates and stores a fresh array on first access.
Incorrect:
def group_bad(pairs)
  h = Hash.new([])
  pairs.each { |k, v| h[k] << v }
  h
end
Correct:
def group(pairs)
  h = Hash.new { |hash, key| hash[key] = [] }
  pairs.each { |k, v| h[k] << v }
  h
end
Complexity: O(n)

Ruby · Hash · iteration · L3
Concept: Adding a key while iterating a hash raises; iterate over a snapshot or build a new hash
Misconception: You can add keys to a hash inside its own each loop.
Explanation: A hash cannot grow during iteration: the insertion raises RuntimeError (can't add a new key into hash during iteration). Updating the value of an existing key is allowed. Iterate over h.to_a or h.keys, or build the result with transform_values, each_with_object or merge.
Incorrect:
def double_keys_bad(h)
  h.each { |k, v| h[k.to_s * 2] = v }
  h
end
Correct:
def double_keys(h)
  out = h.dup
  h.each { |k, v| out[k.to_s * 2] = v }
  out
end
Complexity: O(n)

Ruby · Hash · transformation · L3
Concept: merge keeps the second hash's value on conflicts; pass a block to combine them
Misconception: a.merge(b) adds up values for keys present in both hashes.
Explanation: Without a block, merge lets the argument win and the first value is lost. With a block { |key, old, new| ... } you decide how conflicts combine, for example by summing counters. merge returns a new hash; merge! updates the receiver. Cost is O(size of the argument).
Incorrect:
def combine_bad(a, b)
  a.merge(b)
end
Correct:
def combine(a, b)
  a.merge(b) { |_key, x, y| x + y }
end
Complexity: O(m)

Ruby · Hash · mutation · L3
Concept: Mutating an array used as a key breaks lookup until rehash; freeze or copy the key
Misconception: A key can be changed after it is stored and still be found.
Explanation: A hash stores each key under its hash code at insertion time. If the key object is mutated afterwards, its code changes and h[key] no longer finds the entry, although the entry is still there. Strings are copied and frozen when used as keys, arrays are not. Use frozen keys (key.dup.freeze) or call rehash after a deliberate change.
Incorrect:
def lookup_bad
  key = [1]
  h = { key => :found }
  key << 2
  h[key]
end
Correct:
def lookup
  key = [1].freeze
  h = { key => :found }
  h[[1]]
end
Complexity: O(1)

Ruby · Hash · ordering · L3
Concept: A hash keeps insertion order; reassigning a key keeps its place, delete then insert moves it to the end
Misconception: h[key] = value moves the key to the end of the hash.
Explanation: Since Ruby 1.9 a Hash iterates in insertion order. Assigning to an existing key only changes its value and leaves its position. To mark a key as most recently used, delete it and insert it again. That gives an LRU cache from one Hash: evict h.first (the oldest) when the capacity is exceeded. All operations are O(1) on average.
Incorrect:
def touch_bad(h, key)
  h[key] = h[key]
  h
end
Correct:
def touch(h, key)
  value = h.delete(key)
  h[key] = value
  h
end
def evict_oldest(h)
  h.delete(h.first[0])
end
Complexity: O(1)

Ruby · heaps · creation · L2
Concept: Build a heap in O(n) by sifting down from the last parent to the root
Misconception: Sifting down from index 0 upward to the last parent builds the heap.
Explanation: Sift-down assumes both child subtrees are already heaps, so the work must start at the bottom: from index n / 2 - 1 down to 0. Going from the root downwards fixes the root before its subtrees are ordered and leaves violations behind. Most nodes are near the leaves and move little, so the total is O(n), better than n pushes at O(n log n).
Incorrect:
def build_bad(items)
  a = items.dup
  n = a.size
  (0...(n / 2)).each do |start|
    i = start
    while 2 * i + 1 < n
      l = 2 * i + 1
      r = l + 1
      s = i
      s = l if a[l] < a[s]
      s = r if r < n && a[r] < a[s]
      break if s == i
      a[s], a[i] = a[i], a[s]
      i = s
    end
  end
  a
end
Correct:
class MinHeap
  def build(items)
    @a = items.dup
    (@a.size / 2 - 1).downto(0) { |i| sift_down(i) }
    self
  end
end
Complexity: O(n)

Prompt: Why is building a heap bottom-up with sift-down O(n) although each sift-down can cost O(log n)?

payload.answer: Sift-down from a node costs at most the height of its subtree. Half of the nodes are leaves and need no work, a quarter have height 1, an eighth have height 2, and so on. The total work is the sum of height times the number of nodes at that height, which converges to a constant times n. Only the few nodes near the root pay the full logarithmic cost.

Ruby · heaps · patterns · L3
Concept: The kth largest element comes from a min-heap capped at k items, trimmed after each push
Misconception: Trim the heap before adding the new value to keep it at k items.
Explanation: Trimming before the push evicts the smallest stored value even when the new value is smaller still, so a small newcomer displaces a larger value that belongs in the top k. Push first, then pop while the size exceeds k; the root is then the smallest of the k largest values, which is the kth largest. Time O(n log k) and O(k) space, better than sorting when k is small.
Incorrect:
def kth_largest_bad(nums, k)
  h = MinHeap.new
  nums.each do |x|
    h.pop if h.size >= k
    h.push(x)
  end
  h.peek
end
Correct:
def kth_largest(nums, k)
  h = MinHeap.new
  nums.each do |x|
    h.push(x)
    h.pop if h.size > k
  end
  h.peek
end
Complexity: O(n log k)

Ruby · heaps · ordering · L2
Concept: A max-heap can reuse a min-heap by negating keys, and must negate again on the way out
Misconception: Pushing negated values is enough; pop and peek already return the right numbers.
Explanation: The negation trick turns the smallest negated value into the largest original one, but the heap stores and returns negated numbers. Negate on push and negate again on pop and peek. It works for numeric keys only; for other types pass a comparator or store an ordering key. Operations stay O(log n).
Incorrect:
class MaxHeapBad
  def initialize
    @h = MinHeap.new
  end
  def push(v)
    @h.push(-v)
    self
  end
  def pop
    @h.pop
  end
end
Correct:
class MaxHeap
  def initialize
    @h = MinHeap.new
  end
  def push(v)
    @h.push(-v)
    self
  end
  def pop
    v = @h.pop
    v && -v
  end
  def peek
    v = @h.peek
    v && -v
  end
  def size
    @h.size
  end
end
Complexity: O(log n)

Ruby · heaps · insertion-and-deletion · L2
Concept: Sift-down swaps with the smaller of the two children, not always the left one
Misconception: After moving the last element to the root, swapping it with the left child when it is larger is enough.
Explanation: If the right child is smaller than the left one, swapping with the left child leaves the right child smaller than its new parent, which breaks the heap order. Compare with both children and swap with the smallest. Children of i are 2i + 1 and 2i + 2, and each must be checked against the array size. pop is O(log n).
Incorrect:
def sift_down_bad(a, i)
  n = a.size
  while 2 * i + 1 < n
    l = 2 * i + 1
    break if a[l] >= a[i]
    a[l], a[i] = a[i], a[l]
    i = l
  end
  a
end
Correct:
def sift_down_ok(a, i)
  n = a.size
  loop do
    l = 2 * i + 1
    r = l + 1
    small = i
    small = l if l < n && a[l] < a[small]
    small = r if r < n && a[r] < a[small]
    break if small == i
    a[small], a[i] = a[i], a[small]
    i = small
  end
  a
end
Complexity: O(log n)

Ruby · heaps · insertion-and-deletion · L1
Concept: Sift-up must stop at index 0, because in Ruby (0 - 1) / 2 is -1 and -1 indexes the last element
Misconception: The loop can end naturally when the parent is not larger than the value.
Explanation: A binary heap stores node i's parent at (i - 1) / 2. Ruby integer division rounds toward negative infinity, so for i = 0 the parent index is -1, and @a[-1] is the last element of the array, not an error. Without an i > 0 guard the root is compared with the last element and the two can be swapped, corrupting the heap. push is O(log n).
Incorrect:
def sift_up_bad(a, i)
  parent = (i - 1) / 2
  while a[parent] > a[i]
    a[parent], a[i] = a[i], a[parent]
    i = parent
    parent = (i - 1) / 2
  end
  a
end
Correct:
class MinHeap
  attr_reader :size
  def initialize
    @a = []
  end
  def size
    @a.size
  end
  def empty?
    @a.empty?
  end
  def peek
    @a.first
  end
  def push(v)
    @a.push(v)
    sift_up(@a.size - 1)
    self
  end
  def pop
    return nil if @a.empty?
    top = @a[0]
    last = @a.pop
    unless @a.empty?
      @a[0] = last
      sift_down(0)
    end
    top
  end
  private
  def sift_up(i)
    while i > 0
      parent = (i - 1) / 2
      break if @a[parent] <= @a[i]
      @a[parent], @a[i] = @a[i], @a[parent]
      i = parent
    end
  end
  def sift_down(i)
    n = @a.size
    loop do
      l = 2 * i + 1
      r = l + 1
      small = i
      small = l if l < n && @a[l] < @a[small]
      small = r if r < n && @a[r] < @a[small]
      break if small == i
      @a[small], @a[i] = @a[i], @a[small]
      i = small
    end
  end
end
Complexity: O(log n)

Ruby · Matrix and Vector (require "matrix") · patterns · L4
Concept: Raise [[1, 1], [1, 0]] to the n-th power to get Fibonacci numbers in O(log n) multiplications
Misconception: Any 2x2 matrix of ones gives Fibonacci numbers.
Explanation: The matrix [[1, 1], [1, 0]] raised to n has F(n) in its top-right cell. Matrix#** uses repeated squaring, so it takes O(log n) 2x2 multiplications. A matrix of all ones, [[1, 1], [1, 1]], grows as powers of 2 instead, because its rows are identical.
Incorrect:
require "matrix"
def fib_bad(n)
  (Matrix[[1, 1], [1, 1]] ** n)[0, 1]
end
Correct:
require "matrix"
def fib(n)
  (Matrix[[1, 1], [1, 0]] ** n)[0, 1]
end
Complexity: O(log n)

Ruby · Matrix and Vector (require "matrix") · exercise · explain-why · L4
Prompt: Why does raising [[1, 1], [1, 0]] to the n-th power compute Fibonacci numbers in O(log n) steps?

payload.answer: Multiplying the vector (F(k+1), F(k)) by the matrix gives (F(k+2), F(k+1)), so the n-th power of the matrix applies the Fibonacci recurrence n times at once and its top-right cell is F(n). Matrix exponentiation uses repeated squaring, which needs only about log2(n) matrix multiplications of a fixed 2x2 size, instead of n additions.

Ruby · Matrix and Vector (require "matrix") · edge-cases · L3
Concept: inverse of an integer matrix has Rational entries and a singular matrix raises ErrNotRegular
Misconception: The inverse of an integer matrix is made of floats, and every square matrix has one.
Explanation: Matrix#inverse uses exact arithmetic: integer input gives Rational entries such as (3/2). A matrix with determinant 0 has no inverse and raises ExceptionForMatrix::ErrNotRegular. Test determinant.zero? first, or use rescue. Determinant and inverse are O(n^3).
Incorrect:
require "matrix"
def invert_bad(m)
  m.inverse
end
Correct:
require "matrix"
def invert(m)
  return nil if m.determinant.zero?
  m.inverse
end
Complexity: O(n^3)

Ruby · Matrix and Vector (require "matrix") · transformation · L2
Concept: * is the matrix product; use hadamard_product for element-wise multiplication
Misconception: Multiplying two matrices with * multiplies matching elements.
Explanation: * computes the row-by-column matrix product, so [[1, 2], [3, 4]] squared is [[7, 10], [15, 22]]. Element-wise multiplication is hadamard_product (also called entrywise_product). The product of an r x k and a k x c matrix takes O(r * k * c) operations.
Incorrect:
require "matrix"
def square_bad(m)
  Matrix.build(m.row_count, m.column_count) { |r, c| m[r, c] * m[r, c] }
end
Correct:
require "matrix"
def square(m)
  m * m
end
def entrywise(m)
  m.hadamard_product(m)
end
Complexity: O(n^3)

Concept: Matrix rows must have equal length; a ragged literal raises ErrDimensionMismatch
Misconception: Matrix[[1, 2], [3]] pads the short row with zeros.
Explanation: Every row of a Matrix must have the same number of columns. A ragged row list raises ExceptionForMatrix::ErrDimensionMismatch. Build matrices with Matrix[[...]], Matrix.build(rows, cols) { |r, c| ... }, Matrix.identity(n) or Matrix.zero(r, c). Matrix needs require "matrix" (a bundled gem since Ruby 3.1).
Incorrect:
require "matrix"
def ragged_bad
  Matrix[[1, 2], [3]]
end
Correct:
require "matrix"
def built
  Matrix.build(2, 2) { |r, c| r * 2 + c + 1 }
end
Complexity: O(r * c)

Ruby · Matrix and Vector (require "matrix") · edge-cases · L2
Concept: Multiplying needs left columns equal to right rows; otherwise ErrDimensionMismatch is raised
Misconception: Any two matrices can be multiplied.
Explanation: The product A * B requires A.column_count == B.row_count. A 1 x 2 matrix times a 1 x 2 matrix raises ExceptionForMatrix::ErrDimensionMismatch. Check the shapes before multiplying, or transpose one operand: A * B.transpose is 1 x 1 here.
Incorrect:
require "matrix"
def product_bad(a, b)
  a * b
end
Correct:
require "matrix"
def product(a, b)
  return nil unless a.column_count == b.row_count
  a * b
end
Complexity: O(1)

Concept: Use inner_product for the dot product; Vector * Vector is not defined
Misconception: v * w computes the dot product of two vectors.
Explanation: Vector * Vector raises ExceptionForMatrix::ErrOperationNotDefined; * with a number scales the vector and * with a Matrix multiplies. The dot product is v.inner_product(w) (also dot), the length is v.norm (also magnitude). Both are O(n).

require "matrix"
def dot_bad(v, w)
  v * w
end
Correct:
require "matrix"
def dot(v, w)
  v.inner_product(w)
end

Ruby · priority queues · ordering · L2
Concept: A priority queue comparator must return an Integer like <=>, not true or false
Misconception: The ordering block can return a boolean such as a > b.
Explanation: The heap needs to know less than, equal and greater than, which is what <=> returns as -1, 0 or 1. A block returning true or false cannot be tested with < 0 and raises NoMethodError, or silently misorders if it is used as a truthy value. For a max-first queue swap the operands: { |a, b| b <=> a }. Without a block the queue is a min-queue on <=>. push and pop are O(log n).
Incorrect:
def less_bad?(cmp, x, y)
  cmp.call(x, y) < 0
end
Correct:
class PQ
  def initialize(&cmp)
    @cmp = cmp || proc { |a, b| a <=> b }
    @a = []
  end
  def size
    @a.size
  end
  def empty?
    @a.empty?
  end
  def peek
    @a.first
  end
  def push(v)
    @a.push(v)
    sift_up(@a.size - 1)
    self
  end
  def pop
    return nil if @a.empty?
    top = @a[0]
    last = @a.pop
    unless @a.empty?
      @a[0] = last
      sift_down(0)
    end
    top
  end
  private
  def before?(i, j)
    @cmp.call(@a[i], @a[j]) < 0
  end
  def sift_up(i)
    while i > 0
      parent = (i - 1) / 2
      break unless before?(i, parent)
      @a[i], @a[parent] = @a[parent], @a[i]
      i = parent
    end
  end
  def sift_down(i)
    n = @a.size
    loop do
      l = 2 * i + 1
      r = l + 1
      first = i
      first = l if l < n && before?(l, first)
      first = r if r < n && before?(r, first)
      break if first == i
      @a[first], @a[i] = @a[i], @a[first]
      i = first
    end
  end
end
Complexity: O(log n)

Ruby · priority queues · patterns · L3
Concept: Dijkstra finalises a node when it is popped, so skip stale entries instead of marking on push
Misconception: Mark a node as done when it is first pushed, as in breadth-first search.
Explanation: With weights the first path found to a node is not necessarily the shortest. Marking on push freezes the first, possibly longer, distance. Push every improvement, and when popping skip entries whose distance is larger than the best known. The queue has no decrease-key, so duplicates are allowed. O((V + E) log V).
Incorrect:
def dijkstra_bad(graph, src)
  dist = { src => 0 }
  seen = { src => true }
  q = PQ.new { |a, b| a[0] <=> b[0] }
  q.push([0, src])
  until q.empty?
    d, u = q.pop
    graph[u].each do |v, w|
      next if seen[v]
      seen[v] = true
      dist[v] = d + w
      q.push([d + w, v])
    end
  end
  dist
end
Correct:
def dijkstra(graph, src)
  dist = Hash.new(Float::INFINITY)
  dist[src] = 0
  q = PQ.new { |a, b| a[0] <=> b[0] }
  q.push([0, src])
  until q.empty?
    d, u = q.pop
    next if d > dist[u]
    graph[u].each do |v, w|
      nd = d + w
      next unless nd < dist[v]
      dist[v] = nd
      q.push([nd, v])
    end
  end
  dist
end
Complexity: O((V+E) log V)

Ruby · priority queues · patterns · L3
Concept: When merging with a heap, tied keys must not fall through to comparing non-comparable objects
Misconception: Pushing [value, node] pairs is enough because the value decides the order.
Explanation: Array#<=> moves to the next element when the first elements are equal. Two different node objects have no ordering, so <=> returns nil and the heap raises when two lists have equal values. Add a unique, comparable tie-breaker such as the list index before the node. Merging k sorted lists of n items in total costs O(n log k).
Incorrect:
BNode = Struct.new(:val, :nxt)
def merge_bad(heads)
  q = PQ.new
  heads.each { |h| q.push([h.val, h]) if h }
  out = []
  until q.empty?
    _, node = q.pop
    out << node.val
    q.push([node.nxt.val, node.nxt]) if node.nxt
  end
  out
end
Correct:
LNode = Struct.new(:val, :nxt)
def build_list(values)
  head = nil
  values.reverse_each { |v| head = LNode.new(v, head) }
  head
end
def merge_lists(heads)
  q = PQ.new
  heads.each_with_index { |h, i| q.push([h.val, i, h]) if h }
  out = []
  until q.empty?
    _, i, node = q.pop
    out << node.val
    q.push([node.nxt.val, i, node.nxt]) if node.nxt
  end
  out
end
Complexity: O(n log k)

payload.answer: Sifting swaps elements between distant positions in the array, so the relative order of items with equal keys is not preserved. Ruby · queues · patterns · L2
Concept: Breadth-first search marks a node as seen when it is enqueued, not when it is dequeued
Misconception: Marking a node visited when it is dequeued avoids repeats.
Explanation: A node reachable by two paths is enqueued twice if it is only marked on dequeue, producing duplicates in the visiting order and wasted work. Mark on enqueue so each node enters the queue once. An Array works as the queue because shift is O(1) amortised in CRuby. BFS is O(V + E).
Incorrect:
def bfs_bad(graph, start)
  order = []
  seen = {}
  queue = [start]
  until queue.empty?
    node = queue.shift
    seen[node] = true
    order << node
    graph[node].each { |n| queue.push(n) unless seen[n] }
  end
  order
end
Correct:
def bfs(graph, start)
  order = []
  seen = { start => true }
  queue = [start]
  until queue.empty?
    node = queue.shift
    order << node
    graph[node].each do |n|
      next if seen[n]
      seen[n] = true
      queue.push(n)
    end
  end
  order
end
Complexity: O(V+E)

Ruby · queues · insertion-and-deletion · L1
Concept: A linked queue must reset its tail when the last node is dequeued
Misconception: dequeue only needs to move the head pointer.
Explanation: When the last node is removed the head becomes nil but the tail still points to the removed node. The next enqueue then links the new node behind the dead node, and the queue looks empty or loses elements. Reset the tail to nil whenever the head becomes nil. enqueue and dequeue are O(1).
Incorrect:
class QueueBad
  def initialize
    @head = @tail = nil
  end
  def enqueue(v)
    node = [v, nil]
    if @tail
      @tail[1] = node
    else
      @head = node
    end
    @tail = node
  end
  def dequeue
    return nil unless @head
    v = @head[0]
    @head = @head[1]
    v
  end
  def to_a
    out = []
    node = @head
    while node
      out << node[0]
      node = node[1]
    end
    out
  end
end
Correct:
class QNode
  attr_accessor :value, :next
  def initialize(value)
    @value = value
  end
end
class LinkedQueue
  include Enumerable
  attr_reader :size
  def initialize
    @head = @tail = nil
    @size = 0
  end
  def enqueue(v)
    node = QNode.new(v)
    if @tail
      @tail.next = node
    else
      @head = node
    end
    @tail = node
    @size += 1
    self
  end
  def dequeue
    return nil unless @head
    v = @head.value
    @head = @head.next
    @tail = nil unless @head
    @size -= 1
    v
  end
  def front
    @head && @head.value
  end
  def empty?
    @size.zero?
  end
  def each
    return to_enum(:each) unless block_given?
    node = @head
    while node
      yield node.value
      node = node.next
    end
  end
end
Complexity: O(1)

payload.document:
Ruby · queues · exercise · explain-why · L3
Prompt: Why is dequeue O(1) amortised in a queue built from two stacks even though one call can move many elements?

payload.answer: Each element is pushed onto the input stack once, moved to the output stack at most once, and popped once. A single dequeue may transfer many elements, but the transfer only happens when the output stack is empty, so across n operations the total number of moves is at most n. The cost spread over all operations is constant per operation.

Ruby · Range · patterns · L4
Concept: Range#bsearch needs a monotone block: false then true; testing == is not monotone
Misconception: bsearch { |x| x * x == n } finds the square root.
Explanation: In find-minimum mode the block must be false for small values and true from some point on. The test x * x == n is false again after the root, so it is not monotone and the search may return nil even though a root exists. Search for the first x with x * x > n and subtract one to get the floor of the square root. Binary search over an integer range is O(log n).
Incorrect:
def isqrt_bad(n)
  (0..n).bsearch { |x| x * x == n }
end
Correct:
def isqrt(n)
  (0..n + 1).bsearch { |x| x * x > n } - 1
end
Complexity: O(log n)

payload.document:
Ruby · Range · exercise · explain-why · L4
Prompt: Why must a Range#bsearch block in find-minimum mode be monotone?

payload.answer: Binary search discards half of the range after each probe, assuming that if the block is true at some x it stays true for every larger x, and false for every smaller one. A block such as x * x == n is true at one point only, so a probe on the wrong side of it throws away the part that contains the answer. A condition like x * x > n is false then true, so each probe is safe.

Ruby · Range · iteration · L2
Concept: An endless range cannot be turned into an array; take from it or use lazy
Misconception: (1..).to_a returns the numbers from 1 upwards.
Explanation: An endless range (1..) has no last element, so to_a raises RangeError (cannot convert endless range to an array). Use first(n), take_while, find, or lazy to consume only what you need. The same range works as a slice end: a[1..] is the array without its first element.
Incorrect:
def first_squares_bad(n)
  (1..).to_a.first(n).map { |x| x * x }
end
Correct:
def first_squares(n)
  (1..).lazy.map { |x| x * x }.first(n)
end
Complexity: O(n)

Concept: A Float range cannot be iterated with each; use step
Misconception: (0.0..1.0).each walks the values with a step of 0.1.
Explanation: Iteration needs a successor, and Float has none, so each on a Float range raises TypeError (can't iterate from Float). Use (0.0..1.0).step(0.25) for evenly spaced values, or iterate over integers and scale. step is O(number of values).
Incorrect:
def samples_bad
  out = []
  (0.0..1.0).each { |x| out << x }
  out
end
Correct:
def samples
  (0.0..1.0).step(0.25).to_a
end
Complexity: O(n)

Ruby · Range · equality · L3
Concept: cover? tests the bounds, include? tests membership; they differ for string ranges
Misconception: include? and cover? give the same answer for every range.
Explanation: For numeric ranges both compare against the bounds. For a string range ("a".."z"), include? checks whether the value is one of the generated elements, while cover? only checks begin <= value <= end by string comparison, so "bb" is covered but not included. cover? is O(1); include? on a string range may iterate.
Incorrect:
def in_letters_bad?(s)
  ("a".."z").cover?(s)
end
Correct:
def in_letters?(s)
  ("a".."z").include?(s)
end
Complexity: O(1)

Ruby · red-black trees · equality · L3
Concept: Verifying a red-black tree requires equal black heights, not only local color rules
Misconception: If the root is black and no red node has a red child, the tree is a valid red-black tree.
Explanation: The third rule says every path from a node to its nil leaves has the same number of black nodes. A tree of black nodes with one side deeper passes the local rules but violates it. Compute the black height recursively, count nil as one, and return nil on any mismatch or red-red pair. In this left-leaning variant a red right child is also invalid. O(n).
Incorrect:
def local_ok?(node, parent_red = false)
  return true unless node
  return false if node.red && parent_red
  return false if node.right && node.right.red
  local_ok?(node.left, node.red) && local_ok?(node.right, node.red)
end
def rb_bad?(root)
  root.nil? || (!root.red && local_ok?(root))
end
Correct:
def black_height(node)
  return 1 unless node
  return nil if node.right && node.right.red
  return nil if node.red && node.left && node.left.red
  l = black_height(node.left)
  r = black_height(node.right)
  return nil unless l && r && l == r
  l + (node.red ? 0 : 1)
end
def rb_valid?(root)
  return true unless root
  !root.red && !black_height(root).nil?
end
Complexity: O(n)

Ruby · red-black trees · mutation · L3
Concept: The three fix-up rules run one after another with separate ifs, not as an elsif chain
Misconception: The three fix-up rules are mutually exclusive, so elsif is equivalent.
Explanation: A single insert can need several fixes on the same node: a right rotation can produce a node with two red children that must then be flipped. With elsif the flip is skipped and two red children stay in the tree. Apply the three rules in order with independent ifs: rotate left if only the right child is red, rotate right if two reds are in a row on the left, flip if both children are red.
Incorrect:
class RBElsif < RBTree
  private
  def insert_at(h, key)
    if h.nil?
      @size += 1
      return RBNode.new(key)
    end
    if key < h.key
      h.left = insert_at(h.left, key)
    elsif key > h.key
      h.right = insert_at(h.right, key)
    end
    if red?(h.right) && !red?(h.left)
      h = rotate_left(h)
    elsif red?(h.left) && red?(h.left.left)
      h = rotate_right(h)
    elsif red?(h.left) && red?(h.right)
      flip_colors(h)
    end
    h
  end
end
Correct:
class RBTree
  private
  def fixup(h)
    h = rotate_left(h) if red?(h.right) && !red?(h.left)
    h = rotate_right(h) if red?(h.left) && red?(h.left.left)
    flip_colors(h) if red?(h.left) && red?(h.right)
    h
  end
end
Complexity: O(1)

Ruby · red-black trees · complexity · L2
Concept: Color rules bound the height by 2 log2(n + 1), so sorted input stays logarithmic
Misconception: Sorted insertions make any binary search tree as deep as the number of keys.
Explanation: Every root-to-leaf path has the same number of black nodes and red nodes never touch, so the longest path is at most twice the shortest and the height is at most about 2 log2(n + 1). Search, insert and delete stay O(log n) in the worst case. Without the fix-ups the same code is a plain BST with height n.
Incorrect:
class RBNoFix < RBTree
  private
  def insert_at(h, key)
    if h.nil?
      @size += 1
      return RBNode.new(key)
    end
    if key < h.key
      h.left = insert_at(h.left, key)
    elsif key > h.key
      h.right = insert_at(h.right, key)
    end
    h
  end
end
Correct:
def within_bound?(tree)
  tree.height <= 2 * Math.log2(tree.size + 1)
end
Complexity: O(log n)

document:
Ruby · red-black trees · insertion-and-deletion · L1
Concept: New nodes are red, and the root is recolored black after every insert
Misconception: The root can keep whatever color the fix-up left it with.
Explanation: Inserting a red node keeps the black height unchanged, so fixing red violations is cheaper than fixing black ones. A color flip can turn the root red, which would break the rule that the root is black. Set root.red = false after every insert. This left-leaning variant, which stores 2-3 trees as binary trees, supports insert and search; deletion is considerably more complex and is omitted. Insert is O(log n).
Incorrect:
RBN = Struct.new(:key, :left, :right, :red)
class RedRootBad
  attr_reader :root
  def insert(key)
    @root ||= RBN.new(key, nil, nil, true)
    self
  end
end
Correct:
class RBNode
  attr_accessor :key, :left, :right, :red
  def initialize(key, red = true)
    @key = key
    @red = red
  end
end
class RBTree
  include Enumerable
  attr_reader :root, :size
  def initialize
    @root = nil
    @size = 0
  end
  def insert(key)
    @root = insert_at(@root, key)
    @root.red = false
    self
  end
  def height(node = @root)
    node ? 1 + [height(node.left), height(node.right)].max : 0
  end
  def each(&block)
    return to_enum(:each) unless block
    walk(@root, &block)
    self
  end
  private
  def red?(node)
    !node.nil? && node.red
  end
  def rotate_left(h)
    x = h.right
    h.right = x.left
    x.left = h
    x.red = h.red
    h.red = true
    x
  end
  def rotate_right(h)
    x = h.left
    h.left = x.right
    x.right = h
    x.red = h.red
    h.red = true
    x
  end
  def flip_colors(h)
    h.red = true
    h.left.red = false
    h.right.red = false
  end
  def insert_at(h, key)
    if h.nil?
      @size += 1
      return RBNode.new(key)
    end
    if key < h.key
      h.left = insert_at(h.left, key)
    elsif key > h.key
      h.right = insert_at(h.right, key)
    end
    h = rotate_left(h) if red?(h.right) && !red?(h.left)
    h = rotate_right(h) if red?(h.left) && red?(h.left.left)
    flip_colors(h) if red?(h.left) && red?(h.right)
    h
  end
  def walk(node, &block)
    return unless node
    walk(node.left, &block)
    block.call(node.key)
    walk(node.right, &block)
  end
end
Complexity: O(log n)

Ruby · red-black trees · mutation · L2
Concept: A rotation hands the old parent's color to the new subtree root and makes the old parent red
Misconception: A rotation only moves links; the colors can stay where they are.
Explanation: The subtree root keeps the color that the parent link expects, so the new root must take the old root's color and the demoted node becomes red. Leaving the colors alone can create a red node with a red child or a black node where a red one was expected. A rotation is O(1) and keeps the key order.
Incorrect:
RN = Struct.new(:key, :left, :right, :red)
def rotate_left_bad(h)
  x = h.right
  h.right = x.left
  x.left = h
  h.red = true
  x
end
Correct:
class RBTree
  private
  def rotate_left(h)
    x = h.right
    h.right = x.left
    x.left = h
    x.red = h.red
    h.red = true
    x
  end
  def rotate_right(h)
    x = h.left
    h.left = x.right
    x.right = h
    x.red = h.red
    h.red = true
    x
  end
end
Complexity: O(1)

Concept: ^ and $ match at every line; use \A and \z to anchor the whole string
Misconception: /^\w+$/ only matches a string that is one word.
Explanation: In Ruby ^ and $ are line anchors, always on. A string with a newline matches if any line matches, so "abc\nDROP TABLE" passes /^\w+$/. \A matches the start of the string and \z the end (\Z allows a final newline). Use \A...\z for validating input.
Incorrect:

  s.match?(/^\w+$/)
end
Correct:
def valid?(s)
  s.match?(/\A\w+\z/)
end
Complexity: O(n)

Concept: Interpolating user text into a pattern needs Regexp.escape
Misconception: /#{input}/ searches for the literal text of input.
Explanation: Interpolation inserts the text as pattern syntax. A "." matches any character and an unbalanced "(" raises RegexpError. Regexp.escape(input) quotes every metacharacter so the pattern matches the literal text. For substring tests use include? or start_with? and avoid a regular expression.
Incorrect:
def contains_bad?(text, input)
  text.match?(/#{input}/)
end
Correct:
def contains?(text, input)
  text.match?(/#{Regexp.escape(input)}/)
end
Complexity: O(n)

Concept: match returns nil when there is no match, so check it before indexing the result
Misconception: s.match(/(\d{4})/)[1] always returns the year.

end

def year(s)
  m = s.match(/(?<year>\d{4})/)
  m && m[:year]
end
Complexity: O(n)

Ruby · Regexp · Overview
A Regexp is a regular expression object written /pattern/. It is matched with match, match?, =~, scan, gsub and case/when. Ruby uses a backtracking engine (Onigmo), so cost depends on the pattern; since Ruby 3.2 many patterns are memoised and run in linear time, and Regexp.timeout can limit the rest.

Ruby · Regexp (regular expressions) · transformation · L3
Concept: scan with groups returns an array of arrays, one inner array per match
Misconception: scan always returns a flat array of strings.
Explanation: Without groups, scan returns the matched strings. With capture groups it returns one array of captures per match, so [["a", "1"], ["b", "2"]]. Calling a String method on each element then fails because the element is an Array. Destructure in the block or build a hash with to_h { |k, v| ... }.
Incorrect:
def counts_bad(s)
  s.scan(/([a-z])(\d)/).map(&:to_i)
end
Correct:
def counts(s)
  s.scan(/([a-z])(\d)/).map { |k, v| [k, v.to_i] }
end
Complexity: O(n)

Ruby · segment trees · creation · L2
Concept: Split a segment into [l, mid] and [mid + 1, r] so the halves never overlap
Misconception: Splitting a range at mid into [l, mid] and [mid, r] is the natural way to divide it.
Explanation: The two halves share the element at mid, so it is counted twice, and a range of two elements recurses on itself forever (SystemStackError). Use [l, mid] and [mid + 1, r]. Store node i's children at 2i and 2i + 1 and allocate 4n slots, which always suffices for the recursive layout. Building is O(n).
Incorrect:
def build_bad(arr, l, r)
  return arr[l] if l == r
  mid = (l + r) / 2
  build_bad(arr, l, mid) + build_bad(arr, mid, r)
end
Correct:
class SegTree
  attr_reader :tree, :size
  def initialize(arr)
    @size = arr.size
    @tree = Array.new(4 * [@size, 1].max, 0)
    build(arr, 1, 0, @size - 1) if @size > 0
  end
  def total
    @tree[1]
  end
  private
  def build(arr, node, l, r)
    if l == r
      @tree[node] = arr[l]
      return
    end
    mid = (l + r) / 2
    build(arr, 2 * node, l, mid)
    build(arr, 2 * node + 1, mid + 1, r)
    @tree[node] = @tree[2 * node] + @tree[2 * node + 1]
  end
end
Complexity: O(n)

Ruby · segment trees · exercise · explain-why · L2
Prompt: Why is a recursive segment tree usually stored in an array of 4n slots?

payload.answer: The recursive layout puts the children of node i at 2i and 2i + 1 and splits ranges in the middle, so for sizes that are not powers of two the tree is not complete and some indexes are skipped. The deepest level can reach an index of almost 4n, so 4n slots are a simple safe upper bound. A power-of-two padded size of 2 * 2^ceil(log2 n) would also work.

Ruby · segment trees · mutation · L3
Concept: Lazy propagation must push pending additions to the children before descending into them
Misconception: A pending range addition stored on a node can stay there until the whole node is queried.
Explanation: A partial query or update descends into the children, which do not yet know about the addition stored on their parent, so they return stale values. Push the pending value down (apply it to both children and clear it) before recursing. Then range add and range sum are both O(log n) instead of O(n) per update.
Incorrect:
class LazyNoPush
  def initialize(arr)
    @n = arr.size
    @sum = Array.new(4 * @n, 0)
    @lazy = Array.new(4 * @n, 0)
    build(1, 0, @n - 1, arr)
  end
  def add(l, r, v)
    range_add(1, 0, @n - 1, l, r, v)
  end
  def sum(l, r)
    range_sum(1, 0, @n - 1, l, r)
  end
  private
  def build(node, l, r, arr)
    if l == r
      @sum[node] = arr[l]
      return
    end
    mid = (l + r) / 2
    build(2 * node, l, mid, arr)
    build(2 * node + 1, mid + 1, r, arr)
    @sum[node] = @sum[2 * node] + @sum[2 * node + 1]
  end
  def range_add(node, l, r, ql, qr, v)
    return if qr < l || r < ql
    if ql <= l && r <= qr
      @sum[node] += v * (r - l + 1)
      @lazy[node] += v
      return
    end
    mid = (l + r) / 2
    range_add(2 * node, l, mid, ql, qr, v)
    range_add(2 * node + 1, mid + 1, r, ql, qr, v)
    @sum[node] = @sum[2 * node] + @sum[2 * node + 1] + @lazy[node] * (r - l + 1)
  end
  def range_sum(node, l, r, ql, qr)
    return 0 if qr < l || r < ql
    return @sum[node] if ql <= l && r <= qr
    mid = (l + r) / 2
    range_sum(2 * node, l, mid, ql, qr) + range_sum(2 * node + 1, mid + 1, r, ql, qr)
  end
end
Correct:
class LazySeg
  def initialize(arr)
    @n = arr.size
    @sum = Array.new(4 * @n, 0)
    @lazy = Array.new(4 * @n, 0)
    build(1, 0, @n - 1, arr)
  end
  def add(l, r, v)
    range_add(1, 0, @n - 1, l, r, v)
  end
  def sum(l, r)
    range_sum(1, 0, @n - 1, l, r)
  end
  private
  def build(node, l, r, arr)
    if l == r
      @sum[node] = arr[l]
      return
    end
    mid = (l + r) / 2
    build(2 * node, l, mid, arr)
    build(2 * node + 1, mid + 1, r, arr)
    @sum[node] = @sum[2 * node] + @sum[2 * node + 1]
  end
  def apply(node, l, r, v)
    @sum[node] += v * (r - l + 1)
    @lazy[node] += v
  end
  def push(node, l, r)
    return if @lazy[node].zero?
    mid = (l + r) / 2
    apply(2 * node, l, mid, @lazy[node])
    apply(2 * node + 1, mid + 1, r, @lazy[node])
    @lazy[node] = 0
  end
  def range_add(node, l, r, ql, qr, v)
    return if qr < l || r < ql
    if ql <= l && r <= qr
      apply(node, l, r, v)
      return
    end
    push(node, l, r)
    mid = (l + r) / 2
    range_add(2 * node, l, mid, ql, qr, v)
    range_add(2 * node + 1, mid + 1, r, ql, qr, v)
    @sum[node] = @sum[2 * node] + @sum[2 * node + 1]
  end
  def range_sum(node, l, r, ql, qr)
    return 0 if qr < l || r < ql
    return @sum[node] if ql <= l && r <= qr
    push(node, l, r)
    mid = (l + r) / 2
    range_sum(2 * node, l, mid, ql, qr) + range_sum(2 * node + 1, mid + 1, r, ql, qr)
  end
end
Complexity: O(log n)

    apply(2 * node + 1, mid + 1, r, @lazy[node])
    @lazy[node] = 0
  end
  def range_add(node, l, r, ql, qr, v)
    return if qr < l || r < ql
    if ql <= l && r <= qr
      apply(node, l, r, v)
      return
    end
    push(node, l, r)
    mid = (l + r) / 2
    range_add(2 * node, l, mid, ql, qr, v)
    range_add(2 * node + 1, mid + 1, r, ql, qr, v)
    @sum[node] = @sum[2 * node] + @sum[2 * node + 1]
  end
  def range_sum(node, l, r, ql, qr)
    return 0 if qr < l || r < ql
    return @sum[node] if ql <= l && r <= qr
    push(node, l, r)
    mid = (l + r) / 2
    range_sum(2 * node, l, mid, ql, qr) + range_sum(2 * node + 1, mid + 1, r, ql, qr)
  end
end
Complexity: O(log n)

payload.explanation: A partial query or update descends into the children, which do not yet know about the addition stored on their parent, so they return stale values. Ruby · segment trees · access · L3
Concept: A range query returns the identity for disjoint segments, the stored value for covered ones, and combines otherwise
Misconception: A query can return the stored value whenever the segment is covered, and recurse otherwise, without a disjoint case.
Explanation: Without the disjoint check the recursion reaches leaves that lie outside the query and adds their values. For a sum the identity is 0: return 0 when the node range does not intersect the query, return the stored sum when it is fully inside, and otherwise add the answers from both children. At most about 2 log n nodes are expanded, so a query is O(log n).
Incorrect:
def query_bad(t, node, l, r, ql, qr)
  return t[node] if l == r || (ql <= l && r <= qr)
  mid = (l + r) / 2
  query_bad(t, 2 * node, l, mid, ql, qr) +
    query_bad(t, 2 * node + 1, mid + 1, r, ql, qr)
end
Correct:
class SegTree
  def query(ql, qr)
    query_at(1, 0, @size - 1, ql, qr)
  end
  private
  def query_at(node, l, r, ql, qr)
    return 0 if qr < l || r < ql
    return @tree[node] if ql <= l && r <= qr
    mid = (l + r) / 2
    query_at(2 * node, l, mid, ql, qr) + query_at(2 * node + 1, mid + 1, r, ql, qr)
  end
end
Complexity: O(log n)

Ruby · segment trees · mutation · L2
Concept: A point update must recompute every ancestor on the path from the leaf to the root
Misconception: Changing the leaf value is enough, because queries read from the leaves.
Explanation: Queries use the stored sums of inner nodes, so an ancestor that is not recomputed keeps answering with the old value. After changing the leaf, recompute each ancestor as the sum of its children while the recursion unwinds. Only one root-to-leaf path changes, so an update is O(log n).
Incorrect:
def update_bad(t, node, l, r, i, v)
  if l == r
    t[node] = v
    return
  end
  mid = (l + r) / 2
  if i <= mid
    update_bad(t, 2 * node, l, mid, i, v)
  else
    update_bad(t, 2 * node + 1, mid + 1, r, i, v)
  end
end
Correct:
class SegTree
  def update(i, v)
    update_at(1, 0, @size - 1, i, v)
    self
  end
  private
  def update_at(node, l, r, i, v)
    if l == r
      @tree[node] = v
      return
    end
    mid = (l + r) / 2
    if i <= mid
      update_at(2 * node, l, mid, i, v)
    else
      update_at(2 * node + 1, mid + 1, r, i, v)
    end
    @tree[node] = @tree[2 * node] + @tree[2 * node + 1]
  end
end
Complexity: O(log n)

Ruby · Set (require "set") · insertion-and-deletion · L2
Concept: add always returns the set; add? returns nil when the element was already present
Misconception: seen.add(x) returns false for a duplicate.
Explanation: Set#add returns the set itself, which is always truthy, so it cannot tell you whether the element was new. Set#add? returns the set when it inserted the element and nil when it was already there. That makes duplicate detection a single O(1) call per element.
Incorrect:
require "set"
def first_dup_bad(items)
  seen = Set.new
  items.each { |x| return x unless seen.add(x) }
  nil
end
Correct:
require "set"
def first_dup(items)
  seen = Set.new
  items.each { |x| return x unless seen.add?(x) }
  nil
end
Complexity: O(n)

Concept: Set.new takes an enumerable; Set.new(5) raises, so convert a scalar or string with to_a or chars first
Misconception: Set.new accepts any value and wraps it as one element.
Explanation: Set.new(enum) iterates its argument, so an Integer raises ArgumentError (value must be enumerable) and a String is not enumerable either. Use Set[1, 2, 3] for literal members, enum.to_set for a collection, and "abc".chars.to_set for characters. A Set is backed by a Hash, so add and include? are O(1) on average.
Incorrect:
require "set"
def letters_bad(word)
  Set.new(word)
end
Correct:
require "set"
def letters(word)
  word.chars.to_set
end
Complexity: O(n)

Ruby · Set (require "set") · equality · L2
Concept: Sets are equal when they hold the same elements, in any order; arrays also compare order
Misconception: Set[1, 2] and [1, 2] behave the same when compared with their reversed versions.
Explanation: Set#== ignores order, so Set[1, 2] == Set[2, 1], while [1, 2] == [2, 1] is false. Use <= (subset?), < (proper_subset?), disjoint? and intersect? for relations. Comparing a Set with an Array is never equal, even with the same elements.

def same_items_bad?(a, b)
  a == b
end
Correct:
require "set"
def same_items?(a, b)
  a.to_set == b.to_set
end
Complexity: O(n)

Ruby · Set (require "set") · mutation · L3
Concept: Changing an element after it was added makes a Set lose it; add frozen elements
Misconception: An array stored in a Set can be modified and still be found.
Explanation: A Set stores each element under its hash code, like Hash keys. If an element such as an array is mutated afterwards, its hash code changes and include? returns false, although the element is still in the set. Add frozen copies (item.dup.freeze) or immutable values such as Data.
Incorrect:
require "set"
def lost_bad
  s = Set.new
  item = [1]
  s << item
  item << 2
  s.include?(item)
end
Correct:
require "set"
def kept
  s = Set.new
  item = [1].freeze
  s << item
  s.include?([1])
end
Complexity: O(1)

Ruby · Set (require "set") · patterns · L3
Concept: Check for the complement before adding the current number in a two-sum search
Misconception: Adding x to the seen set first and then testing target - x is fine.
Explanation: If x is added before the check, a number can pair with itself: with target 6 and the list [3], 6 - 3 = 3 is already in the set. Test target - x against the elements seen so far, then add x. One pass with a Set is O(n) time and space.
Incorrect:
require "set"
def pair_bad?(nums, target)
  seen = Set.new
  nums.each do |x|
    seen << x
    return true if seen.include?(target - x)
  end
  false
end
Correct:
require "set"
def pair?(nums, target)
  seen = Set.new
  nums.each do |x|
    return true if seen.include?(target - x)
    seen << x
  end
  false
end
Complexity: O(n)

Ruby · Set (require "set") · ordering · L3
Concept: A Set iterates in insertion order and has no sorting; SortedSet was removed, so call sort
Misconception: SortedSet.new keeps the elements ordered.
Explanation: SortedSet was extracted from the standard library in Ruby 3.0 and raises on use. A Set keeps insertion order and offers no ordered access, so sort the elements into an Array when you need order: set.sort (O(n log n)). For a sorted structure with fast insertion use a balanced tree or a heap.
Incorrect:
require "set"
def ordered_bad(items)
  SortedSet.new(items).to_a
end
Correct:
require "set"
def ordered(items)
  items.to_set.sort
end
Complexity: O(n log n)

Ruby · singly linked lists · insertion-and-deletion · L1
Concept: Keep a tail pointer so push_back is O(1), and handle the empty list separately
Misconception: Appending can always start with head.next, even when the list is empty.
Explanation: An empty list has no head node, so head.next raises NoMethodError on nil. push_back must set both head and tail when the list is empty, and otherwise link the new node after the tail and move the tail. With a tail pointer append is O(1); walking from the head to find the end is O(n). push_front is O(1) with or without a tail.
Incorrect:
def append_bad(list, v)
  node = list.head
  node = node.next while node.next
  node.next = SLNode.new(v)
end
Correct:
class SLNode
  attr_accessor :value, :next
  def initialize(value, nxt = nil)
    @value = value
    @next = nxt
  end
end
class SinglyList
  include Enumerable
  attr_reader :head, :tail, :size
  def initialize
    @head = @tail = nil
    @size = 0
  end
  def push_front(v)
    node = SLNode.new(v, @head)
    @head = node
    @tail ||= node
    @size += 1
    self
  end
  def push_back(v)
    node = SLNode.new(v)
    if @tail
      @tail.next = node
    else
      @head = node
    end
    @tail = node
    @size += 1
    self
  end
  def each
    return to_enum(:each) unless block_given?
    node = @head
    while node
      yield node.value
      node = node.next
    end
  end
end
Complexity: O(1)

Ruby · singly linked lists · patterns · L3
Concept: Floyd cycle detection moves the pointers first and compares afterwards
Misconception: Comparing slow and fast before moving them detects a cycle.
Explanation: Both pointers start at the head, so comparing them before the first step is always true and reports a cycle in every list. Advance slow by one and fast by two, then compare. If fast reaches nil the list ends. Floyd's method uses O(n) time and O(1) space; a Set of visited nodes needs O(n) space.
Incorrect:
def cycle_bad?(head)
  slow = fast = head
  while fast && fast.next
    return true if slow.equal?(fast)
    slow = slow.next
    fast = fast.next.next
  end
  false
end
Correct:
def cycle?(head)
  slow = fast = head
  while fast && fast.next
    slow = slow.next
    fast = fast.next.next
    return true if slow.equal?(fast)
  end
  false
end
Complexity: O(n)

Ruby · singly linked lists · patterns · L3
Concept: Find the middle with slow and fast pointers; the loop test must be fast && fast.next
Misconception: while fast.next is a sufficient loop condition for the fast pointer.
Explanation: With an even number of nodes, fast.next.next becomes nil after the last step and the next test fast.next calls a method on nil. Test fast && fast.next so both fast and its successor exist. The slow pointer ends on the second middle node for even lengths and on the middle node for odd lengths. One pass, O(n) time, O(1) space.
Incorrect:
def middle_bad(head)
  slow = fast = head
  while fast.next
    slow = slow.next
    fast = fast.next.next
  end
  slow.value
end
Correct:
def middle(head)
  return nil unless head
  slow = fast = head
  while fast && fast.next
    slow = slow.next
    fast = fast.next.next
  end
  slow.value
end
Complexity: O(n)

Ruby · singly linked lists · insertion-and-deletion · L2
Concept: Removing a node needs the previous node; also update head when removing the first node and tail when removing the last
Misconception: Deleting the first node whose value matches only needs prev.next = node.next.
Explanation: The first node has no previous node, so removing it must move head instead. Removing the last node must move tail to the previous node, otherwise later push_back calls attach to a node that is no longer in the list. Finding the node costs O(n); unlinking is O(1).
Incorrect:
def remove_bad(list, v)
  prev = nil
  node = list.head
  while node && node.value != v
    prev = node
    node = node.next
  end
  prev.next = node.next if node
  node
end
Correct:
class SinglyList
  def remove(v)
    prev = nil
    node = @head
    while node && node.value != v
      prev = node
      node = node.next
    end
    return false unless node
    if prev
      prev.next = node.next
    else
      @head = node.next
    end
    @tail = prev if node.equal?(@tail)
    @size -= 1
    true
  end
end
Complexity: O(n)

Prompt: Why must a singly linked list remove method update the tail pointer when it removes the last node?

payload.answer: The tail pointer is used by push_back to attach the next node in O(1). If the last node is unlinked but the tail still points to it, the next push_back links the new node after a node that is no longer reachable from the head, so the new element silently disappears from the list. The remove method must move the tail to the previous node.

Ruby · singly linked lists · mutation · L3
Concept: Reverse in place by saving node.next before redirecting it
Misconception: Setting node.next = prev and then moving to node.next walks the old list.
Explanation: After node.next = prev the old successor is unreachable, so the walk stops after one node and the rest of the list is lost. Save nxt = node.next first, redirect, then advance prev and node. Reversal is O(n) time and O(1) extra space; head and tail swap roles.
Incorrect:
def reverse_bad(list)
  prev = nil
  node = list.head
  while node
    node.next = prev
    prev = node
    node = node.next
  end
  prev
end
Correct:
class SinglyList
  def reverse!
    prev = nil
    node = @head
    @tail = @head
    while node
      nxt = node.next
      node.next = prev
      prev = node
      node = nxt
    end
    @head = prev
    self
  end
end
Complexity: O(n)

Ruby · stacks · patterns · L2
Concept: Balanced brackets need a stack because a counter cannot check the order of different kinds
Misconception: Counting opening and closing brackets of each kind is enough to validate a string.
Explanation: Equal counts do not mean proper nesting: "([)]" has one of each kind and ")(" has equal counts but closes before it opens. Push each opener, and on a closer pop and compare with the matching opener. The string is balanced only if no mismatch occurs and the stack ends empty. One pass, O(n).
Incorrect:
def balanced_bad?(s)
  s.count("([{") == s.count(")]}")
end
Correct:
PAIRS = { ")" => "(", "]" => "[", "}" => "{" }
def balanced?(s)
  stack = Stack.new
  s.each_char do |ch|
    if PAIRS.value?(ch)
      stack.push(ch)
    elsif PAIRS.key?(ch)
      return false if stack.empty? || stack.pop != PAIRS[ch]
    end
  end
  stack.empty?
end
Complexity: O(n)

Ruby · stacks · patterns · L3
Concept: A monotonic stack finds each next greater element in one pass; use a strict comparison
Misconception: Popping while arr[top] <= x gives the next greater element.
Explanation: With <= an equal value is popped and gets an equal value as its next greater element, but "greater" means strictly larger. Keep a stack of indexes whose answer is still unknown and pop while arr[top] < x. Each index is pushed and popped once, so the total is O(n), not O(n squared).
Incorrect:
def next_greater_bad(arr)
  res = Array.new(arr.size, -1)
  st = []
  arr.each_with_index do |x, i|
    res[st.pop] = x while !st.empty? && arr[st.last] <= x
    st.push(i)
  end
  res
end
Correct:
def next_greater(arr)
  res = Array.new(arr.size, -1)
  st = []
  arr.each_with_index do |x, i|
    res[st.pop] = x while !st.empty? && arr[st.last] < x
    st.push(i)
  end
  res
end
Complexity: O(n)

Ruby · stacks · insertion-and-deletion · L1
Concept: A stack pops from the same end it pushes to, and popping an empty stack must be handled
Misconception: Array#pop on an empty array is a safe way to read the top of a stack.
Explanation: Array#pop and Array#last return nil on an empty array instead of raising, so a missing element travels onward until a later call such as nil + nil fails far from the cause. A Stack class can raise a clear error on pop and peek of an empty stack. push, pop and peek are O(1). Iterating from the top gives last-in, first-out order.
Incorrect:
def add_top_bad(items)
  items.pop + items.pop
end
Correct:
class EmptyStackError < StandardError; end
class Stack
  include Enumerable
  def initialize
    @items = []
  end
  def push(v)
    @items.push(v)
    self
  end
  def pop
    raise EmptyStackError, "pop from empty stack" if @items.empty?
    @items.pop
  end
  def peek
    raise EmptyStackError, "peek at empty stack" if @items.empty?
    @items.last
  end
  def empty?
    @items.empty?
  end
  def size
    @items.size
  end
  def each(&block)
    return to_enum(:each) unless block
    @items.reverse_each(&block)
    self
  end
end
Complexity: O(1)

Ruby · stacks · patterns · L2
Concept: In reverse Polish evaluation the first pop is the right operand
Misconception: For a - b, pop a first and then b.
Explanation: The stack holds operands in the order they appeared, so the first pop returns the right operand and the second the left one. Swapping them is harmless for + and * but reverses - and /. Pop b, pop a, then compute a op b. Evaluation is O(n).
Incorrect:
def rpn_bad(tokens)
  st = []
  tokens.each do |t|
    if t =~ /\A-?\d+\z/
      st.push(t.to_i)
    else
      a = st.pop
      b = st.pop
      st.push(a.send(t, b))
    end
  end
  st.pop
end
Correct:
def eval_rpn(tokens)
  st = Stack.new
  tokens.each do |t|
    if t =~ /\A-?\d+\z/
      st.push(t.to_i)
    else
      b = st.pop
      a = st.pop
      st.push(a.send(t, b))
    end
  end
  st.pop
end
Complexity: O(n)

Ruby · String · transformation · L3
Concept: Build strings with << or join; += creates a new string object every iteration
Misconception: s += piece appends to the same string in a loop.
Explanation: s += x is s = s + x: it allocates a new string and copies the old one each time, so a loop is O(n^2) in the total length. << appends in place, and Array#join builds the result in one pass. Use << on a string you own.
Incorrect:
def build_bad(parts)
  s = ""
  ids = []
  parts.each { |x| s += x; ids << s.object_id }
  [s, ids.uniq.size]
end
Correct:
def build(parts)
  s = +""
  ids = []
  parts.each { |x| s << x; ids << s.object_id }
  [s, ids.uniq.size]
end
Complexity: O(n)

Ruby · String · exercise · explain-why · L3
Prompt: Why is building a long string with += in a loop slower than with <<?

payload.answer: Each s += x evaluates s + x, which allocates a new string and copies all of s plus x, then rebinds s. Over n appends the copying adds up to O(n^2) characters and creates garbage. << appends into the existing buffer, which grows geometrically, so the loop is O(n) overall.

Misconception: a.equal?(b) is true whenever a and b hold the same text.

  a.equal?(b)

def same_text?(a, b)
  a == b
end

Concept: << and bang methods mutate the receiver, so a method that appends to its argument changes the caller's string
Misconception: A method can append to its string parameter without affecting the caller.

def shout_bad(s)
  s << "!"
end
Correct:
def shout(s)
  s + "!"
end
Complexity: O(n)

Ruby · String · patterns · L3
Concept: Normalise with downcase and gsub before comparing to its reverse for a palindrome check
Misconception: s == s.reverse is a correct palindrome test for sentences.
Explanation: Case, spaces and punctuation break a direct comparison. Normalise first: downcase, then delete everything that is not a letter or digit with gsub(/[^a-z0-9]/, ""), then compare with the reverse. This is O(n) time and space; two pointers do it in O(1) extra space.
Incorrect:
def palindrome_bad?(s)
  s == s.reverse
end
Correct:
def palindrome?(s)
  t = s.downcase.gsub(/[^a-z0-9]/, "")
  t == t.reverse
end
Complexity: O(n)

Ruby · String · iteration · L2
Concept: split(" ") treats runs of whitespace as one separator, split(/ /) keeps empty strings
Misconception: split(/ /) and split(" ") give the same words.
Explanation: split(" ") is awk-style: it ignores leading whitespace and splits on runs of spaces and tabs. split(/ /) splits at every single space, so double spaces produce empty strings. Trailing empty strings are dropped unless you pass a negative limit.
Incorrect:
def word_count_bad(s)
  s.split(/ /).size
end
Correct:
def word_count(s)
  s.split(" ").size
end
Complexity: O(n)

Ruby · Struct and OpenStruct · creation · L1
Concept: Struct.new generates a class; too many arguments raise, too few leave nil, and keyword_init makes the call explicit
Misconception: A Struct accepts any number of arguments and ignores the extra ones.
Explanation: Struct.new(:x, :y) returns a class with accessors for the members. new(1) leaves y as nil, which later raises NoMethodError when used, and new(1, 2, 3) raises ArgumentError (struct size differs). With keyword_init: true the call names every member, unknown names are rejected and the order no longer matters.
Incorrect:
PointBad = Struct.new(:x, :y)
def point_bad(x, y, z)
  PointBad.new(x, y, z)
end
Correct:
Pt = Struct.new(:x, :y, keyword_init: true)
def point(x:, y:)
  Pt.new(x: x, y: y)
end
Complexity: O(1)

Ruby · Struct and OpenStruct · equality · L2
Concept: Struct instances are equal when all members are equal; a plain class needs == and hash
Misconception: Two objects with the same fields are always ==.
Explanation: A Struct defines ==, eql? and hash from its members, so equal structs deduplicate in uniq, Set and as hash keys. A plain class compares by identity unless you define ==, eql? and hash. Mutating a struct used as a hash key changes its hash code and loses the entry.
Incorrect:
class PlainPoint
  attr_reader :x, :y
  def initialize(x, y)
    @x = x
    @y = y
  end
end
def unique_plain(points)
  points.map { |x, y| PlainPoint.new(x, y) }.uniq.size
end
Correct:
Cell = Struct.new(:row, :col)
def unique_cells(points)
  points.map { |r, c| Cell.new(r, c) }.uniq.size
end
Complexity: O(n)

Ruby · Struct and OpenStruct · access · L2
Concept: OpenStruct returns nil for an unknown attribute, hiding typos; a Struct rejects them
Misconception: OpenStruct and Struct behave the same for an unknown attribute.
Explanation: OpenStruct creates attributes on demand, so a misspelled reader such as cfg.timout returns nil and the failure shows up later. A Struct has a fixed member list: an unknown reader raises NoMethodError and an unknown keyword raises ArgumentError. OpenStruct is also slower; use it for throwaway data and Struct or Data for fixed shapes.
Incorrect:
require "ostruct"
def timeout_bad(opts)
  OpenStruct.new(opts).timout + 1
end
Correct:
Config = Struct.new(:timeout, keyword_init: true)
def timeout(opts)
  Config.new(**opts).timeout + 1
end
Complexity: O(1)

Ruby · Struct and OpenStruct · access · L3
Concept: Destructure a Struct with case/in; without an else branch an unmatched value raises NoMatchingPatternError
Misconception: A case/in expression returns nil when no pattern matches.
Explanation: Struct defines deconstruct and deconstruct_keys, so case/in can match on members: in { x: 0.., y: 0.. }. Unlike case/when, a case/in with no matching branch and no else raises NoMatchingPatternError. Add an else branch, or rescue the error when failure is expected.
Incorrect:
def quadrant_bad(pt)
  case pt
  in { x: 0.., y: 0.. } then :first
  in { x: ...0, y: 0.. } then :second
  end
end
Correct:
def quadrant(pt)
  case pt
  in { x: 0.., y: 0.. } then :first
  in { x: ...0, y: 0.. } then :second
  in { x: ...0, y: ...0 } then :third
  else :fourth
  end
end
Complexity: O(1)

Ruby · Symbol · ordering · L3
Concept: Symbols and strings cannot be compared with each other in sort; convert to one type first
Misconception: A mixed array of symbols and strings can be sorted.
Explanation: Symbol#<=> only compares symbols with symbols and String#<=> only strings with strings, so sorting a mixed array raises ArgumentError (comparison of Symbol with String failed). Convert with map(&:to_s) before sorting. Symbols sort by their names.
Incorrect:
def sorted_bad(items)
  items.sort
end
Correct:
def sorted(items)
  items.map(&:to_s).sort
end
Complexity: O(n log n)

Ruby · Symbol · equality · L2
Concept: The same symbol is always the same object; equal strings are separate objects
Misconception: Every use of "name" refers to the same string object, like :name does.
Explanation: Symbols are interned in a symbol table, so :a.equal?(:a) is always true and comparing them is a pointer comparison. Each string literal creates a new object, so repeated "a" literals allocate separately. That makes symbols cheap hash keys and labels, but they are for identifiers, not for text that changes.
Incorrect:
def distinct_strings(n)
  Array.new(n) { "a".object_id }.uniq.size
end
Correct:
def distinct_symbols(n)
  Array.new(n) { :a.object_id }.uniq.size
end
Complexity: O(n)

payload.document:
Ruby · Symbol · exercise · explain-why · L2
Prompt: Why are symbols a better choice than strings for hash keys that are fixed identifiers?

payload.answer: A symbol is interned, so each name is one object and equal symbols are the identical object. Hashing and comparing a symbol does not need to look at characters, and no new object is allocated each time the name appears in the code. Strings are separate mutable objects and must be hashed and compared by content, and a string key has to be copied and frozen by the hash.

Ruby · Symbol · access · L1
Concept: A Symbol key and a String key are different keys; normalise with transform_keys(&:to_sym)
Misconception: h[:name] finds the entry stored under "name".
Explanation: The symbol :name and the string "name" are different objects and different hash keys. Data from JSON.parse or form input has string keys unless symbolize_names is used. fetch(:name) then raises KeyError and h[:name] returns nil. Convert once at the boundary with transform_keys(&:to_sym).
Incorrect:
def name_bad(h)
  h.fetch(:name)
end
Correct:
def name(h)
  h.transform_keys(&:to_sym).fetch(:name)
end
Complexity: O(n)

document:
Ruby · Symbol · patterns · L3
Concept: Compare a symbol state with a symbol; :open == "open" is false
Misconception: A state stored as :open equals the string "open".
Explanation: A symbol never equals a string, even with the same characters. A state machine that stores symbols should compare and branch on symbols (case state when :open), and convert text input once with to_sym on a whitelist of known values. A table of allowed transitions keyed by symbol is an O(1) lookup.
Incorrect:
def open_bad?(state)
  state == "open"
end
Correct:
TRANSITIONS = { open: [:closed], closed: [:open, :archived], archived: [] }.freeze
def open?(state)
  state == :open
end
def can_move?(from, to)
  TRANSITIONS.fetch(from, []).include?(to)
end
Complexity: O(1)

Ruby · Symbol · transformation · L2
Concept: &:name turns a method name into a block, but it cannot pass arguments
Misconception: map(&:round(1)) calls round with an argument.
Explanation: The & operator on a symbol calls Symbol#to_proc, which builds a block that calls that method with no arguments. Adding arguments after the symbol is a syntax error. When a method needs arguments, write the block out: map { |x| x.round(1) }. &:method is O(1) overhead per element.
Incorrect (does not parse: ):
def rounded_bad(xs)
  xs.map(&:round(1))
end
Correct:
def rounded(xs)
  xs.map { |x| x.round(1) }
end
def lengths(words)
  words.map(&:length)
end
Complexity: O(n)

payload.concept: Close the queue to stop all workers; a single sentinel value stops only one of them
payload.explanation: Each :done is consumed by exactly one worker, so with two workers one sentinel leaves the other blocked forever in pop. Queue#close wakes every waiting consumer: pop returns nil once a closed queue is empty, so workers can loop with while (job = q.pop). After close, push raises ClosedQueueError.

payload.document:
Ruby · Queue and SizedQueue (thread-safe queues) · exercise · explain-why · L3
Prompt: Why does closing a Queue stop all workers while a single sentinel value does not?

payload.answer: A sentinel is an ordinary item and is taken by exactly one consumer, so the others stay blocked in pop. Closing the queue changes its state: every blocked pop wakes up and returns nil once the remaining items are gone, and later pops return nil immediately. Each worker sees the nil and exits its loop, whatever the number of workers.

Ruby · Queue and SizedQueue (thread-safe queues) · creation · L2
Concept: Queue.new takes initial items, not a capacity; use SizedQueue.new(n) for a limit
Misconception: Queue.new(5) creates a queue with room for five items.
Explanation: Queue.new accepts an enumerable of initial items (Ruby 3.1+), so Queue.new(5) raises TypeError (can't convert Integer into Array). A plain Queue is unbounded. A capacity needs SizedQueue.new(5). Both live in the core as Thread::Queue and Thread::SizedQueue; require "thread" is no longer needed.
Incorrect:
def limited_bad
  Queue.new(5)
end
Correct:
def limited
  SizedQueue.new(5)
end
def preloaded
  Queue.new([1, 2, 3])
end
Complexity: O(1)

Ruby · Queue and SizedQueue (thread-safe queues) · ordering · L3
Concept: Results arrive in completion order; tag each result with its index and sort
Misconception: Results pushed by worker threads come out in the order the jobs were started.
Explanation: A Queue is FIFO by arrival, not by job start. A thread that finishes first pushes first, so slow jobs appear late. Tag each result with its job index, collect all of them and sort by index to restore the submission order.
Incorrect:
def run_bad(delays)
  out = Queue.new
  ts = delays.each_with_index.map { |d, i| Thread.new { sleep d; out << i } }
  ts.each(&:join)
  Array.new(out.size) { out.pop }
end
Correct:
def run(delays)
  out = Queue.new
  ts = delays.each_with_index.map { |d, i| Thread.new { sleep d; out << [i, d] } }
  ts.each(&:join)
  Array.new(out.size) { out.pop }.sort.map(&:last)
end
Complexity: O(n log n)

Ruby · Queue and SizedQueue (thread-safe queues) · access · L1
Concept: pop blocks on an empty Queue; pop(true) raises ThreadError and pop(timeout:) returns nil
Misconception: q.pop(true) waits politely for an item.
Explanation: Queue#pop blocks until an item arrives. With non_block = true it never waits and raises ThreadError (queue empty) when there is nothing to take. Since Ruby 3.2 pop(timeout: seconds) waits up to the limit and returns nil if nothing arrived. Use the timeout form for polling loops.
Incorrect:
def poll_bad(q)
  q.pop(true)
end
Correct:
def poll(q)
  q.pop(timeout: 0.05)
end
Complexity: O(1)

Ruby · Queue and SizedQueue (thread-safe queues) · insertion-and-deletion · L3
Concept: A SizedQueue blocks the producer when full; a non-blocking push raises ThreadError
Misconception: Pushing more items than the SizedQueue limit just waits for room.
Explanation: SizedQueue.new(n) limits the queue to n items and gives back-pressure: push blocks while the queue is full, so a fast producer cannot outrun a slow consumer. push(x, true) never waits and raises ThreadError (queue full); push(x, timeout: s) returns nil on timeout. A consumer thread must be running, or the blocking push never returns.
Incorrect:
def fill_bad(items, cap)
  q = SizedQueue.new(cap)
  items.each { |x| q.push(x, true) }
  q.size
end
Correct:
def pipeline(items, cap)
  q = SizedQueue.new(cap)
  producer = Thread.new do
    items.each { |x| q << x }
    q.close
  end
  out = []
  while (x = q.pop)
    out << x
  end
  producer.join
  out
end
Complexity: O(n)

Ruby · tries · iteration · L2
Concept: Autocomplete walks the subtree and builds each word with prefix + ch, never by mutating a shared string
Misconception: Appending the character with << to the prefix as the recursion descends builds the words.
Explanation: The same String object is passed to every recursive call, so << keeps lengthening it and siblings see the leftovers of earlier branches, producing words like "abc" for "ac". Build a new string with prefix + ch for each child. Sort the results for a deterministic order. Cost is O(L + size of the subtree).
Incorrect:
def collect_bad(node, prefix, out)
  out << prefix.dup if node.terminal
  node.children.each { |ch, child| collect_bad(child, prefix << ch, out) }
  out
end
Correct:
class Trie
  def words_with_prefix(prefix)
    node = find(prefix)
    return [] unless node
    out = []
    collect(node, prefix, out)
    out.sort
  end
  private
  def collect(node, prefix, out)
    out << prefix if node.terminal
    node.children.each { |ch, child| collect(child, prefix + ch, out) }
  end
end
Complexity: O(L+k)

Ruby · tries · patterns · L2
Concept: Counting words with a prefix reads one pass counter instead of traversing the subtree
Misconception: The number of words with a prefix is 1 if the prefix node is terminal, otherwise 0.
Explanation: That only counts the prefix itself. Every node stores how many inserted words pass through it, so the count for a prefix is the pass counter of its node, or 0 when the path is missing. Duplicate inserts must be ignored or the counters inflate. The query is O(L), independent of the number of matches.
Incorrect:
def count_bad(trie, prefix)
  node = trie.send(:find, prefix)
  node && node.terminal ? 1 : 0
end
Correct:
class Trie
  def count_prefix(prefix)
    node = find(prefix)
    node ? node.pass : 0
  end
end
Complexity: O(L)

Ruby · tries · insertion-and-deletion · L3
Concept: Deleting a word must not remove longer words that share its path
Misconception: Deleting a word means removing the last character's node from its parent.
Explanation: Removing that node also removes every longer word below it, so deleting "app" would delete "apple". Keep a pass count on each node (how many words go through it). Decrement along the path, delete the first child whose count reaches zero, and otherwise just clear the terminal flag. Delete costs O(L).
Incorrect:
def delete_bad(trie, word)
  node = trie.root
  parent = nil
  word.each_char do |ch|
    parent = node
    node = node.children[ch]
    return false unless node
  end
  parent.children.delete(word[-1])
  true
end
Correct:
class Trie
  def delete(word)
    existing = find(word)
    return false unless existing && existing.terminal
    node = @root
    word.each_char do |ch|
      child = node.children[ch]
      child.pass -= 1
      if child.pass.zero?
        node.children.delete(ch)
        @size -= 1
        return true
      end
      node = child
    end
    node.terminal = false
    @size -= 1
    true
  end
end
Complexity: O(L)

Ruby · tries · creation · L1
Concept: Each trie node needs its own children Hash; Hash.new({}) shares one default Hash between all nodes
Misconception: Hash.new({}) is a convenient way to give every node an empty children Hash that fills itself in.
Explanation: The default value of Hash.new({}) is a single shared Hash object, and reading a missing key returns it without storing anything, so children[ch] ||= is never true and the code walks into a bare Hash that has no node methods. Writes through the default would be visible from every node. Use a plain {} per node and create children with ||=. Insert costs O(L) for a word of length L.
Incorrect:
BadNode = Struct.new(:children, :terminal)
def new_bad_node
  BadNode.new(Hash.new({}), false)
end
def insert_bad(root, word)
  node = root
  word.each_char { |ch| node = (node.children[ch] ||= new_bad_node) }
  node.terminal = true
end
Correct:
class TrieNode
  attr_reader :children
  attr_accessor :terminal, :pass
  def initialize
    @children = {}
    @terminal = false
    @pass = 0
  end
end
class Trie
  attr_reader :root, :size
  def initialize
    @root = TrieNode.new
    @size = 0
  end
  def insert(word)
    existing = find(word)
    return false if existing && existing.terminal
    node = @root
    word.each_char do |ch|
      node = (node.children[ch] ||= TrieNode.new)
      node.pass += 1
    end
    node.terminal = true
    @size += 1
    true
  end
  private
  def find(str)
    node = @root
    str.each_char do |ch|
      node = node.children[ch]
      return nil unless node
    end
    node
  end
end
Complexity: O(L)

class TrieNode
  attr_reader :children
  attr_accessor :terminal, :pass
  def initialize
    @children = {}
    @terminal = false
    @pass = 0
  end
end
class Trie
  attr_reader :root, :size
  def initialize
    @root = TrieNode.new
    @size = 0
  end
  def insert(word)
    existing = find(word)
    return false if existing && existing.terminal
    node = @root
    word.each_char do |ch|
      node = (node.children[ch] ||= TrieNode.new)
      node.pass += 1
    end
    node.terminal = true
    @size += 1
    true
  end
  private
  def find(str)
    node = @root
    str.each_char do |ch|
      node = node.children[ch]
      return nil unless node
    end
    node
  end
end

Writes through the default would be visible from every node. Use a plain {} per node and create children with ||=. Insert costs O(L) for a word of length L.

Concept: A word exists only if its last node is terminal; a prefix exists if the path exists
Misconception: A word is in the trie when its path of characters exists.
Explanation: The path for "app" exists as soon as "apple" is inserted, but "app" was never added as a word. Words need a terminal flag on the last node, while a prefix check only needs the path. Both walk L nodes, O(L), independent of how many words are stored.
Incorrect:
def search_bad(trie, word)
  !trie.send(:find, word).nil?
end
Correct:
class Trie
  def include?(word)
    node = find(word)
    !node.nil? && node.terminal
  end
  def prefix?(prefix)
    !find(prefix).nil?
  end
end
Complexity: O(L)

payload.concept: new Array(n).fill([]) puts one array in every slot; build rows with Array.from
payload.explanation: fill stores the same value in every slot. For a primitive that is fine; for an array or object all slots point to one object, so pushing to one row changes all rows. metadata.concept: filter(Boolean) does not narrow the element type; use a type predicate, which TypeScript 5.5 can infer

payload.concept: filter(Boolean) does not narrow the element type; use a type predicate, which TypeScript 5.5 can infer
payload.explanation: The compiler does not know that Boolean removes undefined, so the result is still (number | undefined)[]. Boolean also removes 0 and empty strings, which is usually a bug. Write filter((x): x is number => x !== undefined). Since TypeScript 5.5 the arrow function x => x !== undefined is inferred as a type predicate and narrows by itself.
payload.misconception: arr.filter(Boolean) turns (number | undefined)[] into number[].

payload.document:

Prompt: compactBad does not compile. Which error does the compiler report, why, and how do you fix it without changing what the function returns?

payload.answer: Error TS2322: the result of filter(Boolean) is still (number | undefined)[], so it is not assignable to number[]. The compiler does not treat Boolean as a type predicate. Use a type predicate, xs.filter((x): x is number => x !== undefined). Note that Boolean would also drop 0, so the predicate version is also more correct.

metadata.concept: A generic helper that may find nothing must return T | undefined, not T

payload.concept: A generic helper that may find nothing must return T | undefined, not T
payload.explanation: Reading xs[0] is typed T, but an empty array returns undefined, so the declared return type lies and callers skip the check. Declare T | undefined, or take a non-empty tuple type [T, ...T[]] when the caller guarantees one element. The compiler then forces the check at every call site.
payload.misconception: function first<T>(xs: T[]): T is correctly typed, because the element type is T.

metadata.concept: includes on a readonly tuple of literals rejects a plain string; write a type guard that widens the array once

payload.concept: includes on a readonly tuple of literals rejects a plain string; write a type guard that widens the array once
payload.explanation: With const ALLOWED = ["a", "b"] as const, includes expects "a" | "b", so passing a string is error TS2345. Widen the array to readonly string[] inside a small type guard, function isAllowed(x: string): x is Allowed. The guard then narrows x everywhere it is used, which a plain boolean cannot.
payload.misconception: ALLOWED.includes(x) is the way to check that a string is one of the allowed literals.

metadata.concept: Indexing an array is typed T even when the index is out of range; at() and a check give T | undefined

payload.concept: Indexing an array is typed T even when the index is out of range; at() and a check give T | undefined
payload.explanation: By default TypeScript types nums[i] as number, but an index past the end gives undefined at runtime, and arithmetic on it yields NaN. The compiler only reports it if you turn on noUncheckedIndexedAccess. Array.prototype.at(i) is typed number | undefined, and also accepts negative indexes, so the compiler makes you handle the missing case.
payload.misconception: nums[i] is always a number, because the array is typed number[].

metadata.concept: readonly number[] removes the mutating methods from the type, so a function can promise not to change its argument

payload.concept: readonly number[] removes the mutating methods from the type, so a function can promise not to change its argument
payload.explanation: A parameter typed number[] allows push, sort and splice, so callers cannot tell whether their array survives the call. readonly number[] (or ReadonlyArray<number>) hides the mutating methods, and the compiler rejects them. A mutable array can be passed where readonly is expected, but not the other way round. Return a new array instead of changing the input.
payload.misconception: A function that takes number[] and does not change it is as safe as one that takes readonly number[].
