TypeScript · Array · Overview
A TypeScript array is a JavaScript array with an element type: number[] or Array. Everything about runtime behaviour is unchanged: arrays are objects, they are resized dynamically, indexes past the end give undefined, and most methods either mutate in place or return a new array. The types add a layer that can catch some mistakes and silently allow others.

payload.explanation: Spread, slice and Array.from copy only the first level. The inner arrays are the same objects in both, so writing copy[0][0] changes the original too. Copy each level you intend to change, for example grid.map(row => [...row]), or use structuredClone for plain data. The type readonly number[][] does not protect the inner arrays; use readonly (readonly number[])[].

metadata.concept: A view needs the buffer length to be a multiple of its element size, or the constructor throws RangeError

payload.concept: A view needs the buffer length to be a multiple of its element size, or the constructor throws RangeError
payload.explanation: Each Uint32 element takes four bytes, so a six-byte buffer cannot be covered and the constructor throws RangeError. Pass an explicit length that fits, new Uint32Array(buf, 0, buf.byteLength >> 2), and handle the leftover bytes yourself. A non-zero byteOffset must also be a multiple of the element size.
payload.misconception: new Uint32Array(buf) works for any buffer length.

metadata.concept: Only a buffer created with maxByteLength can resize; a fixed buffer throws TypeError

payload.concept: Only a buffer created with maxByteLength can resize; a fixed buffer throws TypeError
payload.explanation: A normal ArrayBuffer is fixed in size. resize works only on a resizable buffer, created with new ArrayBuffer(n, { maxByteLength }), and never beyond that maximum. A typed array created with no explicit length on a resizable buffer tracks the length automatically. Otherwise, allocate a bigger buffer and copy.
payload.misconception: Any ArrayBuffer can grow with buf.resize(n).

metadata.concept: ArrayBuffer.slice copies the bytes; to change the original, write through a view over it

payload.concept: ArrayBuffer.slice copies the bytes; to change the original, write through a view over it
payload.explanation: slice returns a new buffer holding a copy of the range. Writes to the copy never reach the original. To update a region in place, create a view with an offset and length, new Uint8Array(buf, 0, 4), and write to that.
payload.misconception: Writing to buf.slice(0, 4) changes the first four bytes of buf.

TypeScript · arraybuffer · exercise · choose-the-structure · L3
Prompt: You must hand a 1 MB buffer to a worker without copying it. Compare postMessage with a transfer list, structuredClone, and SharedArrayBuffer.

payload.answer: Passing the ArrayBuffer in the transfer list of postMessage moves ownership with no copy, and the sender's buffer is detached (length 0). Without the transfer list the data is copied. A SharedArrayBuffer is shared by both threads at once, so no handover is needed, but access needs Atomics to avoid races. Choose transfer for one-way handoff, SharedArrayBuffer for concurrent access.

metadata.concept: Several views over one ArrayBuffer share the same bytes; new Uint8Array(view) copies but new Uint8Array(view.buffer) does not

payload.concept: Several views over one ArrayBuffer share the same bytes; new Uint8Array(view) copies but new Uint8Array(view.buffer) does not
payload.explanation: A view is a window onto the buffer. A second view on the same buffer sees every write. Passing a typed array to a constructor copies its elements, but passing its .buffer shares the memory (and ignores the original offset and length). Use u.slice() for an independent copy.
payload.misconception: new Uint8Array(u.buffer) makes an independent copy of u.

payload.document:
TypeScript · avltree · exercise · choose-the-structure · L4
Prompt: Compare AVL trees with red-black trees. When would you pick each?

payload.answer: AVL trees keep a stricter balance (heights differ by at most one), so lookups are faster and the height is at most about 1.44 log n, at the cost of more rotations on insert and delete. Red-black trees allow a height up to 2 log n but need fewer rotations per update. Pick AVL for read-heavy workloads and red-black for write-heavy ones.
payload.prompt: Compare AVL trees with red-black trees. When would you pick each?

metadata.concept: Delete can unbalance an ancestor far above the removed node, so rebalance after every recursive call

payload.concept: Delete can unbalance an ancestor far above the removed node, so rebalance after every recursive call
payload.explanation: Removing a node shortens one side of its ancestors, which can make a sibling side too tall by two. After the recursive removal (including the successor removal) every ancestor must be rebalanced. A delete may need several rotations along the path, where an insert needs at most one.
payload.misconception: Only inserts need rotations; a delete can only shorten a tree.

payload.explanation: When the left child is itself right-heavy (balance factor negative), a single right rotation only moves the problem to the other side. metadata.concept: The worst AVL height is about 1.44 log n, set by the sparsest valid tree, not by a perfect tree

payload.concept: The worst AVL height is about 1.44 log n, set by the sparsest valid tree, not by a perfect tree
payload.explanation: That formula is the height of a perfect tree, the best case. The tallest AVL tree is the sparsest one, where each subtree of height h has the fewest nodes: minNodes(h) = minNodes(h-1) + minNodes(h-2) + 1, a Fibonacci recurrence. The maximum height for n nodes is the largest h with minNodes(h) <= n.
payload.misconception: An AVL tree with n nodes has height floor(log2 n) + 1.

payload.concept: An iterative preorder pushes the right child first so the left child pops first

payload.misconception: Push left then right to visit left first.

payload.answer: Recursion uses the call stack, which is limited to roughly ten thousand frames in JavaScript engines. A degenerate tree, such as a linked list shaped tree with a hundred thousand nodes, throws a RangeError. An explicit stack lives on the heap and can be as deep as memory allows, and it also lets a traversal pause and resume, as an iterator does.

payload.answer: A Set is exact but stores every key. metadata.concept: A Bloom filter needs k different bit positions per item; repeating one hash makes k meaningless

payload.concept: A Bloom filter needs k different bit positions per item; repeating one hash makes k meaningless
payload.explanation: Each item sets k bits. If all k positions come from the same hash value they collapse to one bit, so the filter behaves as if k = 1 and its false positive rate is much higher than designed. Derive k positions from two independent hashes: index_i = (h1 + i * h2) mod m, with h2 made odd so that it is never zero.

metadata.concept: Inserting sorted keys one by one builds a chain; build from the sorted middle instead

payload.concept: Inserting sorted keys one by one builds a chain; build from the sorted middle instead
payload.explanation: Inserting keys in ascending order makes every new key a right child, so the tree becomes a linked list with height n - 1 and every operation is O(n). To build a balanced tree from sorted data, take the middle as the root and recurse on each half. Self-balancing trees fix this on every insert.
payload.misconception: A BST is balanced no matter what order keys are inserted in.

payload.concept: The height is about log base t of n, so a wide node keeps the tree very shallow
payload.explanation: A node with at least t children divides the keys by t at each level, so the height is at most log base t of (n + 1) / 2. With t = 50 and a million keys the height is 3 edges, not 19. Fewer levels means fewer disk reads, which is why databases use B-trees.

payload.document:
TypeScript · btree · exercise · choose-the-structure · L3
Prompt: Why do databases and file systems use B-trees instead of binary search trees?

payload.answer: Disk and network reads move whole pages, so the cost of a lookup is the number of pages read. A B-tree node is sized to fill one page and holds many keys, so the tree is very shallow (three or four levels for millions of keys) and a lookup reads few pages. A binary tree needs about log2 n levels and each is a separate read.
payload.prompt: Why do databases and file systems use B-trees instead of binary search trees?

metadata.concept: An internal node with k keys has k+1 children, so in-order traversal visits one more child after the last key

payload.concept: An internal node with k keys has k+1 children, so in-order traversal visits one more child after the last key
payload.explanation: A node with k keys has k+1 children. A loop over the keys visits the first k children; the last child is to the right of the last key and needs a separate visit after the loop. Forgetting it drops the largest keys of every internal node.
payload.misconception: Visit child i, then key i, for every key.

metadata.concept: Search checks for an equal key in every node, because keys live in internal nodes too

payload.concept: Search checks for an equal key in every node, because keys live in internal nodes too
payload.explanation: Unlike a B+ tree, a B-tree stores keys in internal nodes. After finding the first key that is not smaller than the target, check whether it is equal and stop; otherwise the search descends into the child left of that key and misses the key.
payload.misconception: Search can always descend to a leaf.

payload.explanation: The deque holds indexes whose values decrease from front to back, so the front is the maximum. The front can be an old index that has slid out of the window, and then it must be removed. Forgetting that check returns a stale maximum. Each index is pushed and popped once: O(n).

payload.document:
TypeScript · deque · exercise · choose-the-structure · L3
Prompt: Explain why a deque gives O(n) sliding window maximum and why indexes (not values) are stored.

payload.answer: The deque keeps indexes of candidate maxima in decreasing value order: the front is the current maximum. When a new value arrives, smaller values at the back can never be a maximum again and are popped. Storing indexes lets you drop the front when it falls out of the window (index <= i - k). Each index is pushed and popped at most once, so the total is O(n); recomputing the maximum for every window is O(nk).

metadata.concept: 0-1 BFS puts zero-weight neighbours at the front and must not mark a node final when it is first reached

payload.concept: 0-1 BFS puts zero-weight neighbours at the front and must not mark a node final when it is first reached
payload.explanation: With edge weights 0 and 1 a node can be reached first by a weight-1 edge and later by a cheaper path of zero-weight edges. Marking it seen on discovery freezes the worse distance. Use the distance array as the check (relax when strictly better), pushFront for weight 0 and pushBack for weight 1. Total work stays O(V + E).
payload.misconception: Marking a node seen when it is first discovered gives shortest distances.

metadata.concept: Shortest hop count needs BFS; the first path found by DFS can be much longer

payload.concept: Shortest hop count needs BFS; the first path found by DFS can be much longer
payload.explanation: BFS reaches nodes in order of distance, so the first time a node is reached is the shortest. DFS follows one branch to the end, so the first time it reaches a node may be through a long path. Use a queue for unweighted shortest paths.
payload.misconception: Any traversal that sets dist when it first reaches a node gives the shortest distance.

metadata.concept: Kosaraju runs the second pass on the transposed graph in reverse finishing order

payload.concept: Kosaraju runs the second pass on the transposed graph in reverse finishing order
payload.explanation: The first DFS records the finishing order. The second pass must run on the reversed graph, in reverse finishing order, so each search stays inside one component. Running it on the original graph leaks into every component that can be reached, which merges them.
payload.misconception: Run DFS twice on the same graph to find strongly connected components.

payload.concept: A DFS finishing order must be reversed to be a topological order; Kahn removes sources
payload.explanation: DFS finishes a node after all of its descendants, so the finishing order lists dependencies first, which is the reverse of what a schedule needs. Reverse it, or use Kahn's algorithm: repeatedly take a vertex with indegree zero. If fewer than n vertices come out, the graph has a cycle.
payload.misconception: The order in which DFS finishes nodes is a topological order.

payload.document:
TypeScript · directedgraph · exercise · choose-the-structure · L3
Prompt: How does a topological sort detect a cycle, and why does it matter for build systems?

payload.answer: Kahn's algorithm removes vertices with indegree zero one at a time. If the graph has a cycle, the vertices on the cycle never reach indegree zero, so fewer than n vertices are output. A build system needs a dependency order, so a cycle means no valid build order exists and the tool must report the cycle instead of looping.
payload.prompt: How does a topological sort detect a cycle, and why does it matter for build systems?

metadata.concept: Union by size attaches the smaller tree under the larger, keeping trees shallow

payload.concept: Union by size attaches the smaller tree under the larger, keeping trees shallow
payload.explanation: If every union attaches the first root under the second, a sequence of unions can build one long chain of depth n. Attaching the smaller tree under the larger one limits the height to log n. Track sizes at the roots and update the larger root after merging.
payload.misconception: Always attaching the first root under the second gives balanced trees.

TypeScript · disjointset · exercise · choose-the-structure · L3
Prompt: Why do path compression and union by size together make union-find nearly O(1)?

payload.document:
TypeScript · disjointset · exercise · choose-the-structure · L3
Prompt: Why do path compression and union by size together make union-find nearly O(1)?

payload.answer: Union by size keeps every tree shallow, at most log n high, because the smaller tree always goes under the larger one. Path compression flattens the path walked by each find so later finds on those nodes take one step. Together the amortised cost per operation is the inverse Ackermann function, which is at most 4 for any realistic n.
payload.prompt: Why do path compression and union by size together make union-find nearly O(1)?

metadata.concept: Path compression points every visited node at the root so later finds are nearly constant

payload.concept: Path compression points every visited node at the root so later finds are nearly constant
payload.explanation: Without compression a chain of unions can leave a path of length n, and every find walks it. Compression rewrites each node on the path to point directly at the root, flattening the tree. Combined with union by size it gives the inverse-Ackermann bound, which is practically constant.
payload.misconception: Walking to the root without compression keeps find fast.

metadata.concept: Decrement the component count only when a union really merges two different sets

payload.concept: Decrement the component count only when a union really merges two different sets
payload.explanation: A union of two elements that are already in the same set changes nothing. Counting it makes the component total too small. Return a boolean from union (true when a merge happened) and decrement the count only then.
payload.misconception: Every call to union reduces the number of components by one.

payload.concept: Detect a cycle by testing whether union merged two sets; testing connectivity after the union is always true
payload.explanation: Immediately after union the two endpoints are connected, so the check always reports a cycle. Detect the cycle before merging, or use the boolean returned by union: false means the endpoints were already connected, so the edge creates a cycle.
payload.misconception: After union(a, b), connected(a, b) tells whether the edge closed a cycle.

payload.answer: After union(a, b) the endpoints are in the same set, so connected(a, b) is always true. Check before merging, or use the boolean result of union: it returns false when the endpoints were already connected, which means the edge closes a cycle.

metadata.concept: find must follow parents all the way to the root; returning the direct parent is only correct for depth one

payload.concept: find must follow parents all the way to the root; returning the direct parent is only correct for depth one
payload.explanation: The representative of a set is its root, the element that is its own parent. After several unions an element may be several levels below the root, so a single hop returns an intermediate node and two members of one set compare as different. Loop until parent[x] === x.
payload.misconception: find(x) can return parent[x], since that is the set representative.

metadata.concept: Kruskal sorts edges by weight with a numeric comparator; the default sort orders arrays as strings

payload.concept: Kruskal sorts edges by weight with a numeric comparator; the default sort orders arrays as strings
payload.explanation: Default sort converts each edge array to a string such as "0,1,10" and compares the text, so edges are ordered by the first vertex, not by weight. Sort with (a, b) => a[2] - b[2]. Then add an edge to the tree whenever union merges two components.
payload.misconception: edges.sort() orders the edges by their last element, the weight.

payload.document:
TypeScript · doublylinkedlist · exercise · choose-the-structure · L2
Prompt: Compare a doubly linked list with a singly linked list and an array for removing a known element from the middle.

payload.answer: With a reference to the node, a doubly linked list removes it in O(1) because prev and next are available; a singly linked list needs the predecessor, found in O(n); an array shifts later elements, O(n). The doubly linked list pays an extra pointer per node and loses cache locality, so use it for LRU caches, editors and queues with arbitrary removal.
payload.prompt: Compare a doubly linked list with a singly linked list and an array for removing a known element from the middle.

metadata.concept: Inserting after a node needs four pointer updates; skipping next.prev breaks backward traversal

payload.concept: Inserting after a node needs four pointer updates; skipping next.prev breaks backward traversal
payload.explanation: Inserting after node n changes four links: new.prev = n, new.next = n.next, n.next.prev = new and n.next = new. Missing n.next.prev leaves the following node pointing back at n, so reversed traversal skips the new value. If n was the tail, the tail pointer must move.
payload.misconception: Linking the new node forward is enough for a correct list.

metadata.concept: An LRU cache pairs a hash map with a doubly linked list so reads and evictions are O(1)

payload.concept: An LRU cache pairs a hash map with a doubly linked list so reads and evictions are O(1)
payload.explanation: A Map can track recency through insertion order, but a hand-built LRU with a doubly linked list and a Map from key to node is the classic design for interviews and for languages without ordered maps. On get, unlink the node and push it to the front; on put, insert at the front and evict the tail when full. A get that does not move the node makes the cache FIFO.
payload.misconception: A Map alone gives O(1) recency updates for any key type.

payload.answer: A numeric enum has reverse mappings (Object.keys doubles) and accepts unvalidated numbers. A string enum prints readable values and is safer, but it is TypeScript-only syntax that emits runtime code. metadata.concept: Build in linear time by pushing each node into its parent; copying the array is not a tree

payload.concept: Build in linear time by pushing each node into its parent; copying the array is not a tree
payload.explanation: Each tree node holds a partial sum, so the raw array is not a valid tree. Calling add for every element costs O(n log n). A linear build puts the values at indexes 1..n, then adds each node into its parent at i + lowbit(i) once.
payload.misconception: A Fenwick tree can be created by copying the input array.

metadata.concept: The tree is 1-based internally, so a 0-based index must be shifted by one before walking

payload.concept: The tree is 1-based internally, so a 0-based index must be shifted by one before walking
payload.explanation: Index 0 has no lowest set bit, so a 1-based tree cannot store it. Public methods take a 0-based index and shift it with x = i + 1. Starting a query at i leaves out element i, and an update starting at i = 0 would loop forever because x & -x is 0.
payload.misconception: Start a query at x = i for a 0-based index i.

metadata.concept: Compress values to ranks with a numeric sort before counting inversions

payload.concept: Compress values to ranks with a numeric sort before counting inversions
payload.explanation: Counting inversions uses a Fenwick tree indexed by rank. The default sort compares strings, so 10 comes before 9 and the ranks are wrong. Sort with (x, y) => x - y, map each value to its rank, and for each element count the earlier elements with a larger rank as i minus prefix(rank).
payload.misconception: Sorting the distinct values with sort() gives their ranks.

payload.concept: x & -x isolates the lowest set bit, which is the size of the range a node covers
payload.explanation: A Fenwick node at 1-based index x stores the sum of the lowbit(x) elements ending at x. lowbit(x) is the value of the lowest set bit, computed as x & -x using two's complement. x % 2 and x & 1 only report whether the lowest bit is set, so they return 0 or 1, never 4 or 8.
payload.misconception: The lowest set bit of x can be found with x % 2 or x & 1.

metadata.concept: Setting a value means adding the difference from the stored value, not the new value

payload.concept: Setting a value means adding the difference from the stored value, not the new value
payload.explanation: A Fenwick tree stores sums, so add always accumulates. To replace a value, keep a plain array of the current values and add v minus the old value. Calling add with the new value doubles the element on a repeated set.
payload.misconception: set(i, v) can call add(i, v).

metadata.concept: An update walks up by adding the lowbit, touching every node whose range covers the index

payload.concept: An update walks up by adding the lowbit, touching every node whose range covers the index
payload.explanation: A query walks down, removing the lowest bit each step, to collect disjoint ranges. An update must reach every node whose range contains the index, which means walking up with x += x & -x. Walking down updates only the nodes below the index and later prefix sums miss the change.
payload.misconception: An update can walk down with x -= x & -x, like a query.

TypeScript · fenwicktree · exercise · choose-the-structure · L3
Prompt: When would you choose a Fenwick tree over a segment tree for range queries?

payload.answer: Choose a Fenwick tree when the operation is invertible, such as sum or xor, and the work is point updates with prefix or range queries. It uses n+1 numbers, a few lines of code and small constants. Choose a segment tree when the operation has no inverse (min, max, gcd), or when lazy range updates and range queries are both needed.

metadata.concept: Separate chaining keeps a list per bucket; storing one entry per bucket loses colliding keys

payload.concept: Separate chaining keeps a list per bucket; storing one entry per bucket loses colliding keys
payload.explanation: Two keys can hash to the same index. A bucket that holds a single entry overwrites the first key when the second arrives. Chaining keeps a list per bucket and appends to it, so colliding keys coexist and lookups scan the short chain. The expected chain length is the load factor.
payload.misconception: Writing buckets[index] = [key, value] stores every key.

metadata.concept: Delete removes one entry from its chain; clearing the chain removes the colliding keys too

payload.concept: Delete removes one entry from its chain; clearing the chain removes the colliding keys too
payload.explanation: The bucket may contain other keys that collided with it. Clearing the whole chain deletes them silently. Find the entry index with findIndex and splice that one entry, then decrement the count.
payload.misconception: Emptying the bucket removes the key.

payload.concept: A string hash must be reduced to an unsigned 32-bit value, or the bucket index can be negative
payload.explanation: The bitwise OR with 0 produces a signed 32-bit integer, which is negative for about half of long strings, and a negative number modulo the capacity is negative or zero. Use >>> 0 to keep the hash as an unsigned 32-bit value before taking the remainder. Multiplying by a small prime such as 31 spreads similar strings across buckets.
payload.misconception: h = (h * 31 + code) | 0 gives a valid bucket index after % size.

payload.misconception: Keys can be compared with == because both are hashed to the same string.

metadata.concept: Resizing must rehash every key: the bucket index depends on the capacity

payload.concept: Resizing must rehash every key: the bucket index depends on the capacity
payload.explanation: The index is hash % capacity, so a different capacity maps keys to different buckets. Copying old buckets as they are leaves keys where lookup will not look. Create the new bucket array and insert every entry again. Doubling the capacity when the load factor passes about 0.75 keeps chains short and makes insertion amortised O(1).
payload.misconception: Copying the old buckets into a larger array keeps lookups working.

payload.document:
TypeScript · hashtable · exercise · choose-the-structure · L2
Prompt: Explain load factor and why a hash table resizes by doubling and rehashing.

payload.answer: The load factor is count divided by capacity: it is the expected chain length. When it grows past about 0.75 chains get long and operations slow down. Resizing allocates a larger bucket array, typically double, and reinserts every key, because the index is hash modulo capacity and changes with the capacity. Doubling makes the cost of rehashing amortised O(1) per insertion.
payload.prompt: Explain load factor and why a hash table resizes by doubling and rehashing.

metadata.concept: put on an existing key must replace its value, not append a duplicate

payload.concept: put on an existing key must replace its value, not append a duplicate
payload.explanation: A second put for the same key adds another entry to the chain, so the count grows, the first entry is found first by get and the stale value is returned. Search the chain for the key and update it in place; only append when it is missing.
payload.misconception: Appending to the chain is enough because get finds the newest entry.

payload.concept: Heapify builds a heap in O(n) by sifting down from the last parent to the root
payload.explanation: Sift-down assumes both subtrees are already heaps, so it must run on the lowest parents first. Start at the last parent, index (n >> 1) - 1, and move toward 0. Running from 0 upward leaves deeper levels unfixed. The total work is O(n), better than n pushes at O(n log n).
payload.misconception: Sifting down from index 0 upwards builds a heap.

payload.document:
TypeScript · heap · exercise · choose-the-structure · L3
Prompt: Why is building a heap with heapify O(n) while n pushes cost O(n log n)?

payload.answer: Heapify sifts down from the last parent. Half of the nodes are leaves and need no work, a quarter sift at most one level, an eighth at most two, and so on, so the total is the sum of h * n / 2^h, which is O(n). Each push may sift up through log n levels, and there are n pushes. Use heapify when all values are known up front.
payload.prompt: Why is building a heap with heapify O(n) while n pushes cost O(n log n)?

metadata.concept: In a 0-indexed array heap the parent of i is (i - 1) >> 1 and the children are 2i + 1 and 2i + 2

payload.concept: In a 0-indexed array heap the parent of i is (i - 1) >> 1 and the children are 2i + 1 and 2i + 2
payload.explanation: Those formulas are for a 1-indexed heap that leaves slot 0 empty. A 0-indexed array uses parent = (i - 1) >> 1, left = 2i + 1, right = 2i + 2. With the 1-indexed formulas, index 2 gets parent 1 instead of 0 and the heap property is checked against the wrong node.
payload.misconception: The parent of index i is floor(i / 2) and the children are 2i and 2i + 1.

payload.explanation: The invariant is that every parent is not larger than either child (for a min-heap). A check that tests only the left child accepts arrays where the right child is smaller. Loop over all indexes i > 0 and compare with parent (i - 1) >> 1.
payload.misconception: Comparing each parent with its left child is enough to validate a heap.

metadata.concept: The running median uses a max-heap for the lower half and a min-heap for the upper half, rebalanced after each insert

payload.concept: The running median uses a max-heap for the lower half and a min-heap for the upper half, rebalanced after each insert
payload.explanation: The two halves must stay balanced (sizes differ by at most one) and ordered (every lower value is at most every upper value). Insert into the lower half, move its maximum to the upper half, and move one back if the upper half becomes larger. Without the rebalancing the median is read from the wrong heap.
payload.misconception: Pushing every number into one heap and the next into the other keeps the median available.

payload.concept: Sift-down swaps with the smaller child; always taking the left child breaks the heap
payload.explanation: The root must end up smaller than both children, so it should swap with the smaller one. Taking the left child unconditionally can put a larger value above a smaller sibling. Compare both children, pick the smaller (for a min-heap), and stop when neither is smaller than the node.
payload.misconception: After moving the last element to the root, swap it with the left child until it is smaller.

Prompt: A pop implementation always swaps the root with its left child while the left child is smaller. Explain why the heap property can break.

payload.answer: The root must become no larger than both children. If the right child is even smaller than the left one, swapping with the left leaves a larger value above a smaller sibling, so the parent-child invariant is false. payload.explanation: The new value may be smaller than several ancestors. After each swap the value sits at the parent index and must be compared with the next parent. Forgetting to update the index stops after one swap and leaves the root wrong. The loop runs at most log n times.

metadata.concept: Heap sort builds a max-heap and moves the maximum to the end; a min-heap yields descending order

payload.concept: Heap sort builds a max-heap and moves the maximum to the end; a min-heap yields descending order
payload.explanation: Each extraction moves the root to the end of the array. If the root is the smallest value the array ends up in descending order. Heap sort in place needs a max-heap: build it, then repeatedly swap the root with the last unsorted slot and sift down over the shrunken range. It runs in O(n log n) with O(1) extra space.
payload.misconception: Using a min-heap and swapping the root to the end sorts ascending.

TypeScript · interface · exercise · choose-the-structure · L2
Prompt: Compare interface and type alias for describing an object shape. When does the difference matter?

payload.answer: Both describe object shapes and are structurally compatible. An interface can be declared again to merge members (used to augment library types), supports extends with compatibility errors reported at the declaration, and shows a name in messages. A type alias can also name unions, tuples, mapped and conditional types, and cannot be redeclared. Prefer interface for public object contracts that may be extended, and type for unions and computed types.

payload.explanation: Invalid JSON, including single quotes, trailing commas and an empty string, throws SyntaxError. Wrap the call in try/catch and return a discriminated result so callers must handle failure. Parsing user input without a guard crashes the request.
payload.misconception: JSON.parse returns null or undefined for text that is not JSON.

metadata.concept: JSON.parse returns any, which switches type checking off; parse into unknown and validate

payload.concept: JSON.parse returns any, which switches type checking off; parse into unknown and validate
payload.explanation: JSON.parse is typed to return any, so the compiler accepts whatever you do with the result. A missing field gives NaN or a TypeError at run time. Assign the result to unknown, check its shape with a type guard, and only then use it. A cast (as User) does not check anything.
payload.misconception: JSON.parse(text) returns the type I declare, so p.age + 1 is checked.

metadata.concept: A reviver that converts every string to a Date also converts non-dates; match the key or the format

payload.concept: A reviver that converts every string to a Date also converts non-dates; match the key or the format
payload.explanation: The reviver is called for every value. new Date("hello") produces an Invalid Date, so a blanket reviver corrupts ordinary strings. Convert only specific keys, or strings that match a strict ISO pattern, and keep everything else unchanged.
payload.misconception: Reviving all strings that look like dates is harmless.

metadata.concept: Equal objects can stringify differently; sort keys recursively for a stable string to compare or hash

payload.concept: Equal objects can stringify differently; sort keys recursively for a stable string to compare or hash
payload.explanation: stringify writes keys in insertion order, so {a:1,b:2} and {b:2,a:1} differ. For cache keys, hashes and equality checks, produce a canonical form: sort the keys at every level. Arrays keep their order.
payload.misconception: Two objects with the same fields always produce the same JSON string.

payload.concept: Define toJSON on a class to choose exactly which fields are serialised
payload.explanation: TypeScript visibility (private, protected) is erased, so every own enumerable property is serialised, including a password. If a value has a toJSON method, stringify calls it and serialises the result instead. Return a plain object with only the safe fields.
payload.misconception: JSON.stringify includes only the fields that are public in the TypeScript class.

metadata.concept: Build a list by walking the array backwards, or prepending in forward order reverses it

payload.concept: Build a list by walking the array backwards, or prepending in forward order reverses it
payload.explanation: A singly linked list grows at the head in O(1), so each prepend puts the new value before all earlier ones. Looping forward therefore produces the reverse order. Walk the input from the end, or keep a tail pointer when appending. A ListNode<T> holds a value and a next reference that is null at the end.
payload.misconception: Prepending each element while looping forward keeps the original order.

metadata.concept: Floyd cycle detection must move the pointers before comparing them

payload.concept: Floyd cycle detection must move the pointers before comparing them
payload.explanation: Both pointers start at the head, so comparing them before moving always succeeds for any list with at least two nodes. Move first (slow one step, fast two) and then compare. A list with no cycle ends when fast or fast.next becomes null, in O(n) time and O(1) space.
payload.misconception: Comparing slow and fast at the top of the loop detects a cycle.

metadata.concept: Merging two sorted lists needs a dummy head and must attach the remaining nodes at the end

payload.concept: Merging two sorted lists needs a dummy head and must attach the remaining nodes at the end
payload.explanation: When one list is exhausted, the other still holds its largest values. Forgetting to attach the remainder truncates the result. Use a dummy head to avoid special-casing the first node and finish with tail.next = a ?? b.
payload.misconception: The merge loop is finished when one list runs out.

metadata.concept: Slow and fast pointers find the middle; the loop condition decides which middle an even list returns

payload.concept: Slow and fast pointers find the middle; the loop condition decides which middle an even list returns
payload.explanation: The slow pointer moves one step while fast moves two. For [1, 2, 3, 4] the loop condition fast && fast.next ends with slow on 3 (second middle). The condition fast.next && fast.next.next ends on 2 (first middle). Decide which middle the problem wants before writing the condition.
payload.misconception: Stopping when fast.next is null returns the second middle of an even list.

metadata.concept: Delete with a dummy head: it handles removing the first node and does not skip the node after a deletion

payload.concept: Delete with a dummy head: it handles removing the first node and does not skip the node after a deletion
payload.explanation: Looking ahead from the head never examines the head itself, so a matching first node stays. Advancing cur after a deletion also skips the next node, so consecutive matches survive. A dummy node before the head removes the special case, and cur advances only when nothing was deleted.
payload.misconception: Looking one node ahead (cur.next) is enough to delete any value.

payload.document:
TypeScript · linkedlist · exercise · choose-the-structure · L2
Prompt: Explain why deleting nodes from a singly linked list is easier with a dummy head, and when you should not advance the cursor.

payload.answer: A dummy node before the head means the node being removed always has a predecessor, so deleting the first node is the same as any other. Advance the cursor only when no deletion happened; after cur.next = cur.next.next the new next node has not been examined yet, so advancing would skip consecutive matches.

metadata.concept: Reverse in place by saving next before redirecting the pointer

payload.concept: Reverse in place by saving next before redirecting the pointer
payload.explanation: After cur.next = prev, cur.next no longer points forward, so advancing through it walks backwards and the loop ends after one step. Save next first, redirect, then advance with the saved reference. The three pointers prev, cur and next make the reversal O(n) time and O(1) space.
payload.misconception: Setting cur.next = prev and then moving to cur.next walks the original list.

TypeScript · map · exercise · choose-the-structure · L3
Prompt: Design an LRU cache with O(1) get and set in TypeScript. Which structure do you use, and how do you track recency and evict?

payload.answer: Use a Map<K, V>. It looks up in O(1) and iterates in insertion order. On get, delete the key and set it again so it becomes newest. On set, delete then set, and if size exceeds capacity delete the first key from map.keys().next().value. An object cannot guarantee order for integer-like keys, and an array makes recency updates O(n).

TypeScript · queue · exercise · choose-the-structure · L3
Prompt: Why does breadth-first search use a queue, and how do you separate the levels?

payload.answer: BFS visits nodes in order of distance from the start, which is first in, first out: nodes discovered earlier are processed earlier. To separate levels, record the queue length at the start of each iteration and process exactly that many nodes, collecting their values in a row. Use an index-based queue or a linked list to avoid the O(n) cost of Array.shift on big inputs.

metadata.concept: Without compaction an index-based queue never frees consumed slots

payload.concept: Without compaction an index-based queue never frees consumed slots
payload.explanation: Consumed slots stay in the array, so a long-running queue grows without bound even when it holds one element. Compact the array when the head passes half the length (slice from head and reset to 0); the cost is amortised O(1) per operation.
payload.misconception: Advancing the head index frees memory for consumed items.

metadata.concept: A queue with a head index is O(1) per dequeue, but size must subtract the head offset

payload.concept: A queue with a head index is O(1) per dequeue, but size must subtract the head offset
payload.explanation: Array.shift is O(n) because every element moves. A head index avoids that: dequeue reads items[head] and advances. The live length is then items.length - head, not items.length. Counting consumed slots makes isEmpty false forever. Mnemonist (npm) has a Queue class with the same operations.
payload.misconception: The size of an index-based queue is items.length.

payload.concept: A ring buffer needs a count (or a spare slot) to tell a full buffer from an empty one
payload.explanation: In a circular array, head and tail are equal both when it is empty and when it is full after tail wraps. Without a separate count the two cases are indistinguishable. Keep an explicit count; enqueue fails (or overwrites) when count equals capacity.
payload.misconception: head === tail means the ring buffer is empty.

metadata.concept: A queue from two stacks moves items only when the output stack is empty

payload.concept: A queue from two stacks moves items only when the output stack is empty
payload.explanation: Items are pushed on an input stack and popped from an output stack. Transferring reverses their order once. If you transfer on every dequeue, items already in the output stack end up beneath newer ones, so the order breaks. Transfer only when the output stack is empty; each element moves at most once, giving amortised O(1).
payload.misconception: Moving all items to the output stack on every dequeue keeps FIFO order.

TypeScript · record · exercise · choose-the-structure · L2
Prompt: You map each event type to a handler. Compare a switch statement, Record<string, Handler> and Record<EventType, Handler>.

payload.answer: Record<EventType, Handler> is best when the types are a fixed union: the compiler requires an entry for every member, the lookup is O(1) and always defined, and adding a type to the union flags missing handlers. Record<string, Handler> accepts any key and can return undefined. A switch is verbose but can be made exhaustive with assertNever. Use a Map for keys known only at run time.

payload.explanation: The result type is { [k: string]: V }, so assigning it to Record<"a" | "b", V> is error TS2739 (missing properties). Cast after you know all keys are present, or build the record with a typed loop that checks every key.

metadata.concept: Record<"a" | "b", V> requires every key of the union; a missing key is error TS2741

payload.concept: Record<"a" | "b", V> requires every key of the union; a missing key is error TS2741
payload.example_bad: const scoresB: Record<"a" | "b", number> = { a: 1 };
payload.explanation: Record<K, V> with a union K means every member must be present. Omitting one is error TS2741 ("property is missing"). Use Partial<Record<K, V>> when keys are optional, or Record<string, V> when keys are dynamic.
payload.misconception: A Record over a union of keys can leave some keys out.

metadata.concept: Record<number, V> still has string keys at run time; Object.keys gives strings

payload.misconception: Object.keys of a Record<number, string> returns numbers.

payload.explanation: Red-black trees need three things: a black root, no red node with a red child, and the same number of black nodes on every path from a node to a leaf. metadata.concept: Every insert fixes the path with three checks in order: lean left, balance, split

payload.concept: Every insert fixes the path with three checks in order: lean left, balance, split
payload.explanation: A new red node can create a right-leaning red link, two reds in a row on the left, or two red children. A left-leaning tree repairs them in order: rotate left when only the right child is red, rotate right when two left links are red, and flip when both children are red. Omitting the first check leaves red right links.
payload.misconception: Only the red-red case needs fixing after an insert.

payload.document:
TypeScript · redblacktree · exercise · choose-the-structure · L4
Prompt: Why do red-black trees guarantee O(log n) height?

payload.answer: Two rules give the bound. Every path from a node to a leaf has the same number of black nodes, and no red node has a red child. So the shortest path has only black nodes and the longest alternates black and red, which is at most twice as long. With n nodes the black height is at most log2(n + 1), so the height is at most 2 log2(n + 1).
payload.prompt: Why do red-black trees guarantee O(log n) height?

metadata.concept: A colour flip toggles the parent and both children, which splits a temporary 4-node

payload.concept: A colour flip toggles the parent and both children, which splits a temporary 4-node
payload.explanation: A node with two red children represents a temporary 4-node. Flipping turns both children black and the parent red, which sends the extra red link up one level without changing any black height. Toggling only the children changes the black height of the paths below and breaks the invariant.
payload.misconception: A flip toggles the two children only.

payload.concept: Colour rules cap the height at 2 log2(n + 1); an unbalanced insert gives a chain
payload.explanation: The colours only help if the fix-up runs. Because every path has the same number of black nodes and no path has two reds in a row, the longest path is at most twice the shortest, so the height is at most 2 log2(n + 1). Plain insertion of sorted keys with no fix-up builds a chain of height n.

metadata.concept: Quantifiers are greedy: .+ takes as much as possible; use .+? or a negated class to stop early

payload.concept: Quantifiers are greedy: .+ takes as much as possible; use .+? or a negated class to stop early
payload.explanation: A greedy .+ consumes up to the last > on the line, so two adjacent tags become one match. Use the lazy form .+? or a negated class [^>]+ to stop at the first >. Nested quantifiers such as (a+)+ can also backtrack catastrophically; prefer simple, anchored patterns for untrusted input.
payload.misconception: /<.+>/g finds each HTML tag separately.

metadata.concept: String.match returns RegExpMatchArray | null; indexing the result without a check is error TS2531

payload.concept: String.match returns RegExpMatchArray | null; indexing the result without a check is error TS2531
payload.explanation: match returns null when nothing matches, and the compiler types it as RegExpMatchArray | null. Reading [0] directly is error TS2531 ("Object is possibly null"). Use optional chaining with a default, or test the result first. Do not silence it with !, which fails at runtime on the first non-matching input.
payload.misconception: str.match(re)[0] is safe whenever the pattern looks likely to match.

payload.concept: Lazy propagation pushes pending range adds to the children before a query descends
payload.explanation: A range add that covers a node completely updates only that node and stores a pending tag for its children. A later query that descends below this node must push the tag down first, or the children still hold the old sums. Skipping the push gives stale results.

metadata.concept: A recursive segment tree needs an array of 4n slots; 2n is not enough when n is not a power of two

payload.concept: A recursive segment tree needs an array of 4n slots; 2n is not enough when n is not a power of two
payload.explanation: A recursive tree with children at 2*node and 2*node+1 leaves gaps when n is not a power of two, so node numbers can pass 2n. For n = 6 the highest node used is 13, which is past 12. Allocating 4n is always enough. An iterative bottom-up tree can use exactly 2n because it uses a different layout.
payload.misconception: A segment tree over n items fits in 2n slots.

metadata.concept: A point update must recompute every ancestor on the way back up

payload.concept: A point update must recompute every ancestor on the way back up
payload.explanation: Ancestors store combined values. After changing a leaf, each node on the path to the root must be recomputed from its children, which the recursion does after returning. Updating the leaf only leaves stale sums in every ancestor, so any query that uses an ancestor is wrong.
payload.misconception: Writing the new value in the leaf is enough.

metadata.concept: union, intersection and difference return new Sets; hand-written loops often mutate an input

payload.concept: union, intersection and difference return new Sets; hand-written loops often mutate an input
payload.explanation: Deleting during iteration is legal, but it changes the input set, which surprises callers. The ES2025 methods a.union(b), a.intersection(b), a.difference(b) and a.symmetricDifference(b) return new Sets and leave both inputs alone. Check the runtime supports them (Node 22 does).
payload.misconception: Removing items from a while iterating is a safe way to compute the intersection with b.

TypeScript · set · exercise · choose-the-structure · L1
Prompt: You must check whether any of 1,000,000 ids has already been seen, many times. Compare an array with includes and a Set.

payload.answer: Use a Set. has is O(1) on average, so each check is constant time; array includes is O(n), so repeated checks cost O(n squared). A Set also drops duplicates, keeps insertion order and has a size property. Use an array only when you need index access or duplicates.

payload.concept: isSubsetOf tests membership of every element; comparing sizes is not a subset test
payload.explanation: A smaller set need not be contained in the larger one. Use a.isSubsetOf(b), isSupersetOf or isDisjointFrom. Two sets are equal when their sizes match and one is a subset of the other.

payload.concept: To keep the first item for each key, track seen keys in a Set; a Map built from pairs keeps the last

metadata.concept: Use Atomics.add for a counter shared between threads; i[0]++ is a separate read and write that can lose updates

payload.concept: Use Atomics.add for a counter shared between threads; i[0]++ is a separate read and write that can lose updates
payload.explanation: A plain increment reads the value, adds one and writes it back. Two threads can read the same value and both write it plus one, so an update is lost. Atomics.add performs the whole operation indivisibly and returns the previous value. The plain version is wrong only sometimes, which is what makes it dangerous.
payload.misconception: i[0]++ on a shared Int32Array is safe because it is one statement.

payload.document:
TypeScript · sharedarraybuffer · exercise · choose-the-structure · L3
Prompt: Compare transferring an ArrayBuffer and sharing a SharedArrayBuffer between a main thread and workers. When do you pick each?

payload.answer: Transfer moves ownership of one ArrayBuffer to the receiver with no copy and detaches it on the sender, so only one thread uses it at a time and no synchronisation is needed. SharedArrayBuffer lets several threads read and write the same memory at once, which needs Atomics for counters, flags and locks. Choose transfer for pipelines and handoff, SharedArrayBuffer for concurrent shared state, and note that browsers require cross-origin isolation for SharedArrayBuffer.

metadata.concept: A growable SharedArrayBuffer can only grow, never shrink; grow below the current size throws RangeError

payload.concept: A growable SharedArrayBuffer can only grow, never shrink; grow below the current size throws RangeError
payload.explanation: grow(n) requires the buffer to be created with maxByteLength, and n must be at least the current byteLength and at most the maximum. Shrinking throws RangeError. Existing views with no fixed length follow the new size.
payload.misconception: A growable SharedArrayBuffer can be resized to any size up to its maximum.

metadata.concept: Atomics works only on integer typed arrays; a Float64Array is error TS2769

payload.concept: Atomics works only on integer typed arrays; a Float64Array is error TS2769
payload.explanation: Atomics operations are defined for Int8, Uint8, Int16, Uint16, Int32, Uint32, BigInt64 and BigUint64 arrays. Float arrays and Uint8ClampedArray are rejected by the compiler (TS2769) and throw TypeError at run time. For floats, store an integer representation or use a lock.
payload.misconception: Atomics.add works on any typed array over a SharedArrayBuffer.

payload.explanation: When the minimum element is popped, the previous minimum is lost if only one variable is kept. Keep a second stack that records the minimum at every depth, or store pairs (value, minSoFar). Both give O(1) push, pop and getMin.

metadata.concept: A monotonic stack finds the next greater element; use while, not if, when popping smaller values

payload.concept: A monotonic stack finds the next greater element; use while, not if, when popping smaller values
payload.explanation: A new value can be greater than several stack entries, and each of them has just found its answer. Using if pops only one, leaving unresolved entries behind and producing wrong answers. The while loop pops every smaller value, so each index is pushed and popped once: O(n).
payload.misconception: Popping one smaller value per new element is enough.

TypeScript · stack · exercise · choose-the-structure · L3
Prompt: Explain how a monotonic stack finds the next greater element for every position in O(n), and why the inner loop is while rather than if.

payload.answer: Scan left to right keeping a stack of indexes whose next greater value is not yet known, in decreasing order of value. For each new value, pop while the top value is smaller and record the new value as their answer, then push the current index. A new value may resolve several entries, so a while loop is required. Each index is pushed and popped at most once, so the total work is O(n).

payload.explanation: A single counter accepts "([)]" because the counts match, but the nesting is wrong. A stack remembers the order of open brackets: on a closer, the top of the stack must be the matching opener. The string is balanced only if the stack is empty at the end.
payload.misconception: Counting opening and closing brackets is enough to validate nesting.

payload.explanation: Words share their prefixes, which is the point of a trie. Insert must look for an existing child first and create one only when it is missing. TypeScript · trie · exercise · choose-the-structure · L3
Prompt: When is a trie a better choice than a Set of strings?

payload.answer: Use a trie when queries are about prefixes: startsWith, autocomplete, longest common prefix and wildcard matching, because the shared prefix path answers them without scanning every word. A Set answers only exact membership in O(L) and would need a scan of all words for prefix queries. A trie costs more memory per character, so prefer a Set when only exact lookups are needed.

payload.misconception: Follow single-child nodes to find the longest common prefix.

TypeScript · tuple · exercise · choose-the-structure · L2
Prompt: A function returns a start and an end position. Compare returning a tuple, an object and a two-element array.

payload.answer: A tuple [start, end] is compact and checked by position, good for short, obvious pairs, and destructuring gives local names. An object { start, end } names its fields, so callers cannot swap them silently and it is easier to extend. A plain number[] loses the length and position checks. Prefer an object when there are more than two values or the order is not obvious.

metadata.concept: Optional and rest elements make a tuple flexible, but an optional element can be undefined

payload.concept: Optional and rest elements make a tuple flexible, but an optional element can be undefined
payload.explanation: The ? marks an element that may be missing, so its type is number | undefined, and arithmetic on it is error TS2532. A rest element ([number, ...string[]]) allows any number of trailing items. Handle the optional case with ?? or a check.
payload.misconception: In [string, number?] the second element is always a number.

metadata.concept: TypeScript allows push on a tuple, so the runtime length can differ from the type; return a new tuple instead

payload.concept: TypeScript allows push on a tuple, so the runtime length can differ from the type; return a new tuple instead
payload.explanation: Methods such as push, pop and splice are still available on a mutable tuple and the compiler does not track them. After t.push(3) the value has three elements while its type says two. Treat tuples as immutable: declare them readonly, or build a new tuple with spread and an explicit return type.
payload.misconception: A [number, number] tuple cannot grow, because its length is part of the type.

metadata.concept: Conditional types distribute over unions; wrap both sides in a tuple to stop distribution

payload.example_good:
type ToArray<T> = [T] extends [unknown] ? T[] : never;
const mixed: ToArray<string | number> = ["a", 1];
payload.explanation: A conditional type on a naked type parameter applies to each union member, so ToArray<string | number> is string[] | number[], and a mixed array is error TS2322. Wrapping the check in [T] extends [unknown] disables distribution and gives (string | number)[].

payload.answer: Use Uint8ClampedArray. It clamps values above 255 to 255 and below 0 to 0 and rounds, so brightening does not wrap around to dark. A Uint8Array wraps modulo 256, turning 300 into 44. Canvas ImageData uses Uint8ClampedArray for this reason.

A typed array is a fixed-length array of one numeric type, stored in an ArrayBuffer. There are eleven concrete classes: Int8Array, Uint8Array, Uint8ClampedArray, Int16Array, Uint16Array, Int32Array, Uint32Array, Float32Array, Float64Array, BigInt64Array and BigUint64Array. They share one API, but the element type changes the range and the rounding.

payload.document:
TypeScript · undirectedgraph · exercise · choose-the-structure · L3
Prompt: When is an adjacency list better than an adjacency matrix for an undirected graph?

payload.answer: An adjacency list uses O(V + E) space and visits only real neighbours, so it is better for sparse graphs, where E is far below V squared, and for traversals. An adjacency matrix uses O(V squared) space but answers "is there an edge between u and v" in O(1), so it suits dense graphs and algorithms that probe arbitrary pairs.
payload.prompt: When is an adjacency list better than an adjacency matrix for an undirected graph?

metadata.concept: An undirected edge is stored in both neighbour sets, and a Set ignores duplicates

payload.concept: An undirected edge is stored in both neighbour sets, and a Set ignores duplicates
payload.explanation: An undirected edge connects u and v both ways. Storing it once makes hasEdge(v, u) false and traversals from v miss the edge. Add both ends. Using a Set per vertex also makes repeated addEdge calls harmless.
payload.misconception: Adding v to the neighbours of u is enough.

metadata.concept: The edge count is half the sum of degrees, with each self-loop added back once

payload.concept: The edge count is half the sum of degrees, with each self-loop added back once
payload.explanation: Each ordinary edge appears in two neighbour sets, so halving the sum works. A self-loop appears once in its own set, so the halved sum is fractional. Add the number of loops to the sum before halving, which counts each loop as degree two.
payload.misconception: edges = sum of neighbour counts / 2.

metadata.concept: Cache results per object in a WeakMap so cached entries do not keep the objects alive

payload.concept: Cache results per object in a WeakMap so cached entries do not keep the objects alive
payload.explanation: A Map holds strong references to its keys, so every object ever cached stays in memory for the life of the cache. A WeakMap holds keys weakly: when the object is otherwise unreachable, its entry can be collected. The trade-off is that a WeakMap cannot be listed, counted or cleared.
payload.misconception: A Map keyed by object is an equivalent cache.

Prompt: You cache an expensive computation per DOM-like node object. Compare a Map and a WeakMap, and say when each is the right choice.

payload.document:
TypeScript · weakmap · exercise · choose-the-structure · L2
Prompt: You cache an expensive computation per DOM-like node object. Compare a Map and a WeakMap, and say when each is the right choice.

payload.answer: Use a WeakMap when entries should live only as long as the key object: it holds keys weakly, so the cache does not prevent garbage collection and needs no cleanup. Use a Map when you must list, count or clear entries, or when keys are primitives. A Map keyed by objects leaks them until you delete the entry.
payload.prompt: You cache an expensive computation per DOM-like node object. Compare a Map and a WeakMap, and say when each is the right choice.

metadata.concept: A WeakMap has no size, keys or forEach; track counts yourself or use a Map

payload.concept: A WeakMap has no size, keys or forEach; track counts yourself or use a Map
payload.explanation: Entries can disappear whenever the garbage collector runs, so the API hides them: only get, set, has and delete exist. Reading size is error TS2339 and undefined at runtime. If you need to list or count entries, use a Map and manage removal yourself.
payload.misconception: A WeakMap can be listed and counted like a Map.

metadata.concept: Keep private per-object data in a WeakMap instead of adding a property that shows up in keys and JSON

payload.concept: Keep private per-object data in a WeakMap instead of adding a property that shows up in keys and JSON
payload.explanation: A property added to an object is enumerable: it appears in Object.keys, spread copies and JSON.stringify, so it can leak. A module-level WeakMap keyed by the object stores the secret outside the object, is dropped with it when collected, and works on frozen objects.
payload.misconception: Adding a hidden field to an object keeps it out of serialised output.

payload.misconception: V - 1 rounds of relaxation are enough, and the result is always valid.

payload.answer: Use Dijkstra for a single source with non-negative weights: O(E log V) with a heap. Use Bellman-Ford for a single source when weights can be negative, because it also detects negative cycles, at O(V E). Use Floyd-Warshall for all pairs on small dense graphs at O(V cubed), or run Dijkstra from every vertex on sparse graphs with non-negative weights.
