Go modules, packages, and dependency versions

A Go package is the unit named by a package clause and used through imports; a module is a versioned collection of one or more related packages. A repository may contain one or more modules, though a single root module is a common layout. The module path declared in go.mod is both the module's identity for Go tooling and the prefix used in package import paths.

Use `go mod init <module-path>` to create go.mod. It records the module path, the Go version declaration, and dependency requirements and other module directives. `go get` changes dependency requirements; `go mod tidy` reconciles requirements with packages used by the module. The precise effect of commands can vary by Go release, so consult that release's command documentation before automating dependency updates.

A package name is not itself the full import path. Files in one package directory normally share a package clause, while imported package paths identify packages within modules. Identifiers beginning with an upper-case Unicode letter are exported from their package; lower-case identifiers are package-private.

Common debugging sequence: check the current directory and `go env GOMOD`; inspect go.mod and go.sum; run `go list ./...` to surface package and dependency resolution issues; then use `go mod tidy` only when you intend to reconcile module requirements. Do not treat a repository, module, and package as interchangeable terms.

Go slices: length, capacity, and shared storage

A slice describes a contiguous segment of an underlying array. Its length is the number of elements visible through that slice; its capacity measures how far the slice can be extended within the associated array. A slice is not the array itself. Slicing or assigning a slice can produce values that share the same underlying array, so writes through one view may be observable through another when their ranges overlap.

`append` returns a slice value. If the existing capacity is sufficient, the appended elements can use the same underlying array; if not, append may allocate a different array. Code must use the returned slice and must not rely on whether storage was reused. To make an independent copy of elements, allocate a destination and use `copy`, or use an appropriate `slices.Clone` where available in the project's Go version.

This sharing has practical consequences: a short subslice can keep a larger backing array reachable, and mutating a subslice can change elements seen in another alias. Copy when independent ownership is needed. Do not infer allocation behavior from a particular run or compiler implementation.

The Go specification defines slice semantics; implementation representation details are not a language-level guarantee.

Go interfaces and error handling

A Go interface specifies a type set. For ordinary value interfaces, a concrete type satisfies an interface implicitly when its method set meets the interface's requirements; no declaration on the concrete type is required. This supports small interfaces at the point where behavior is consumed.

An interface value can be understood conceptually as holding a dynamic type and a dynamic value. An interface compares equal to nil only when it has no dynamic type and no dynamic value. Therefore, returning a typed nil pointer as an `error` can produce a non-nil error interface. Prefer returning a literal `nil` on success and construct an error only on failure.

Errors are values implementing the built-in `error` interface. Callers should usually test or wrap errors according to the contract of the operation. Use `errors.Is` or `errors.As` when the wrapped error chain and sentinel/type identity matter; string matching is brittle. Add context with `%w` when the caller should be able to inspect the underlying error, and use `%v` when you deliberately do not expose that relationship.

Go 1.18 added type parameters and constraint interfaces. Interfaces containing type terms such as `~int` or unions are constraints and are not ordinary runtime value types. Check the language version and specification for the constructs in use.

Go concurrency: goroutines, channels, and shared memory

A goroutine is a concurrently executing function. Starting one does not by itself make shared-memory access safe. A data race occurs when goroutines access the same memory concurrently and at least one access is a write, unless the accesses are properly synchronized or atomic under the Go memory model.

Use channels to communicate values or coordinate ownership, and use synchronization primitives such as `sync.Mutex`, `sync.RWMutex`, `sync.WaitGroup`, or `sync/atomic` when they fit the shared-state design. A channel send/receive or mutex operation establishes synchronization only according to the memory model's specified rules; merely starting a goroutine or sleeping is not a reliable synchronization strategy.

Pass `context.Context` explicitly to operations that need cancellation or deadlines. Cancellation is a signal; each goroutine and blocking operation must cooperate by observing the context or another documented shutdown signal. A caller returning does not automatically stop goroutines it started.

Run `go test -race ./...` during development to help detect races in exercised paths. The race detector is dynamic evidence, not a proof that all interleavings are race-free. Avoid promises about goroutine scheduling order unless your program explicitly synchronizes it.

C# projects and the .NET SDK

Modern .NET projects use MSBuild project files such as `.csproj`. An SDK-style project names an SDK, commonly `Microsoft.NET.Sdk`; the SDK supplies build targets and tasks and provides defaults for common source and resource items. The `dotnet` CLI invokes SDK functionality, while the .NET runtime executes applications. These are related components but are not synonyms.

The target framework declared by a project determines the API surface and runtime target; the installed SDK version is a separate selection. A project can target a framework different from the SDK's version, subject to installed targeting packs and supported tooling. Use `dotnet --info` to inspect installed SDKs and runtimes, `dotnet build` to compile, and `dotnet test` to run configured tests.

SDK defaults can include source files by globbing. Explicitly adding a file already included by a default glob can cause duplicate-item errors. Inspect evaluated MSBuild properties and items when project behavior differs from the visible project file; `dotnet msbuild -preprocess` can show imported project content.

Keep SDK, target framework, and language version distinctions clear when explaining a compiler diagnostic. Project templates and defaults change across .NET releases, so state the target framework when behavior depends on it.

C# nullable reference types: annotations and analysis

C# nullable reference types let source express whether a reference is intended to be possibly null and let the compiler issue warnings based on static flow analysis. `string` and `string?` annotations communicate different intent when nullable analysis is enabled. They do not create distinct runtime reference types, insert automatic null checks, or guarantee that a value cannot be null.

The nullable context has separate annotation and warning settings and can be configured in source with directives or in project settings such as `<Nullable>enable</Nullable>`. Defaults depend on project/template and compiler context; inspect the effective setting instead of assuming all projects enable it.

A warning is a prompt to inspect the flow and contract. Use a runtime guard when a boundary must reject null, and use `?` when null is a valid part of the API contract. The null-forgiving operator suppresses a warning at a point; it does not validate the value.

When documenting an API, state both the intended null contract and the compiler configuration. Nullable annotations improve static analysis but are not a substitute for runtime validation of external input.

C# asynchronous methods with async and await

The `async` modifier allows `await` expressions in a method or lambda and shapes how its result is represented, commonly as `Task`, `Task<T>`, or `ValueTask` forms. `await` asynchronously waits for an awaitable operation to complete and then continues the method; it does not mean that the awaited work necessarily runs on a new thread. I/O operations may complete without occupying a thread for their entire wait, while CPU-bound work requires an explicit scheduling decision if it must run elsewhere.

Exceptions from an awaited task are observed at the await point. If a method returns a task without awaiting it, the caller may observe faults through that returned task, but local try/catch blocks around the task creation do not catch a later asynchronous failure unless the operation is awaited or otherwise observed there.

Cancellation is cooperative. Pass a `CancellationToken` to APIs that support it and honor it in your own long-running operations. Calling `Cancel` requests cancellation; it does not forcibly terminate arbitrary code.

Avoid blocking asynchronous code with `.Wait()` or `.Result` when an asynchronous call chain can be used. Blocking can waste threads and can cause deadlocks in some synchronization contexts. The exact scheduling behavior depends on the awaited operation and runtime context; do not promise a particular thread switch.

C# deterministic resource disposal

The `using` statement and `using` declaration arrange for a disposable object to be disposed when control leaves the relevant scope, including when control exits through an exception or return. Synchronous disposal uses `IDisposable.Dispose`; `await using` is for asynchronous disposal through `IAsyncDisposable.DisposeAsync`. The compiler implements the cleanup guarantee with try/finally-like behavior.

Disposal is distinct from garbage collection. Garbage collection manages memory reachability; it does not provide a deterministic time for releasing files, sockets, database handles, or other external resources. After disposal, do not continue using the object unless its contract explicitly permits it.

If a method receives an object it does not own, it should not dispose it unless ownership is explicitly transferred by the API contract. For resources acquired locally, scope disposal as narrowly as practical. Async disposal must itself be awaited when required.

Compiler diagnostics can help distinguish a type that supports `IDisposable` from one that supports `IAsyncDisposable`. Framework and API ownership conventions vary, so follow the specific API's contract.

Java packages and modules: separate organization and access controls

A package groups related top-level types and gives them a namespace. A module can group packages and declares dependencies on other modules. In a named module, `requires` declares a dependency and `exports` makes a package available to code in other modules. A public class in a package that the module does not export is not generally accessible to ordinary code outside that module.

This means Java access checks can involve more than the `public` modifier: inspect the type's member access, its package, and whether its containing module exports that package. `opens` is about reflective access and should not be treated as a synonym for `exports`. The module declaration is conventionally stored in `module-info.java`.

When diagnosing “package is not visible” or module resolution errors, verify the module path and `requires` directives, then check the package's export/open directives. When diagnosing a traditional classpath application, first establish whether it is running as named or unnamed modules; not every project needs an explicit module descriptor.

Module behavior is specified by the Java Language Specification and Java runtime module system. Build-tool configuration affects how those modules are compiled and launched, so state the JDK and build setup when giving commands.

Java resource lifetime and try-with-resources

Objects that own external resources such as files, streams, or sockets often expose `AutoCloseable` or `Closeable`. A try-with-resources statement closes each declared resource when control leaves the statement, including exceptional exits. Declare multiple resources in the header when they are acquired together; they are closed in reverse declaration order.

If the body throws and closing also throws, the body exception remains the primary exception and close failures are recorded as suppressed exceptions. This avoids the common `finally` pattern where a cleanup exception accidentally hides the original failure. Suppressed failures can be inspected with `Throwable.getSuppressed()`.

Try-with-resources manages a resource's close protocol; it does not imply that every object needs closing, nor does it replace ownership documentation. Close resources your code owns or whose API contract assigns cleanup to you. Avoid using a resource after it has been closed.

The core language feature is available since Java SE 7. When a question depends on specific library behavior or language changes, check the target JDK documentation.

Java Stream API: lazy pipelines and safe behavior

A stream is a computation pipeline over a source, not a collection that stores elements. Intermediate operations such as `filter` and `map` are lazy; the source is traversed when a terminal operation such as `collect`, `count`, or `reduce` begins. After a terminal operation, the stream is consumed and should not be reused. Obtain another stream from the source for another traversal.

Behavioral functions should not interfere with a non-concurrent source, and should usually be stateless. Mutating the list being streamed can yield incorrect behavior or exceptions. Side effects in pipeline functions are risky, especially for parallel streams: execution order and thread can vary, and an implementation may elide work when the result is unaffected. Prefer a reduction or collector over mutating an external accumulator.

Parallel streams do not make arbitrary code thread-safe and are not automatically faster. Consider source size, splitting, operation cost, shared state, ordering requirements, and the execution environment. Measure with a representative workload before choosing parallel execution.

Streams are single-use abstractions; their exact optimizations are implementation choices constrained by the API contract. Consult the Java SE version targeted by the application for available operations and behavior.

Java concurrency: tasks, executors, and lifecycle

An `Executor` separates task submission from the mechanism that runs a task; the interface does not require that execution be asynchronous. `ExecutorService` adds task tracking and lifecycle operations. Submitting a `Runnable` or `Callable` can return a `Future` that represents completion and, for a result-bearing task, its value or failure.

An executor has an ownership lifecycle. `shutdown()` stops accepting new tasks while allowing submitted tasks to complete; `shutdownNow()` attempts to stop active work and returns tasks that have not started. It does not forcibly terminate code that ignores interruption. Applications should define who owns the executor, how it is shut down, and how task failures and cancellation are observed.

Do not create an unbounded number of threads or assume a particular executor scheduling order. Select an execution policy according to workload, resource limits, latency goals, and the JDK version. Newer Java releases include virtual-thread APIs; they change the cost model for thread-per-task designs but do not remove the need to bound scarce downstream resources.

Use documented synchronization and task completion boundaries to coordinate shared state. A `Future.get()` retrieves completion and establishes the API's stated memory-consistency relationship; unsynchronized shared mutation remains unsafe.

JavaScript promises, async functions, and error flow

A Promise represents the eventual fulfillment or rejection of an asynchronous operation. Calling `.then()` schedules its reaction as a microtask; it is not called synchronously just because the promise is already fulfilled. Promise reactions run after the current JavaScript job completes, according to the host's event-loop rules. A timer callback is a different kind of queued task, so do not infer that `setTimeout(fn, 0)` runs before promise reactions.

An `async` function always returns a Promise. `await` pauses that async function's continuation until the awaited value settles; it does not block the whole JavaScript agent. A rejected awaited promise throws at the `await` expression and can be handled with `try/catch`, or by handling the returned promise. A missing `return` or missing rejection handler can cause a failure to be lost from the caller's expected error path.

Sequential awaits express dependency between operations. For independent operations, `Promise.all` can start/await them together, but it rejects when an input rejects and does not automatically cancel the remaining operations. Cancellation must be supported by the underlying API, often through an `AbortSignal`.

Browser and Node.js hosts provide different APIs and event-loop details. The language-level promise rules are shared, but scheduling specifics and available cancellation/IO APIs should be stated for the actual host.

JavaScript modules: exports, resolution, and loading

ES modules use `export` to expose bindings and `import` to consume them. Static imports are resolved and linked as part of module loading before the importing module's body runs. Named exports and default exports have different import syntax; use the form that matches the declaration. Imported bindings are live read-only views of the exported binding, not ordinary copied local variables.

Module resolution is host-defined. Browsers resolve URL-like specifiers relative to the importing module and generally require a supported URL or import-map mapping; Node.js has its own resolution rules and package conventions. A relative import that works in one host or bundler may fail in another. Include file extensions and package configuration according to the target host's rules.

Dynamic `import()` returns a Promise for a module namespace object and is useful when code should load conditionally. It has asynchronous failure behavior, so handle rejection. Cyclic imports are supported but can expose uninitialized bindings during evaluation; reduce surprising cycles when module initialization order matters.

A script must be loaded as a module by the host (for example, with `type=module` in HTML) for browser static import syntax. Treat bundler conveniences as tooling behavior, not universal JavaScript language behavior.

Generics invariance and bounded wildcards
Baseline: Java SE 21; JUnit 5 API concepts

`List<Integer>` is not a subtype of `List<Number>`: otherwise a consumer could insert a Double into an Integer list. A producer view `List<? extends Number>` lets the caller read Number values but prevents adding arbitrary non-null elements. A consumer view `List<? super Integer>` accepts Integer values, but reads expose Object because the actual element type might be Object. Use a type parameter when multiple arguments or a result must share a type relationship. Type erasure means runtime checks cannot generally distinguish parameterizations such as List<String> and List<Integer>. Raw types discard static guarantees and can move a failure to a later cast. Diagnose compiler errors by writing the required read/write operations before choosing a wildcard; adding unchecked casts usually hides the mismatch.

Checked exceptions must be caught or declared, while RuntimeException and Error subclasses follow different compiler rules. Choose an exception contract that exposes a failure the caller can act on. Catching Exception and continuing with a success result can conceal corruption or incomplete work. Thread interruption is a cooperative signal; code that catches InterruptedException should either propagate it or, when propagation is impossible, normally restore the interrupt flag with `Thread.currentThread().interrupt()` and stop the interrupted operation. Cleanup belongs in a finally block or a resource protocol. A cancellation request cannot guarantee that arbitrary blocking/native operations terminate immediately. Separate retryable failure, invalid input, cancellation and programming defects instead of treating every exception as the same outcome.

Baseline: Java SE 21; JUnit 5 API concepts

Java 21 virtual threads support blocking task-per-thread designs with a much smaller scheduling cost than dedicating an operating-system thread to every task. They do not accelerate CPU-bound work or remove database, memory and remote-service limits. Use bounded admission or a semaphore to constrain a scarce dependency, rather than pooling virtual threads merely to reduce their number. Shared mutable objects still require synchronization. Lifecycle, cancellation and failure propagation remain explicit design responsibilities. Diagnose throughput by measuring the bottleneck and resource saturation before changing thread type. Advice about monitor pinning and particular runtime scheduling behavior must identify the JDK release, because those details evolve after Java 21.

`thenApply` transforms a successful value; `thenCompose` flattens a transformation that itself returns a CompletionStage. `thenCombine` combines independent results. Async variants schedule work through an executor; non-async continuations can run in a completing or caller thread, so do not rely on an unstated thread identity. `handle` observes success or failure and produces a new outcome, while `whenComplete` is intended for observing the existing outcome subject to its exception rules. `orTimeout` changes future completion; it does not establish that the underlying I/O was cancelled. Observe terminal failures and define executor ownership. CompletableFuture cancellation also does not supply a general mechanism to interrupt the underlying computation; consult the API contract before promising that cancelled work has stopped.

For a multi-statement invariant, disable auto-commit, commit only after all steps succeed, and roll back on failure. Use parameterized PreparedStatements for data values; concatenating untrusted values into SQL creates injection risk. Bind parameters cannot substitute arbitrary table names or SQL syntax, which require an allowlist. Close ResultSet, Statement and owned Connection resources with try-with-resources. Pooled connection close usually returns the connection to a pool rather than destroying the physical connection; restore required state according to the pool's contract. TreeMap and TreeSet use their ordering to determine key equivalence, so an ordering inconsistent with equals can produce behavior surprising to callers expecting the general Map/Set equality contract. Big-O claims belong to a specific implementation and operation: a Collection interface alone does not promise ArrayList indexing or HashMap lookup cost. Check both route-level and resource/ownership authorization where needed. Store passwords with an appropriate adaptive password encoder rather than reversible encryption or plain hashes. Baseline: Python 3.13; CPython details identified explicitly

Python binds arguments to parameter names according to positional, keyword, positional-only and keyword-only rules. A default expression is evaluated when the function definition executes, rather than on every call. A mutable default list can therefore retain mutations between calls; use None plus per-call construction when a fresh container is intended. Arguments bind object references to local names. Rebinding the local name does not replace the caller's binding, while mutating a shared object can be visible to the caller. Copying a container shallowly does not duplicate its nested mutable members. Diagnose mutation bugs by drawing the object-sharing relationships instead of describing Python as universally pass-by-reference or pass-by-value in the C sense.

Iterators generators and exhaustion
Baseline: Python 3.13; CPython details identified explicitly

An iterable supplies an iterator through iter; an iterator supplies successive values through next and raises StopIteration at exhaustion. A generator function returns a generator when called and resumes its body at each iteration. It does not eagerly compute and store all yielded results. Iterators are commonly single-pass; calling list on an exhausted iterator does not repeat its original computation. If two consumers must traverse independently, create independent iterators from a reusable source or deliberately materialize the data, accounting for memory. Resource-owning generators need explicit lifecycle care when iteration stops early. Distinguish generator laziness from async iteration, which uses separate protocols and can suspend on asynchronous operations.

Baseline: Python 3.13; CPython details identified explicitly

The with statement enters a context manager, runs its body and calls the exit protocol on both normal and exceptional paths after a successful entry. An exit method can suppress an exception by returning a true value, so suppression must be intentional and narrow. A contextlib.contextmanager generator normally yields exactly once; put resource release in finally so errors in the body still trigger cleanup. Cleanup failure can itself affect exception propagation. Use `raise ... from ...` when an API translates a failure while preserving causal context. Catch the specific expected failure and avoid hiding unrelated programming errors with a bare except. Do not rely on CPython reference counting as the portable resource-release mechanism.

Python type hints support static tools and documentation; runtime data from JSON, a database or a network still needs validation. Baseline: Python 3.13; CPython details identified explicitly

Calling an async def function produces a coroutine object; scheduling or awaiting it drives its execution. Asyncio normally runs tasks cooperatively on an event-loop thread: a task permits other work when it suspends at a suitable await. A blocking file or network call, or a long CPU loop, can stall that loop. Use an async API, an appropriate executor/thread helper for blocking I/O, or a process strategy for CPU work according to the workload. Cancellation is requested and delivered at cooperative suspension points. Keep cleanup in finally and do not swallow CancelledError without a deliberate structured-concurrency reason. TaskGroup coordinates child task lifetime and failures; detached tasks require explicit ownership and error observation.

Multiplication that wraps before malloc receives the size can allocate a buffer smaller than the later writes require. Use a temporary pointer for realloc so failure does not overwrite the only reference to the old block. realloc's size-zero details vary by C revision and implementation; handle zero explicitly instead of relying on them. Baseline: ISO C++20; C++17 and C++23 differences identified explicitly

An object's lifetime is separate from the lifetime of a pointer, reference or view that names it. RAII ties resource cleanup to an owning object's destruction, including stack unwinding. Prefer standard owners such as vector and unique_ptr to manual new/delete when they express the intended ownership. string_view and span are non-owning; they can dangle when the underlying storage is destroyed or reallocated. Returning a view into a local string is invalid even though returning the view object itself is allowed. A reference extending one temporary's lifetime does not generally extend every temporary transitively. Baseline: ISO C++20; C++17 and C++23 differences identified explicitly

std::move is a cast that enables move-aware overload resolution; it does not itself transfer storage or ensure the chosen operation is cheap. A moved-from standard-library object is generally valid but in an unspecified state unless the type's contract says more. Assign or destroy it safely, and do not assume it is empty. RAII owners simplify exception paths, but a compound operation still needs an explicit guarantee: no effects on failure, preserved invariants with changed state, or merely no resource leak. noexcept influences exception behavior and container implementation choices. Avoid an unchecked noexcept promise on an operation that can throw, because an escaping exception then terminates the program.

A vector growth that reallocates invalidates pointers, references and iterators to its elements; reserving capacity changes that condition but does not make all later operations harmless. An erased element's iterator is invalid regardless of remaining capacity. Ordered containers and sorting require a suitable strict weak ordering; subtracting integer keys to implement a comparator can overflow and violate the contract. Complexity claims must include comparator cost and distinguish average, amortized and worst-case guarantees. A node-based container's stable addresses do not imply superior cache behavior or constant-time search. A trait bound constrains supported behavior, while a lifetime bound constrains how long referenced data must remain valid in that context. Baseline: Rust 2021 edition core concepts; compiler and crate versions recorded per project

Calling an async function creates a Future representing suspended computation; it must be polled to make progress. An executor schedules polling, while the operating-system/runtime I/O integration wakes tasks when work may proceed. A future is not inherently a dedicated thread, and a blocking call within a task can block its executor thread. Pin expresses restrictions on moving a pinned value relevant to self-referential future implementations; it is not a general claim that all async variables must be heap-allocated. Dropping a future cancels further polling of that future, but does not necessarily undo effects or stop independently spawned/background operations. RefCell checks borrow conflicts at runtime and can panic; it does not make an object thread-safe. Mutex coordinates access across threads according to its contract. Rc provides single-threaded shared ownership, while Arc provides atomic reference counting; Arc does not make its contained value automatically safe for concurrent mutation. Send concerns transferring ownership between threads, and Sync concerns safe sharing through references. These traits propagate according to type composition and unsafe contracts. Goroutine stacks can grow under runtime control but still have limits; Go promises no universal safe recursion depth. Negative remainder normalization must avoid an intermediate overflow, so prefer a branch after taking a remainder when the domain permits it. Complexity claims about maps are implementation-sensitive; include hashing/key size and avoid deriving a language guarantee from one runtime benchmark.

Baseline: C# 12 and .NET 8 conceptual baseline; newer API support checked per target

A variable of value type contains a value, while a reference-type variable holds a reference to an object. Passing an argument normally copies that variable's value: a copied reference can still name the same mutable object. ref/out/in alter parameter passing under their own rules. A struct containing a reference can share the referenced object after the struct is copied. Record classes provide generated value-oriented equality over their defined components, while ordinary classes generally retain reference identity unless equality is overridden. A record is not recursively immutable merely because its declaration is concise or uses init accessors. Choose equality and mutation contracts explicitly before using objects as keys.

LINQ deferred repeated and provider execution
Baseline: C# 12 and .NET 8 conceptual baseline; newer API support checked per target

Many LINQ-to-Objects operators create deferred sequences: work happens when the result is enumerated. Enumerating again can repeat computation and side effects, and it may observe changed source data. ToList materializes a snapshot of the sequence's current elements at the cost of allocation and traversal; it does not recursively clone those elements. Some terminal operations execute immediately, and operators such as sorting must buffer before producing results. IQueryable delegates query interpretation to a provider whose supported translations and database behavior differ from ordinary in-memory delegates. Inspect generated SQL for database performance. LINQ is not categorically slow or fast; identify the operators, data size, provider and number of enumerations before assessing cost.

Cancellation tokens locks and asynchronous ownership
Baseline: C# 12 and .NET 8 conceptual baseline; newer API support checked per target

CancellationToken communicates a cooperative request. Pass it to supporting I/O APIs and observe it in long-running work; cancelling a source does not forcibly terminate arbitrary code or undo committed work. Task represents an operation, not a guarantee of a dedicated thread. Protect shared invariants with an appropriate synchronization abstraction. Ordinary lock does not support awaiting inside its body; an async-compatible gate such as SemaphoreSlim can be appropriate when its acquisition/release and cancellation paths are correct. Avoid holding a resource longer than the operation needs it, and dispose owned token sources and asynchronous resources according to their contracts. Preserve ownership of child tasks so failures are observed and shutdown can wait appropriately.

Baseline: C# 12 and .NET 8 conceptual baseline; newer API support checked per target

Overflow behavior depends on numeric type and checked/unchecked context; checked contexts apply lexically and do not automatically change arithmetic inside a called method. A larger destination type does not repair a narrower overflowing intermediate expression. Decimal and floating-point types have different ranges, precision and exception behavior. C# string indexing counts UTF-16 code units, so an index is not necessarily a Unicode code point or visible grapheme. Stack size and available recursion depth depend on runtime/thread environment. Baseline: WHATWG HTML living standard; support claims require browser/assistive-technology baseline

HTML elements have content models and attribute-specific rules; a tag catalogue alone cannot explain valid nesting or interaction. A button inside a form defaults to submit behavior unless its type/association specifies otherwise. Boolean attributes are true by presence, so disabled="false" still represents presence rather than a false boolean. Content attributes and live DOM properties can diverge: an input's current value is not always the same as its initial value attribute. A browser parser may repair invalid markup, making the resulting DOM differ from the source indentation. Inspect the parsed tree and the element's normative definition when diagnosing a form or nesting issue instead of assuming the browser preserved the source literally.

Cascade layers specificity inheritance and values
Baseline: CSS modules; cascade layers as specified in Cascade Level 5; browser baseline required

The cascade resolves competing declarations using origin/importance, layer ordering and other cascade criteria before specificity and order decide eligible ties. A more specific selector does not override a declaration that wins at an earlier cascade criterion. Normal unlayered author declarations outrank normal layered author declarations; important layer ordering is reversed, so document the layer strategy rather than assuming all important rules behave like normal rules. Inheritance supplies values for inherited properties when appropriate and is distinct from a selector directly matching an element. Declared, cascaded, specified, computed, used and actual values describe different stages; a percentage's computed representation need not be its eventual pixel size.

Percentage sizing needs a relevant containing-block reference and cannot always be reduced using the nearest parent's visible size. Flex and grid items have automatic minimum-size behavior that can prevent expected shrinking; setting min-width:0 is useful only when that is the intended constraint. Grid minmax and track sizing interact with intrinsic content, while flex distribution follows its own algorithm. Algorithm invariants preconditions and complexity
Baseline: Language-neutral contracts; language-specific adaptation included by the builder

An algorithm reference should state the input domain, the maintained invariant, why every transition preserves it, how the algorithm terminates and why the result satisfies the postcondition. For binary search, sortedness and a consistent ordering are preconditions; a loop invariant about the remaining interval explains why eliminating one side is valid. Count the cost of comparisons, hashing, copying and arithmetic representation rather than only loop iterations. Distinguish worst-case, average and amortized bounds. Include empty input, duplicates, numeric overflow and Unicode representation where relevant. Language translation must preserve these contracts even when containers, integer types and ownership differ. A plausible implementation or passing example is weaker evidence than an explicit invariant argument.

Primary sources:
https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-006-introduction-to-algorithms-fall-2011/resources/mit6_006f11_lec02/

Language adaptation (java): Apply this contract through explicit interfaces or ordinary functions as appropriate; identify collection, comparator and resource-owner types in Java examples.

Traversal discovery state and partial failure
Baseline: Language-neutral contracts; language-specific adaptation included by the builder

Breadth-first traversal should mark a vertex as discovered when it is enqueued if the queue-capacity argument assumes each vertex enters once. Marking only on removal can enqueue duplicates from multiple predecessors. An adjacency-list traversal has O(V+E) work only under explicit representation and per-edge operation assumptions; input validation, allocation and language-level hashing can add costs. Define behavior for disconnected vertices, self-loops, parallel edges and invalid IDs. For graph mutation, distinguish a fully committed change from a partially constructed representation and preserve the documented invariant on failure. The C adjacency insertion replacement in this dataset uses allocate-before-publish to preserve a two-sided undirected representation on allocation failure.

document:
Dynamic programming state transition and representation
Baseline: Language-neutral contracts; language-specific adaptation included by the builder

A DP state denotes a subproblem, and its key must contain every variable that changes the result. Define base cases, recurrence and dependency order before choosing top-down memoization or bottom-up tabulation. A zero value may be a valid result and cannot automatically mean uncomputed. Shared nested mutable arrays can corrupt independent states even when the mathematical recurrence is correct. Account for table size, transition cost, numeric growth and any retained reconstruction information. Memory optimization is valid only when overwritten states are no longer needed. Language-specific recursion limits, integer representation and container ownership are implementation constraints that must be reconciled with the language-neutral recurrence.

Factory builder and dependency construction choices
Baseline: Language-neutral contracts; language-specific adaptation included by the builder

A factory centralizes object construction when callers should depend on an abstraction rather than select concrete constructors. A builder assembles a value through a controlled sequence when many optional settings or staged validation would make a constructor hard to use. They solve different construction pressures and can be combined, but neither is required for every class. State which invariants hold before and after construction and who owns created resources. A simple function or named constructor may be clearer than a class hierarchy in languages with lightweight functions. Avoid using patterns to hide required dependencies or defer invalid state until first use; make configuration and construction failure visible at the boundary.

Factory builder and dependency construction choices
Baseline: Language-neutral contracts; language-specific adaptation included by the builder

A factory centralizes object construction when callers should depend on an abstraction rather than select concrete constructors. A builder assembles a value through a controlled sequence when many optional settings or staged validation would make a constructor hard to use. They solve different construction pressures and can be combined, but neither is required for every class. State which invariants hold before and after construction and who owns created resources. A simple function or named constructor may be clearer than a class hierarchy in languages with lightweight functions. Avoid using patterns to hide required dependencies or defer invalid state until first use; make configuration and construction failure visible at the boundary.

Adapter decorator and facade boundaries
Baseline: Language-neutral contracts; language-specific adaptation included by the builder

An adapter translates one interface into another expected by a caller. A decorator preserves an interface while adding behavior around delegated operations. A facade presents a simpler entry point to a larger subsystem. These are distinct changes to the public contract, not interchangeable names for every wrapper. A wrapper must preserve relevant failure, cancellation, ownership and ordering guarantees; silently swallowing an exception or caching a mutable result can change semantics. Prefer composition when independently combining concerns, and keep the underlying resource's disposal/close responsibility explicit. In a structural-typing language, a small object or function may implement the needed contract without a large nominal hierarchy.

Primary sources:
https://docs.python.org/3.13/library/functools.html#functools.wraps
https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/java/io/FilterInputStream.html

Language adaptation (java): Apply this contract through explicit interfaces or ordinary functions as appropriate; identify collection, comparator and resource-owner types in Java examples.

document:
Observer subscriptions event delivery and cleanup
Baseline: Language-neutral contracts; language-specific adaptation included by the builder

Observer connects a publisher with interested subscribers while reducing direct knowledge of each consumer. Specify whether delivery is synchronous or queued, whether order matters, what happens when a listener fails and how unsubscribe works. A publisher retaining callbacks can keep subscriber objects reachable after their visual or request lifecycle ends. Weak references can fit some designs but do not replace an explicit lifecycle contract. Avoid assuming every event is delivered exactly once or that observers cannot reenter the publisher. For distributed delivery, retries, duplication and idempotency require additional protocol design beyond the in-process pattern. Test behavior under listener removal, failure and reentrant modification according to the chosen contract.

Primary sources:
https://dom.spec.whatwg.org/#interface-eventtarget

Language adaptation (java): Apply this contract through explicit interfaces or ordinary functions as appropriate; identify collection, comparator and resource-owner types in Java examples.

Command state strategy and iterator responsibilities
Baseline: Language-neutral contracts; language-specific adaptation included by the builder

A command represents an operation as a value for deferred execution, logging or queuing; undo requires stored information and an explicit inverse contract rather than coming for free. State represents behavior that changes with an object's lifecycle state, while strategy supplies an interchangeable algorithm chosen by a caller or context. An iterator exposes traversal without promising independent ownership, repeatability or safe mutation of the source. Match the pattern to the reason behavior varies. First-class functions, tagged unions and native iteration protocols often express these responsibilities more directly than a class hierarchy. Include failure, cancellation and resource lifetime in the chosen abstraction's interface.

Primary sources:
https://docs.python.org/3.13/library/collections.abc.html
https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/iter/trait.Iterator.html

Baseline: Language-neutral contracts; language-specific adaptation included by the builder

A command represents an operation as a value for deferred execution, logging or queuing; undo requires stored information and an explicit inverse contract rather than coming for free. State represents behavior that changes with an object's lifecycle state, while strategy supplies an interchangeable algorithm chosen by a caller or context. An iterator exposes traversal without promising independent ownership, repeatability or safe mutation of the source. Match the pattern to the reason behavior varies. First-class functions, tagged unions and native iteration protocols often express these responsibilities more directly than a class hierarchy. Include failure, cancellation and resource lifetime in the chosen abstraction's interface.

document:
Composite structures cycles and ownership
Baseline: Language-neutral contracts; language-specific adaptation included by the builder

Composite gives leaf and container objects a compatible interface so callers can operate on a tree uniformly. The tree assumption is part of the contract: shared children or cycles change traversal, deletion and aggregation behavior. If cycles are allowed, use a graph model and track visited state rather than recursively assuming every edge descends toward a leaf. Define whether a child has one owner, multiple references or a parent pointer, and how removal affects its lifetime. Uniformity should not force meaningless operations onto leaves. Language ownership tools can enforce some relationships, but an interface alone does not prove acyclicity, bounded recursion depth or correct aggregate results.

Primary sources:
https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.desktop/java/awt/Container.html

Language adaptation (java): Apply this contract through explicit interfaces or ordinary functions as appropriate; identify collection, comparator and resource-owner types in Java examples.

document:
css reference — Boxes, normal flow and positioning

### The box model and intrinsic sizing

The content box is surrounded by padding, border and margin. With content-box, declared width describes content; with border-box it includes padding and border. Margin remains outside both. Minimum and maximum sizes constrain preferred sizes, and intrinsic contributions constrain layout even when percentages or flexible tracks are used. Set border-box consistently on elements and pseudo-elements rather than assuming it is inherited automatically.

```css
*, *::before, *::after { box-sizing: border-box; }
img, video { max-inline-size: 100%; block-size: auto; }
.prose { max-inline-size: 70ch; overflow-wrap: anywhere; }
```

`width: 100%` plus padding can overflow under content-box. `min-inline-size: 0` can allow a flex or grid child to shrink below its automatic minimum; it should be applied to the actual constrained child, not scattered through the whole application. `overflow-wrap: anywhere` affects intrinsic sizing differently from legacy break-word behavior. A fixed height is rarely a good answer to varying text, translation or zoom.

Margins can be negative and vertical margins can collapse in ordinary block flow under defined conditions. Padding cannot be negative and does not collapse. A new block formatting context, including flow-root, changes float interaction and margin behavior. Inline formatting has line boxes and baselines; vertical margins on non-replaced inline boxes do not create block spacing. Replaced elements have intrinsic dimensions and aspect ratios. Tables and ruby have specialized rules.

Logical properties express block/inline directions from writing-mode and direction. Use margin-inline-start, padding-block, inline-size and inset-inline-end where the intention is logical. Top/right/bottom/left remain physical. If physical and logical declarations map to the same side, cascade and mapping determine the result; writing both is not automatically a useful fallback.

document:
css reference — Boxes, normal flow and positioning

### Display, overflow and hiding

Display has outer and inner behavior: block versus inline participation, and flow/flex/grid/table layout within. `inline-flex` is inline outside and flex inside. Display none removes boxes; visibility hidden generally retains layout space; opacity zero still allows focus and hit testing unless other state changes intervene. `content-visibility` can skip rendering work subject to containment, and requires care around intrinsic sizes and offscreen content. `display: contents` removes the principal box but has accessibility and context-specific consequences; test rather than assuming it preserves all semantics identically.

Overflow visible, hidden, clip, scroll and auto differ in clipping and scroll-container behavior. Hidden can still allow programmatic scrolling; clip does not establish the same scroll container. Changing one overflow axis can change computed behavior of the other. A sticky element can attach to an unexpected scrolling ancestor. Reserve necessary scrollbar space with scrollbar-gutter where supported. Do not hide overflow simply to conceal a layout bug or crop focus indicators.

document:
css reference — Boxes, normal flow and positioning

### Positioning and paint order

Static participates in normal flow. Relative retains its place and offsets its box. Absolute is removed from normal flow and positions against a containing block determined by layout rules. Fixed is often viewport-relative, but transformed or containing ancestors can establish another containing block. Sticky participates in flow until constrained by the relevant scroll container and inset; it needs room to move. Insets, opposing constraints, auto margins and intrinsic sizing interact differently for each positioning mode.

A stacking context isolates descendant z-index ordering. Positioned elements with non-auto z-index, certain flex/grid items, opacity, transforms, isolation and other effects can create contexts. A child with z-index 9999 cannot escape its ancestor's stacking context. The browser top layer used by native dialogs and popovers is a different mechanism. Transform changes visual geometry and can create containing blocks without changing the normal-flow allocation.

```css
.page-header { position: sticky; inset-block-start: 0; z-index: 10; background: #fff; }
.anchor-target { scroll-margin-block-start: 6rem; }
.badge-host { position: relative; }
.badge-host .badge { position: absolute; inset-block-start: 0.5rem; inset-inline-end: 0.5rem; }
```

Use this badge pattern only when the badge does not obscure content at zoom or remove meaningful information from source order. Practice: identify every scroll container and stacking context before changing a sticky header's z-index.

Source: https://drafts.csswg.org/css-box-4/
Source: https://drafts.csswg.org/css-display-4/
Source: https://drafts.csswg.org/css-position-3/

document:
css reference — Flexbox in depth

## 5 Flexbox in depth

Flexbox distributes items along one main axis, with an orthogonal cross axis. Direction maps row/column through writing mode; row-reverse changes visual order, not DOM reading order. Flex-wrap creates independent lines. A wrapped flex layout is not a two-dimensional grid with aligned tracks across rows.

The container controls display, flex-direction, flex-wrap, justify-content, align-items, align-content and gap. `flex-flow` combines direction and wrapping. Justify-content distributes main-axis free space after flex sizing and auto margins; align-items supplies cross-axis alignment defaults; align-self overrides an item; align-content distributes multiple lines when there is cross-axis free space. Gap creates gutters between items and lines, not outer container padding.

The item controls order, flex-grow, flex-shrink, flex-basis, align-self and its minimum/maximum sizes. Flex basis supplies the initial main-size input; auto can take the main-size property or content sizing. Grow factors distribute positive free space, not a direct percentage width. Shrink factors are weighted by flex base sizes, so equal shrink factors do not necessarily remove equal pixels. Constraints freeze items during the algorithm; inspect the resulting sizes rather than relying on a one-step ratio.

`flex: 1` commonly expands to grow 1, shrink 1 and a zero-percent basis in browsers; specification expansion details matter when the container's size is indefinite. Use explicit `flex: 1 1 0` when that basis is intended. `flex: auto` means 1 1 auto; `flex: none` means 0 0 auto. Automatic minimum sizes can prevent shrinking long tokens. An auto margin can absorb free space before alignment distribution, making it useful for pushing an action group to the end.

```css
.toolbar { display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; align-items: center; gap: 0.75rem; }
.toolbar__title { margin: 0; flex: 1 1 16rem; min-inline-size: 0; }
.toolbar__actions { display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; gap: 0.5rem; margin-inline-start: auto; }
```

Real use cases: toolbars, wrapping action groups, media objects, one-dimensional navigation, and a page shell with flexible main content. Avoid flex order for a logical sequence that differs between keyboard and visual traversal. Align-items stretch does not force identical heights if item constraints prevent it. Percentage flex bases, min-content and aspect ratio can interact in surprising ways.

Practice: build three cards with long URLs and different text lengths. Measure widths before and after min-inline-size:0. Explain why gap is still present when justify-content changes and why align-content may have no visible effect on a single line.

Source: https://drafts.csswg.org/css-flexbox-1/

document:
css reference — Responsive design, typography and visual systems

### Typography and internationalization

Choose a robust font stack with a generic fallback. Font-family, size, weight, style, stretch/width, line-height and variant features describe different dimensions. Variable-font axis settings are low-level; prefer high-level properties when they express the requirement. Optical sizing depends on the font and feature. Font display is an @font-face descriptor, not an element property. Font loading can change metrics and cause layout shifts; reserve space where appropriate and use a deliberate fallback strategy.

Unitless line-height scales with the descendant's own font size when inherited. A computed length may inherit as that length. Letter-spacing and word-spacing affect text fit and can impair scripts if applied indiscriminately. Use real language metadata for hyphenation and language-sensitive line breaking. White-space, white-space-collapse, text-wrap and overflow-wrap solve different problems. Text-overflow:ellipsis needs a constrained box and appropriate overflow/white-space behavior; it does not expose the missing content to every user.

Support text resizing, 320 CSS-pixel reflow where applicable, user text spacing and long translations. Horizontal scrolling can be appropriate for a code region or data table, but should not become page-wide scrolling for ordinary content. Direction and writing-mode change logical axes, not the text's language. Do not use bidi controls or visual order to falsify meaningful reading order.

document:
css reference — Responsive design, typography and visual systems

### Color, surfaces and states

Create semantic tokens for ink, surfaces, borders, focus, success, warning and error. A palette name alone does not establish contrast. WCAG AA normally requires 4.5:1 for ordinary text and 3:1 for qualifying large text; relevant non-text component boundaries and indicators generally need 3:1 under the applicable criterion. Disabled/inactive controls have exceptions, but must still be understandable. Alpha colors must be evaluated after compositing against actual surfaces. Color contrast tools for sRGB are not enough to reason blindly about every wide-gamut composition.

Use color-scheme to communicate supported native-control modes when the page actually supports them. prefers-color-scheme can provide an initial choice; an explicit user choice should persist according to product policy. Test both schemes. In forced-colors mode, system colors and user-agent adjustments may override authored paint; avoid disabling forced-color-adjust without a strong, tested reason.

Backgrounds can be layered; the first image is painted above later images and color is below them. Each layer can have independent origin, clip, size, repeat, position and attachment; the background shorthand's slash separates position and size. Border-radius shapes corners but does not replace clipping rules. Box-shadow and outline are not layout space. Filters, blending and backdrop filters can produce expensive rendering and unexpected contrast; maintain a clear fallback.

css reference — CSS architecture and production debugging

## 8 CSS architecture and production debugging

A stylesheet needs ownership rules. Tokens describe shared decisions; base styles cover low-specificity semantic defaults; components own local appearance; utilities express intentional single-purpose overrides; state belongs to actual DOM/API state. BEM is one naming convention, CSS Modules provide build-time naming isolation, and Shadow DOM provides tree-scoped styling. None removes the need for accessible markup or a clear theme contract.

Use cascade layers to make override order explicit. A reset should be small and understood; a universal all:unset reset can remove useful native behavior. Keep selectors shallow and stable. Avoid binding styles to incidental DOM depth or database IDs. Scope tokens: public component custom properties are an API, while internal variables can be private by convention but remain observable CSS. Document default values, valid types, inheritance and fallback behavior.

Adopt a spacing scale and semantic color system, but do not generate every possible class and variant. Keep layout primitives reusable: stack, cluster, switcher and grid are compositions of standard layout rules rather than magic framework features. Separate content-specific exceptions from shared primitives so a one-off page fix does not change every card.

Build pipeline: pin compiler and framework versions; resolve modules; compile Sass; apply the chosen CSS transformations and prefix strategy; minify; generate source maps according to deployment policy; hash assets; and verify the actual shipped CSS. A Sass compiler does not automatically add vendor prefixes. A prefixer does not polyfill Grid, container queries or a JavaScript API. CSS purging must understand dynamically generated class names and state selectors; test the production bundle rather than only development output.

Debug a failure through six observations: authored source, matched rules, winning declarations, computed/resolved values, layout geometry and actual interaction. In performance work, measure style recalculation, layout, paint and compositing. Reading geometry after writing style can force synchronous layout; collect reads, compute once and batch writes. A requestAnimationFrame callback alone does not eliminate forced layout if it alternates reads and writes internally.

Acceptance exercises: diagnose a selector defeated by an unlayered framework; locate an automatic minimum causing overflow; repair focus clipped by overflow; compare live state to a stale attribute; explain a transform-created fixed containing block; and remove a DOM-order mismatch introduced with Grid placement. For each exercise, include a deliberately broken variant and an observable test that fails before the repair.

sass reference — Sass modules, built-ins and scalable architecture

### Built-in module map

- `sass:math`: numerical bounds, rounding, trigonometry, logarithms, random values, unit inspection and compatible-unit operations. Random compile-time values produce unstable output unless deliberately controlled outside Sass; avoid them for deterministic design tokens.
- `sass:color`: color-space-aware channel inspection, adjustment, scaling, mixing and conversion. Distinguish an absolute channel change from proportional scaling and verify rendered contrast.
- `sass:string`: quoting/unquoting, insertion, slicing, replacement through composition, indexing and identifiers. Sass indexing conventions differ from JavaScript's zero-based string APIs; inspect the specific function contract.
- `sass:list`: length, nth, set-nth, append, join, zip, index, separator and bracket inspection. A list's comma/space/slash separator affects emitted CSS.
- `sass:map`: get, has-key, keys, values, merge, remove, set and nested map operations, including deep operations where provided. Merging a map does not update derived maps that were already computed elsewhere.
- `sass:selector`: append, nest, extend, replace, unify, parse and superselector checks. Selector values are structured Sass lists; string concatenation is not a substitute for unification.
- `sass:meta`: type inspection, inspect, feature/tool introspection, function/mixin lookup and invocation, module member discovery and load-css. load-css emits CSS; it does not replace a clear @use public API or create access to private members.

The appendix enumerates the public function and mixin names exposed by the installed compiler, grouped by module. Signatures and version behavior belong to the linked official module documentation. This prevents claiming that a remembered function list is complete while omitting newer APIs.

Source: https://sass-lang.com/documentation/modules/

### Migration, compatibility and code quality

Sass @import and global built-in functions were deprecated beginning with Dart Sass 1.80.0. New application modules should use @use/@forward and namespaced built-ins. Bootstrap 5.3 still uses the older import architecture, so its integration is a deliberate compatibility exception. A mechanical replacement of @import with @use can break shared scope, configurable variables and map ordering. Keep that exception at the vendor boundary and plan the migration against the upstream framework version.

Other migration concerns include slash division, color function changes, mixed declarations after nested rules, the legacy JavaScript API, invalid combinators, stricter argument handling and changes to conditional function syntax. Use @if for clear control flow rather than writing new examples around a deprecated legacy if() function. Preserve plain CSS functions when the browser should evaluate them. Run the official Sass migrator on a reviewable branch and inspect compiled diffs; a successful migration command does not prove unchanged design behavior.

Production checks: compile every entry point; test functions against invalid units and types; compare expanded CSS snapshots for deliberate output changes; enforce a selector-depth and output-size budget; verify source-map policy; render component states; and run accessibility checks in the final CSS build. Separate owned-code warnings from upstream dependency warnings. Record which warnings remain and why. Do not silently suppress a warning merely to call a build pristine.

bootstrap reference — Bootstrap 5 ecosystem and layout

### What the framework provides

Bootstrap 5 combines Reboot defaults, typography/content styles, a responsive Flexbox grid, utilities, helpers, forms, components and optional JavaScript plugins. It is utility-rich and component-oriented; calling it purely utility-first hides the component selectors and runtime plugins that are central to the system. Bootstrap Icons is a separate project. Bootstrap 5 does not require jQuery. The bundled JavaScript includes Popper for components that need positioning; the non-bundle build needs the required dependency supplied separately.

Pin CSS and JavaScript to the same version. The integrated lab uses local files from bootstrap@5.3.8, avoiding a live CDN dependency. If using a CDN in a product, verify the exact URL and integrity hash together, include the appropriate crossorigin setting and define the application's CSP. An integrity hash from a different version breaks loading. A framework stylesheet does not supply HTML labels, meaningful content, server validation or a screen-reader-tested interaction by itself.

Load exactly one owner for each interactive component. Do not load both a bundled UMD file and an independently bundled copy of the same plugins. Framework data APIs and a React/Vue state layer can conflict if both mutate the same classes, attributes or children. Either let Bootstrap own its documented component lifecycle through a wrapper, or use a framework-native implementation with compatible styling and an explicitly different API.

Source: https://getbootstrap.com/docs/5.3/getting-started/introduction/

bootstrap reference — Bootstrap 5 ecosystem and layout

### Breakpoints and containers

The default tiers are xs below 576px, sm from 576px, md from 768px, lg from 992px, xl from 1200px and xxl from 1400px. There is no xs infix: `.col-6` starts at the smallest tier. Most min-width responsive classes continue applying at larger widths until overridden. Breakpoints are configuration, not device detection.

`.container` provides width 100% with responsive max-widths: 540, 720, 960, 1140 and 1320px from sm through xxl. `.container-fluid` remains 100% wide. `.container-md`, for example, is fluid below md, then uses responsive max-width behavior from md upward. Container padding and gutters still matter; a max-width is not the final width of all nested content. Custom Sass can change these values, so verify a customized build rather than assuming defaults.

Bootstrap's `.container` class is not a CSS query-container declaration. Its breakpoints are viewport media queries. For a component that appears in a sidebar and a main panel, native container queries may express its layout more accurately than adding more Bootstrap viewport classes.

bootstrap reference — Bootstrap 5 ecosystem and layout ### The 12-column grid The grid relationship is container, row, columns, then content. Rows use flex wrapping and gutter compensation; columns provide padding. `.col` shares remaining space; `.col-auto` sizes to content; `.col-1` through `.col-12` allocate fractions of the 12-column width. `.col-12.col-md-6.col-xl-4` means full width, then half width, then one third. `.row-cols-1.row-cols-md-2` sets a default number of columns per row. A nested grid needs its own row inside an existing column. ```html

Practice courses

JavaScript fundamentals

Practice values, functions and collections.

View JavaScript course

Java fundamentals

Practice types, methods and collections.

View Java course

JavaScript course information is available in this section.

Java course information is available in this section.

``` This is a complete semantic section fragment for a document already loading Bootstrap. The integrated lab includes the document shell. Grid gutters use `.g-*`, `.gx-*` and `.gy-*` and the related `--bs-gutter-x/y` variables. Large gutters combined with poorly placed rows can create overflow. Use `.g-0` intentionally; it removes spacing, not the need for readable separation. Offsets `.offset-md-2` add tier-specific starting space and may need resetting at later tiers. `.order-*` changes visual order; prefer source order that already matches meaning. `.align-items-*`, `.align-self-*` and `.justify-content-*` are Flexbox utilities, not separate grid algorithms. `.w-100` can force a flex line break in a controlled row but should not replace clear markup and layout. Bootstrap's optional CSS Grid implementation is a separate, experimental opt-in build path using `.grid`, `.g-col-*` and CSS custom properties. It is not the default `.row` Flexbox grid, and default compiled CSS does not necessarily include it. Native CSS Grid can also be used directly without that optional framework layer. bootstrap reference — Bootstrap utilities, content, helpers and forms

### Utility grammar and coverage

A utility class maps to actual declarations. Many are generated with `!important` by default, so a later ordinary component rule may not override them. Responsive and state variants are generated only for configured families; do not invent a class because a naming pattern seems plausible. The utility appendix extracts every entry of the installed `$utilities` Sass map and lists its CSS properties, class prefix, values, responsive setting, print setting and generated states. That is the exact build-source contract, not a list remembered from another Bootstrap version.

Spacing uses `{property}{sides}-{breakpoint?}-{size}`: m/p for margin/padding; t/b/s/e/x/y or no side; optional sm through xxl; and default scale 0,1,2,3,4,5 with values 0,0.25,0.5,1,1.5,3rem. Auto belongs to margin where generated. s/e are logical start/end conventions processed by the appropriate LTR/RTL build; loading LTR CSS and expecting every direction-sensitive utility to flip automatically is insufficient. Negative margins are opt-in through Sass and should not be assumed present. Gap utilities follow their configured families.

Display includes none, inline, inline-block, block, grid, inline-grid, table forms, flex and inline-flex with responsive/print variants where configured. Flex families cover direction, wrapping, fill, grow/shrink, alignment and order. Sizing provides selected percentage/auto values, viewport-relative helpers and min/max helpers; arbitrary values such as `.w-37` are not generated by default. Position utilities cover static/relative/absolute/fixed/sticky and selected edges/translations; responsive position variants are not universally available.

Other families cover background and text colors, opacity, borders and rounding, shadows, object fit, overflow, float, vertical alignment, interaction, visibility, link opacity/underlines, font sizing/weight/style, line height, text alignment/wrapping/transformation/decoration and small z-index values. `.invisible` retains layout space and differs from `.d-none`. `.text-truncate` needs a suitable constrained formatting context. `.pe-none` disables pointer targeting, not keyboard focus or programmatic activation. `.user-select-none` should not be used to obstruct normal text use.

bootstrap reference — Bootstrap utilities, content, helpers and forms

### Content and helper layer

Reboot normalizes selected element defaults using box-sizing, typography, margins and native-control adjustments. It is global CSS; assess it before importing into an existing site. Heading utility classes such as h1/h5 change appearance but do not change heading semantics. Use the correct HTML heading level. `.lead`, `.small`, `.mark`, list-unstyled and list-inline are presentational conventions, not substitutes for meaning.

Images can use `.img-fluid`, `.img-thumbnail`, rounded utilities and figure classes; they still need appropriate alternatives and actual width/height information. Tables use `.table` with contextual, striped, hover, bordered, borderless, size and responsive wrappers. A `.table-responsive` wrapper enables horizontal overflow and can clip floating content; preserve header associations and consider how keyboard users reach an overflowing region.

Helpers include clearfix, color/background helpers, colored links, focus-ring, icon-link, fixed/sticky positioning, ratio, hstack/vstack, stretched-link, text-truncation, vertical-rule and visually-hidden. `.visually-hidden` keeps content available to assistive technology while hiding it visually; `.visually-hidden-focusable` is useful for a skip link that appears on focus. A stretched link overlays an anchor's click area and can conflict with other controls; keep its containing block and interaction boundaries deliberate. A ratio helper creates geometry, not an accessible media title.

bootstrap reference — Bootstrap utilities, content, helpers and forms ### Forms and validation `.form-control` styles text-like inputs and textareas; `.form-select` styles selects; `.form-check`, `.form-check-input`, `.form-check-label` and `.form-switch` structure choices; `.form-range` styles range controls. `.input-group` groups controls and visible add-ons, but add-ons do not automatically become labels. Floating labels require the documented order and placeholder relationship; a floating placeholder is not a substitute for the real label element. Use visible labels, correct input types, name attributes, autocomplete tokens and text instructions. Connect help/error text with aria-describedby where appropriate. Reflect actual error state with aria-invalid and provide an understandable error message after validation. A red border or icon is insufficient. Do not display errors for untouched fields indiscriminately. Disabled controls are normally excluded from submission; readonly controls differ and have narrower applicability. Bootstrap's custom client-side validation styles and tooltip feedback have documented accessibility limitations. Prefer native browser validation or a carefully implemented accessible error workflow, and always validate on the server. `.was-validated`, `.is-valid` and `.is-invalid` are style triggers, not proof that a server accepted the data. Server errors must be mapped back to the relevant field and, for longer forms, summarized with useful links and deliberate focus handling. ```html
Used for your learning account.

This demonstration performs a local navigation, not account registration.

``` Use this as a native validation exercise. Production registration needs an actual endpoint, privacy policy and server rules; the lab deliberately makes no account mutation. Test empty, malformed and valid inputs with keyboard and touch. bootstrap reference — Bootstrap component mastery and lifecycle

### Static components and semantic contracts

Accordion combines collapse state with heading/button structure. Use real buttons with matching aria-controls and panel IDs; headings must remain meaningful. Alerts communicate messages; dismissible alerts need a labeled close button and a plan for focus when the alert disappears. Badges supplement labels and should not make unexplained numbers the sole accessible name. Breadcrumbs use navigation labeling, a list and aria-current for the current item.

Buttons should be button elements for actions and anchors for navigation. Outline variants still require contrast checks. Button groups need a useful group label and appropriate control semantics. Cards are visual containers; select headings, links, images and landmarks based on their actual content. Close buttons need an accessible label and sufficient target area. List groups can be lists, navigation or actionable controls; mixing these arbitrarily changes keyboard and screen-reader expectations.

Pagination uses navigation, descriptive labels and aria-current; an anchor with a disabled-looking class is still an anchor unless its behavior and focus are handled. Placeholders represent loading presentation and should not create fake operable controls or repeated meaningless announcements. Progress markup in 5.3 puts progressbar semantics and value attributes on the documented outer progress element; include a label and useful min/max/current values. Spinners need a meaningful status strategy and reduced-motion consideration. Repeated decorative spinners should not each announce the same loading state.

bootstrap reference — Bootstrap component mastery and lifecycle

### Interactive plugins: API contract

Bootstrap plugins generally expose `getInstance(element)`, `getOrCreateInstance(element, options)` and `dispose()`, with component-specific methods. Configuration comes from defaults, data attributes and explicit options under the documented precedence. `data-bs-config` can hold supported JSON configuration, but security-sensitive options such as sanitization settings are restricted. Data attributes use the bs prefix and kebab-case. Do not assume an option supported by one component exists on another.

Methods that start transitions generally return before the transition finishes. Listen for lifecycle events such as shown.bs.modal or hidden.bs.offcanvas when completion matters. A call during an active transition can be ignored according to the plugin contract. The show/hide events are often cancelable; shown/hidden report completion. Event names and payloads differ by component. The appendix extracts the exact default option names, default values and declared types from all 12 JavaScript plugin constructors in the pinned UMD bundle.
