read_u16 always returns 0 to 65535, so scale by 65535 and not by the chip resolution
py-emb-adc-scale   lens: access   level: L1   family: py-emb-adc-access
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: py-emb-adc-median. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. A 10-bit ADC returns 0 to 1023 from read_u16.
machine.ADC.read_u16() normalises every converter to 16 bits, so a 12-bit or 10-bit chip still returns values up to
65535. Convert to millivolts with raw * vref_mv // 65535. Dividing by 1023 or 4095 gives results that are 64 or 16
times too large. vref is the reference voltage, commonly 3300 mV.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 from machine import ADC
def to_mv_bad(raw):
    return raw * 3300 // 1023
Correct:
 from machine import ADC
def to_mv(raw, vref_mv=3300):
    return raw * vref_mv // 65535
Convert an analog temperature sensor with its datasheet offset, not just a scale factor
py-emb-adc-tmp36   lens: creation   level: L2   family: py-emb-adc-creation
Prerequisites: py-emb-adc-divider. Follow-up: py-emb-adc-hysteresis. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. The TMP36 output is 10 mV per degree Celsius, so temperature is mV divided by 10.
The TMP36 outputs 750 mV at 25 degrees Celsius with a slope of 10 mV per degree and a 500 mV offset at 0
degrees. Subtract the offset before dividing: temp_tenths = (mv - 500). Without the offset every reading is 50 degrees
too high. Keep the result in tenths of a degree to stay in integers.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def tmp36_bad(mv):
    return mv // 10
Correct:
 def tmp36(mv):
    return (mv - 500) // 10

Undo a voltage divider by multiplying by (r1 + r2) / r2 to get the real battery voltage
py-emb-adc-divider   lens: mutation   level: L2   family: py-emb-adc-mutation
Prerequisites: py-emb-adc-median. Follow-up: py-emb-adc-tmp36. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. The pin voltage is the battery voltage.
A divider with r1 from the battery to the pin and r2 from the pin to ground gives v_pin = v_batt * r2 / (r1 + r2). To
recover the battery voltage multiply by (r1 + r2) / r2. Choose resistors so that the maximum battery voltage stays
below the ADC reference, and keep the arithmetic in integers (millivolts) to avoid float drift.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def battery_mv_bad(pin_mv, r1, r2):
    return pin_mv * r2 // (r1 + r2)
Correct:
 def battery_mv(pin_mv, r1, r2):
    return pin_mv * (r1 + r2) // r2

Take the median of a few samples to reject a spike that a mean would smear into the result
py-emb-adc-median   lens: transformation   level: L2   family: py-emb-adc-transformation
Prerequisites: py-emb-adc-scale. Follow-up: py-emb-adc-divider. Complexity: O(n log n).
 Common misconception. The mean of several readings is always the most robust value.
Noise on an analog line comes as small jitter and as occasional spikes. The mean moves with a spike, while the
median ignores it. Read an odd number of samples, sort them and take the middle one. Use a mean when the noise
is symmetric and small, and a median when single bad readings occur.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def mean_bad(samples):
    return sum(samples) // len(samples)
Correct:
 def median(samples):
    s = sorted(samples)
    return s[len(s) // 2]
Use two thresholds so a noisy reading near the limit does not toggle an output
py-emb-adc-hysteresis   lens: edge-cases   level: L3   family: py-emb-adc-edge-cases
Prerequisites: py-emb-adc-tmp36. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. One threshold is enough to switch a heater on and off.
A reading that hovers around a single threshold flips the output on every sample. A Schmitt trigger uses a high
threshold to switch on and a lower one to switch off, so the band between them keeps the previous state. Keep the
state in the function arguments or an object so the decision depends on history.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def heater_bad(temp, limit):
    return temp < limit
Correct:
 def heater(temp, was_on, low, high):
    if temp < low:
        return True
    if temp > high:
        return False
    return was_on

3. Core concepts (tested chunks)
3 concept chunks, ordered by level. Read the misconception first and try to predict why it fails before reading the
explanation.
read_u16 always returns 0 to 65535, so scale by 65535 and not by the chip resolution
py-emb-adc-scale   lens: access   level: L1   family: py-emb-adc-access
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: py-emb-adc-median. Complexity: O(1).
Common misconception. A 10-bit ADC returns 0 to 1023 from read_u16.
machine.ADC.read_u16() normalises every converter to 16 bits, so a 12-bit or 10-bit chip still returns values up to
65535. Convert to millivolts with raw * vref_mv // 65535. Dividing by 1023 or 4095 gives results that are 64 or 16
times too large. vref is the reference voltage, commonly 3300 mV.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
from machine import ADC
def to_mv_bad(raw):
return raw * 3300 // 1023
Correct:
from machine import ADC
def to_mv(raw, vref_mv=3300):
return raw * vref_mv // 65535
Convert an analog temperature sensor with its datasheet offset, not just a scale factor
py-emb-adc-tmp36   lens: creation   level: L2   family: py-emb-adc-creation
Prerequisites: py-emb-adc-divider. Follow-up: py-emb-adc-hysteresis. Complexity: O(1).
Common misconception. The TMP36 output is 10 mV per degree Celsius, so temperature is mV divided by 10.
The TMP36 outputs 750 mV at 25 degrees Celsius with a slope of 10 mV per degree and a 500 mV offset at 0
degrees. Subtract the offset before dividing: temp_tenths = (mv - 500). Without the offset every reading is 50 degrees
too high. Keep the result in tenths of a degree to stay in integers.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
def tmp36_bad(mv):
return mv // 10
Correct:
def tmp36(mv):

Python on hardware, ADC analog input · 3. Core concepts (tested chunks) (continued)
return (mv - 500) // 10
Undo a voltage divider by multiplying by (r1 + r2) / r2 to get the real battery voltage
py-emb-adc-divider   lens: mutation   level: L2   family: py-emb-adc-mutation
Prerequisites: py-emb-adc-median. Follow-up: py-emb-adc-tmp36. Complexity: O(1).
Common misconception. The pin voltage is the battery voltage.
A divider with r1 from the battery to the pin and r2 from the pin to ground gives v_pin = v_batt * r2 / (r1 + r2). To
recover the battery voltage multiply by (r1 + r2) / r2. Choose resistors so that the maximum battery voltage stays
below the ADC reference, and keep the arithmetic in integers (millivolts) to avoid float drift.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
def battery_mv_bad(pin_mv, r1, r2):
return pin_mv * r2 // (r1 + r2)
Correct:
def battery_mv(pin_mv, r1, r2):
return pin_mv * (r1 + r2) // r2

4.4 Algorithm chunks
Take the median of a few samples to reject a spike that a mean would smear into the result
py-emb-adc-median   lens: transformation   level: L2   family: py-emb-adc-transformation
Prerequisites: py-emb-adc-scale. Follow-up: py-emb-adc-divider. Complexity: O(n log n).
Common misconception. The mean of several readings is always the most robust value.

Python on hardware, ADC analog input · 4. ADC analog input strategies (continued)
Noise on an analog line comes as small jitter and as occasional spikes. The mean moves with a spike, while the
median ignores it. Read an odd number of samples, sort them and take the middle one. Use a mean when the noise
is symmetric and small, and a median when single bad readings occur.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
def mean_bad(samples):
return sum(samples) // len(samples)
Correct:
def median(samples):
s = sorted(samples)
return s[len(s) // 2]
Use two thresholds so a noisy reading near the limit does not toggle an output
py-emb-adc-hysteresis   lens: edge-cases   level: L3   family: py-emb-adc-edge-cases
Prerequisites: py-emb-adc-tmp36. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(1).
Common misconception. One threshold is enough to switch a heater on and off.
A reading that hovers around a single threshold flips the output on every sample. A Schmitt trigger uses a high
threshold to switch on and a lower one to switch off, so the band between them keeps the previous state. Keep the
state in the function arguments or an object so the decision depends on history.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
def heater_bad(temp, limit):
return temp < limit
Correct:
def heater(temp, was_on, low, high):
if temp < low:
return True
if temp > high:
return False
return was_on

3. Core concepts (tested chunks)
3 concept chunks, ordered by level. Read the misconception first and try to predict why it fails before reading the

MQTT topics and payloads are bytes: encode what you send and decode what you receive
py-emb-mqt-bytes   lens: creation   level: L1   family: py-emb-mqt-creation
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: py-emb-mqt-poll. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. The callback receives strings.
umqtt passes the topic and the payload to your callback as bytes, and publish expects bytes. Encode text with
.encode() before sending, and decode in the callback before comparing with a string. Comparing b"on" with "on" is
never true.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 from umqtt.simple import MQTTClient
got_bad = []
def on_msg_bad(topic, msg):
    got_bad.append(msg == "on")
Correct:
 from umqtt.simple import MQTTClient
got = []
def on_msg(topic, msg):
    got.append(msg.decode() == "on")
def send(client, topic, text):
    client.publish(topic.encode(), text.encode())
Call check_msg() regularly, because incoming messages are only handled when you do
py-emb-mqt-poll   lens: iteration   level: L2   family: py-emb-mqt-iteration
Prerequisites: py-emb-mqt-bytes. Follow-up: py-emb-mqt-topics. Complexity: O(rounds).
 Common misconception. A subscribed callback is called by itself.
umqtt.simple has no background thread. A subscription only queues messages in the connection, and the callback
runs from check_msg() (non-blocking) or wait_msg() (blocking). Call check_msg() in every main loop iteration, and do
not let the loop block for longer than the keep-alive interval.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 from umqtt.simple import MQTTClient
def run_bad(client, cb):
    client.set_callback(cb)
    client.subscribe(b"cmd")
Correct:
 from umqtt.simple import MQTTClient
def run(client, cb, rounds=3):
    client.set_callback(cb)
    client.subscribe(b"cmd")
    for _ in range(rounds):
        client.check_msg()

Send a ping before the keep-alive interval runs out, or the broker drops the client
py-emb-mqt-ping   lens: edge-cases   level: L3   family: py-emb-mqt-edge-cases
Prerequisites: py-emb-mqt-topics. Follow-up: py-emb-mqt-will. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. The connection stays open as long as the program runs.
With keepalive=60 the broker closes the connection if it hears nothing for 1.5 times that interval. When your loop
publishes rarely, call client.ping() on a schedule, for example every half of the keep-alive time. Compare times with
ticks_diff.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def ping_due_bad(now, last, keepalive_s):
    return now - last > keepalive_s
Correct:
 import time
def ping_due(now, last, keepalive_s):
    return time.ticks_diff(now, last) >= keepalive_s * 500

4.4 Algorithm chunks
Match subscriptions with the + and # wildcards, level by level
py-emb-mqt-topics   lens: equality   level: L2   family: py-emb-mqt-equality
Prerequisites: py-emb-mqt-poll. Follow-up: py-emb-mqt-ping. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. A topic matches a subscription when the two strings are equal.
The filter sensors/+/temp matches any one level in the middle, and sensors/# matches everything below sensors.
Compare the filter and the topic level by level after splitting on the slash. A plain string comparison treats the
wildcards as ordinary characters.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def match_bad(flt, topic):
    return flt == topic
Correct:
 def match(flt, topic):
    f = flt.split("/")
    t = topic.split("/")
    for i in range(len(f)):
        if f[i] == "#":
            return True
        if i >= len(t) or (f[i] != "+" and f[i] != t[i]):
            return False
    return len(f) == len(t)

Register a last-will message so subscribers learn when a device disappears
py-emb-mqt-will   lens: patterns   level: L3   family: py-emb-mqt-patterns
Prerequisites: py-emb-mqt-ping. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. A device announces its own shutdown before it goes offline.
A device that loses power cannot send "offline". Set a last will with set_last_will before connect(): the broker
publishes it when the connection ends without a clean disconnect. Publish a retained "online" message after
connecting and make the will a retained "offline" on the same topic.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 from umqtt.simple import MQTTClient
def start_bad(c):
    c.connect()
Correct:
 from umqtt.simple import MQTTClient
def start(c, topic=b"dev/1/status"):
    c.set_last_will(topic, b"offline", retain=True)
    c.connect()
    c.publish(topic, b"online", retain=True)

Prompt. A client is started with start() and its connection then drops without a disconnect (sim_drop). What does
print("RESULT:%s") print for the last published payload on the status topic, written as print("RESULT:%s" %
Broker.published[-1][1])?
Answer key (mentor only, never embedded). b'offline'
py-emb-mqt-will-ex2   format: explain-why   level: L3   grading: rubric   modes: practice, interview
Prompt. What problem does an MQTT last-will message solve, and why is it retained?
Answer key (mentor only, never embedded). A device that crashes or loses power cannot announce that it is gone.
The broker publishes the will on its behalf when the connection ends without a normal disconnect, so subscribers learn
that the device is offline. Retaining it means a client that subscribes later still sees the latest state of the device.

Python on hardware, MQTT messaging · 3. Core concepts (tested chunks)
3. Core concepts (tested chunks)
3 concept chunks, ordered by level. Read the misconception first and try to predict why it fails before reading the
explanation.
MQTT topics and payloads are bytes: encode what you send and decode what you receive
py-emb-mqt-bytes   lens: creation   level: L1   family: py-emb-mqt-creation
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: py-emb-mqt-poll. Complexity: O(n).
Common misconception. The callback receives strings.
umqtt passes the topic and the payload to your callback as bytes, and publish expects bytes. Encode text with
.encode() before sending, and decode in the callback before comparing with a string. Comparing b"on" with "on" is
never true.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
from umqtt.simple import MQTTClient
got_bad = []
def on_msg_bad(topic, msg):
got_bad.append(msg == "on")
Correct:
from umqtt.simple import MQTTClient
got = []
def on_msg(topic, msg):
got.append(msg.decode() == "on")
def send(client, topic, text):
client.publish(topic.encode(), text.encode())
Call check_msg() regularly, because incoming messages are only handled when you do
py-emb-mqt-poll   lens: iteration   level: L2   family: py-emb-mqt-iteration
Prerequisites: py-emb-mqt-bytes. Follow-up: py-emb-mqt-topics. Complexity: O(rounds).
Common misconception. A subscribed callback is called by itself.
umqtt.simple has no background thread. A subscription only queues messages in the connection, and the callback
runs from check_msg() (non-blocking) or wait_msg() (blocking). Call check_msg() in every main loop iteration, and do
not let the loop block for longer than the keep-alive interval.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
from umqtt.simple import MQTTClient
def run_bad(client, cb):
client.set_callback(cb)
client.subscribe(b"cmd")

Python on hardware, MQTT messaging · 3. Core concepts (tested chunks) (continued)
Correct:
from umqtt.simple import MQTTClient
def run(client, cb, rounds=3):
client.set_callback(cb)
client.subscribe(b"cmd")
for _ in range(rounds):
client.check_msg()
Send a ping before the keep-alive interval runs out, or the broker drops the client
py-emb-mqt-ping   lens: edge-cases   level: L3   family: py-emb-mqt-edge-cases
Prerequisites: py-emb-mqt-topics. Follow-up: py-emb-mqt-will. Complexity: O(1).
Common misconception. The connection stays open as long as the program runs.
With keepalive=60 the broker closes the connection if it hears nothing for 1.5 times that interval. When your loop
publishes rarely, call client.ping() on a schedule, for example every half of the keep-alive time. Compare times with
ticks_diff.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
def ping_due_bad(now, last, keepalive_s):
return now - last > keepalive_s
Correct:
import time
def ping_due(now, last, keepalive_s):
return time.ticks_diff(now, last) >= keepalive_s * 500

Match subscriptions with the + and # wildcards, level by level
py-emb-mqt-topics   lens: equality   level: L2   family: py-emb-mqt-equality
Prerequisites: py-emb-mqt-poll. Follow-up: py-emb-mqt-ping. Complexity: O(n).
Common misconception. A topic matches a subscription when the two strings are equal.

Python on hardware, MQTT messaging · 4. MQTT messaging strategies (continued)
The filter sensors/+/temp matches any one level in the middle, and sensors/# matches everything below sensors.
Compare the filter and the topic level by level after splitting on the slash. A plain string comparison treats the
wildcards as ordinary characters.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
def match_bad(flt, topic):
return flt == topic
Correct:
def match(flt, topic):
f = flt.split("/")
t = topic.split("/")
for i in range(len(f)):
if f[i] == "#":
return True
if i >= len(t) or (f[i] != "+" and f[i] != t[i]):
return False
return len(f) == len(t)
Register a last-will message so subscribers learn when a device disappears
py-emb-mqt-will   lens: patterns   level: L3   family: py-emb-mqt-patterns
Prerequisites: py-emb-mqt-ping. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(1).
Common misconception. A device announces its own shutdown before it goes offline.
A device that loses power cannot send "offline". Set a last will with set_last_will before connect(): the broker
publishes it when the connection ends without a clean disconnect. Publish a retained "online" message after
connecting and make the will a retained "offline" on the same topic.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
from umqtt.simple import MQTTClient
def start_bad(c):
c.connect()
Correct:
from umqtt.simple import MQTTClient
def start(c, topic=b"dev/1/status"):
c.set_last_will(topic, b"offline", retain=True)
c.connect()
c.publish(topic, b"online", retain=True)

3. Core concepts (tested chunks)
3 concept chunks, ordered by level. Read the misconception first and try to predict why it fails before reading the
explanation.
connect() returns at once: wait for isconnected() with a timeout
py-emb-wif-wait   lens: edge-cases   level: L1   family: py-emb-wif-edge-cases
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: py-emb-wif-status. Complexity: O(timeout).
 Common misconception. After wlan.connect() the device is online.
connect() only starts the association; the link is up some time later, and it may never come up. Poll
wlan.isconnected() with a short sleep and a deadline, and report failure when the deadline passes. Using the network
too early gives OSError on the first socket.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 import network
def connect_bad(ssid, pw):
    wlan = network.WLAN(network.STA_IF)
    wlan.active(True)
    wlan.connect(ssid, pw)
    return wlan
Correct:
 import time, network
def connect(ssid, pw, timeout_ms=10000):
    wlan = network.WLAN(network.STA_IF)
    wlan.active(True)
    wlan.connect(ssid, pw)
    start = time.ticks_ms()
    while not wlan.isconnected():
        if time.ticks_diff(time.ticks_ms(), start) > timeout_ms:
            return None
        time.sleep_ms(100)
    return wlan
Pick the strongest network by the largest RSSI, and decode the SSID bytes
py-emb-wif-scan   lens: ordering   level: L2   family: py-emb-wif-ordering
Prerequisites: py-emb-wif-status. Follow-up: py-emb-wif-reconnect. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. The smallest RSSI is the strongest signal.
scan() returns tuples (ssid, bssid, channel, rssi, security, hidden) where the SSID is bytes. RSSI is measured in dBm
and is negative, so -40 is stronger than -80. The strongest network has the largest value, which max() finds. Decode
the SSID before comparing it with a configured name.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def best_bad(nets):
    return min(nets, key=lambda n: n[3])[0]
Correct:
 def best(nets):
    top = max(nets, key=lambda n: n[3])
    return top[0].decode()

Read wlan.status() to tell a wrong password from a missing network
py-emb-wif-status   lens: fit-and-alternatives   level: L2   family: py-emb-wif-fit-and-alternatives
Prerequisites: py-emb-wif-wait. Follow-up: py-emb-wif-scan. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. A failed connection always has the same cause and fix.
status() gives the reason while the link is not up. A wrong password (STAT_WRONG_PASSWORD) needs new
credentials and retrying will not help. A missing network (STAT_NO_AP_FOUND) may appear later, so waiting and
retrying makes sense. Compare with the named constants because the numeric values depend on the port.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def reason_bad(status):
    return "failed"
Correct:
 import network
def reason(status):
    if status == network.STAT_WRONG_PASSWORD:
        return "bad password"
    if status == network.STAT_NO_AP_FOUND:
        return "not found"
    return "other"

Switch the radio off between uploads, since an idle connected radio draws power
py-emb-wif-power   lens: complexity   level: L3   family: py-emb-wif-complexity
Prerequisites: py-emb-wif-reconnect. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Leaving Wi-Fi connected costs nothing when idle.
The radio draws tens of milliamps while it is on, far more than a sleeping microcontroller. A battery device should
connect, send, then call wlan.disconnect() and wlan.active(False) before it sleeps. The next cycle pays the
connection time again, so batch the data.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def done_bad(wlan):
    return wlan.isconnected()
Correct:
 def done(wlan):
    wlan.disconnect()
    wlan.active(False)
    return wlan.active()
Check the link in the main loop and reconnect with a delay between attempts
py-emb-wif-reconnect   lens: patterns   level: L3   family: py-emb-wif-patterns
Prerequisites: py-emb-wif-scan. Follow-up: py-emb-wif-power. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Once connected, the link stays up.
Access points restart, signal drops and DHCP leases expire. In the main loop test isconnected() every iteration or so,
and when it is false start a new connect attempt. Use the doubling delay from the retry chapter and a cap, so the
radio is not retried at full speed.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def ensure_bad(wlan, ssid, pw):
    wlan.connect(ssid, pw)
Correct:
 def ensure(wlan, ssid, pw):
    if wlan.isconnected():
        return False
    wlan.connect(ssid, pw)
    return True

Python on hardware, Wi-Fi connectivity · 3. Core concepts (tested chunks)
3. Core concepts (tested chunks)
3 concept chunks, ordered by level. Read the misconception first and try to predict why it fails before reading the
explanation.
connect() returns at once: wait for isconnected() with a timeout
py-emb-wif-wait   lens: edge-cases   level: L1   family: py-emb-wif-edge-cases
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: py-emb-wif-status. Complexity: O(timeout).
Common misconception. After wlan.connect() the device is online.
connect() only starts the association; the link is up some time later, and it may never come up. Poll
wlan.isconnected() with a short sleep and a deadline, and report failure when the deadline passes. Using the network
too early gives OSError on the first socket.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
import network
def connect_bad(ssid, pw):
wlan = network.WLAN(network.STA_IF)
wlan.active(True)
wlan.connect(ssid, pw)
return wlan
Correct:
import time, network
def connect(ssid, pw, timeout_ms=10000):
wlan = network.WLAN(network.STA_IF)
wlan.active(True)
wlan.connect(ssid, pw)
start = time.ticks_ms()
while not wlan.isconnected():
if time.ticks_diff(time.ticks_ms(), start) > timeout_ms:
return None
time.sleep_ms(100)
return wlan
Pick the strongest network by the largest RSSI, and decode the SSID bytes
py-emb-wif-scan   lens: ordering   level: L2   family: py-emb-wif-ordering
Prerequisites: py-emb-wif-status. Follow-up: py-emb-wif-reconnect. Complexity: O(n).
Common misconception. The smallest RSSI is the strongest signal.

Python on hardware, Wi-Fi connectivity · 3. Core concepts (tested chunks) (continued)
scan() returns tuples (ssid, bssid, channel, rssi, security, hidden) where the SSID is bytes. RSSI is measured in dBm
and is negative, so -40 is stronger than -80. The strongest network has the largest value, which max() finds. Decode
the SSID before comparing it with a configured name.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
def best_bad(nets):
return min(nets, key=lambda n: n[3])[0]
Correct:
def best(nets):
top = max(nets, key=lambda n: n[3])
return top[0].decode()
Read wlan.status() to tell a wrong password from a missing network
py-emb-wif-status   lens: fit-and-alternatives   level: L2   family: py-emb-wif-fit-and-alternatives
Prerequisites: py-emb-wif-wait. Follow-up: py-emb-wif-scan. Complexity: O(1).
Common misconception. A failed connection always has the same cause and fix.
status() gives the reason while the link is not up. A wrong password (STAT_WRONG_PASSWORD) needs new
credentials and retrying will not help. A missing network (STAT_NO_AP_FOUND) may appear later, so waiting and
retrying makes sense. Compare with the named constants because the numeric values depend on the port.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
def reason_bad(status):
return "failed"
Correct:
import network
def reason(status):
if status == network.STAT_WRONG_PASSWORD:
return "bad password"
if status == network.STAT_NO_AP_FOUND:
return "not found"
return "other"

4.4 Algorithm chunks
Switch the radio off between uploads, since an idle connected radio draws power
py-emb-wif-power   lens: complexity   level: L3   family: py-emb-wif-complexity
Prerequisites: py-emb-wif-reconnect. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(1).
Common misconception. Leaving Wi-Fi connected costs nothing when idle.

Python on hardware, Wi-Fi connectivity · 4. Wi-Fi connectivity strategies (continued)
The radio draws tens of milliamps while it is on, far more than a sleeping microcontroller. A battery device should
connect, send, then call wlan.disconnect() and wlan.active(False) before it sleeps. The next cycle pays the
connection time again, so batch the data.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
def done_bad(wlan):
return wlan.isconnected()
Correct:
def done(wlan):
wlan.disconnect()
wlan.active(False)
return wlan.active()
Check the link in the main loop and reconnect with a delay between attempts
py-emb-wif-reconnect   lens: patterns   level: L3   family: py-emb-wif-patterns
Prerequisites: py-emb-wif-scan. Follow-up: py-emb-wif-power. Complexity: O(1).
Common misconception. Once connected, the link stays up.
Access points restart, signal drops and DHCP leases expire. In the main loop test isconnected() every iteration or so,
and when it is false start a new connect attempt. Use the doubling delay from the retry chapter and a cap, so the
radio is not retried at full speed.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
def ensure_bad(wlan, ssid, pw):
wlan.connect(ssid, pw)
Correct:
def ensure(wlan, ssid, pw):
if wlan.isconnected():
return False
wlan.connect(ssid, pw)
return True

A task is due when ticks_diff(now, due) is zero or positive
py-emb-sch-due   lens: ordering   level: L1   family: py-emb-sch-ordering
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: py-emb-sch-drift. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. now >= due is a reliable test.
The tick counter wraps, so a due time that was computed just before the wrap is a small number afterwards and now
>= due is wrong. ticks_diff(now, due) >= 0 gives the right answer for any interval below half the counter range.
Compute due times with ticks_add.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def due_bad(now, due):
    return now >= due
Correct:
 import time
def due(now, due_at):
    return time.ticks_diff(now, due_at) >= 0
Schedule the next run from the previous due time, so late starts do not accumulate drift
py-emb-sch-drift   lens: iteration   level: L2   family: py-emb-sch-iteration
Prerequisites: py-emb-sch-due. Follow-up: py-emb-sch-catchup. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Add the period to the current time after each run.
If a task runs 3 ms late and the next due time is "now + period", every run shifts by a few milliseconds and the rate
slowly drifts. Adding the period to the previous due time keeps the long-term rate exact; only the single late run is late.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def next_bad(now, due_at, period):
    return now + period
Correct:
 import time
def next_due(now, due_at, period):
    return time.ticks_add(due_at, period)
If a task is far behind, skip the missed runs instead of running them in a burst
py-emb-sch-catchup   lens: edge-cases   level: L3   family: py-emb-sch-edge-cases
Prerequisites: py-emb-sch-drift. Follow-up: py-emb-sch-order. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. A task that missed five periods should run five times in a row.
After a long block, the due time is several periods in the past. Looping until it is in the future runs the task many times
back to back, which can starve other tasks and repeat stale work. Run it once and move the due time to the next slot
after now.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def reschedule_bad(due_at, now, period):
    return due_at + period
Correct:
 def reschedule(due_at, now, period):
    behind = now - due_at
    if behind >= period:
        due_at += (behind // period) * period
    return due_at + period

Catch exceptions per task so one faulty task does not stop the others
py-emb-sch-isolate   lens: patterns   level: L3   family: py-emb-sch-patterns
Prerequisites: py-emb-sch-order. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. An exception in one task is fine; the scheduler restarts.
If the scheduler loop does not catch an exception, a bug in one rarely used task ends the whole loop and every task
stops. Wrap each call in try and except Exception, record the error, and keep going. Count failures so a repeatedly
failing task can be disabled.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def run_bad(tasks):
    for fn in tasks:
        fn()
Correct:
 def run_all(tasks, errors):
    for name, fn in tasks:
        try:
            fn()
        except Exception as e:
            errors.append(name + ":" + type(e).__name__)
Run the task with the earliest due time first
py-emb-sch-order   lens: patterns   level: L3   family: py-emb-sch-patterns
Prerequisites: py-emb-sch-catchup. Follow-up: py-emb-sch-isolate. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. Running tasks in list order is fair.
With a list order, a task near the end can wait while later-added tasks that are not due yet are examined first, and two
due tasks run in the order they were added and not in the order they became due. Pick the due task whose due time
is earliest, so the most overdue one goes first.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def pick_bad(tasks, now):
    for t in tasks:
        if t["due"] <= now:
            return t["name"]
Correct:
 def pick(tasks, now):
    ready = [t for t in tasks if t["due"] <= now]
    if not ready:
        return None
    return min(ready, key=lambda t: t["due"])["name"]

Prompt. Why does computing the next run as "now + period" make a periodic task drift?
Answer key (mentor only, never embedded). The task never starts at exactly the planned time, so each run is a little
late. If the next run is based on the actual start time, every delay is added to all later runs and the lateness piles up, so

slowly drifts. Adding the period to the previous due time keeps the long-term rate exact; only the single late run is late.

return now + period
Correct:
import time
def next_due(now, due_at, period):
return time.ticks_add(due_at, period)

If a task is far behind, skip the missed runs instead of running them in a burst
py-emb-sch-catchup   lens: edge-cases   level: L3   family: py-emb-sch-edge-cases
Prerequisites: py-emb-sch-drift. Follow-up: py-emb-sch-order. Complexity: O(1).
Common misconception. A task that missed five periods should run five times in a row.
After a long block, the due time is several periods in the past. Looping until it is in the future runs the task many times
back to back, which can starve other tasks and repeat stale work. Run it once and move the due time to the next slot
after now.

def reschedule_bad(due_at, now, period):
return due_at + period
Correct:
def reschedule(due_at, now, period):
behind = now - due_at
if behind >= period:
due_at += (behind // period) * period
return due_at + period

3 concept chunks, ordered by level. Read the misconception first and try to predict why it fails before reading the
explanation.
An XOR checksum folds every byte together with xor, and a sum is a different checksum
py-emb-frame-xor   lens: creation   level: L1   family: py-emb-frame-creation
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: py-emb-frame-crc8. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. Adding the bytes gives the NMEA checksum.
NMEA 0183 sentences end with an XOR of every character between the dollar sign and the asterisk, written as two
hex digits. Addition gives a different value, so a correct message is rejected. Start from 0 and apply ^ to each byte,
and format with "%02X".
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):

    s = 0
    for b in data:
        s = (s + b) & 0xFF
    return s
Correct:
 def checksum(data):
    c = 0
    for b in data:
        c ^= b
    return c
The same polynomial with a different start value is a different CRC-16
py-emb-frame-crc16   lens: equality   level: L2   family: py-emb-frame-equality
Prerequisites: py-emb-frame-crc8. Follow-up: py-emb-frame-parse. Complexity: O(8n).
 Common misconception. Any CRC-16 with polynomial 0x1021 is CRC-CCITT.
The polynomial 0x1021 is shared by several algorithms. CRC-16/CCITT-FALSE starts at 0xFFFF and gives 0x29B1
for b"123456789"; starting at 0x0000 gives the XMODEM variant, 0x31C3. Both ends must agree on initial value,
polynomial, bit order and final xor, so write the parameters into the protocol description.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def crc16_xmodem(data):
    crc = 0x0000
    for b in data:
        crc ^= b << 8
        for _ in range(8):
            crc = ((crc << 1) ^ 0x1021) & 0xFFFF if crc & 0x8000 else (crc << 1) & 0xFFFF
    return crc

 def crc16_ccitt(data, init=0xFFFF):
    crc = init
    for b in data:
        crc ^= b << 8
        for _ in range(8):
            if crc & 0x8000:
                crc = ((crc << 1) ^ 0x1021) & 0xFFFF
            else:
                crc = (crc << 1) & 0xFFFF
    return crc
Compute CRC-8 bit by bit and mask to eight bits after every shift
py-emb-frame-crc8   lens: transformation   level: L2   family: py-emb-frame-transformation
Prerequisites: py-emb-frame-xor. Follow-up: py-emb-frame-crc16. Complexity: O(8n).
 Common misconception. The shift can be left unmasked, since Python integers grow.
A CRC register is eight bits wide. Python integers are unbounded, so an unmasked left shift keeps the high bits and
the result is wrong. Use polynomial 0x07: for each byte xor it into the register, then eight times shift left, xor with the
polynomial when the top bit was set and mask with 0xFF. The check value for b"123456789" is 0xF4.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def crc8_bad(data, poly=0x07):
    crc = 0
    for b in data:
        crc ^= b
        for _ in range(8):
            crc = (crc << 1) ^ poly if crc & 0x80 else crc << 1
    return crc
Correct:
 def crc8(data, poly=0x07):
    crc = 0
    for b in data:
        crc ^= b
        for _ in range(8):
            if crc & 0x80:
                crc = ((crc << 1) ^ poly) & 0xFF
            else:
                crc = (crc << 1) & 0xFF
    return crc

Validate the start byte, the length and the checksum before trusting a frame
py-emb-frame-parse   lens: access   level: L3   family: py-emb-frame-access
Prerequisites: py-emb-frame-crc16. Follow-up: py-emb-frame-slip. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. A frame that starts with the start byte is valid.
A frame here is 0xAA, a length byte, the payload and an XOR checksum of the length and payload. A parser that
trusts the start byte returns garbage when bytes are lost. Check that the buffer is long enough, that the length fits, and
that the checksum matches; return None for anything else so the caller can resynchronise.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def parse_bad(buf):
    if buf and buf[0] == 0xAA:
        return bytes(buf[2:2 + buf[1]])
Correct:
 def parse(buf):
    if len(buf) < 3 or buf[0] != 0xAA:
        return None
    n = buf[1]
    if len(buf) < 3 + n:
        return None
    payload = bytes(buf[2:2 + n])
    if checksum(buf[1:2 + n]) != buf[2 + n]:
        return None
    return payload
def build(payload):
    body = bytes([len(payload)]) + payload
    return bytes([0xAA]) + body + bytes([checksum(body)])
Escape the end marker inside the payload with byte stuffing
py-emb-frame-slip   lens: edge-cases   level: L3   family: py-emb-frame-edge-cases
Prerequisites: py-emb-frame-parse. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. A payload can contain any byte without special treatment.
If a frame ends at byte 0xC0, a payload that contains 0xC0 ends it early. SLIP replaces 0xC0 inside the data with
0xDB 0xDC and 0xDB with 0xDB 0xDD. Escape 0xDB first or the escape bytes are escaped twice, and decode by
reversing the pairs.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def slip_bad(data):
    return bytes(data) + b"\xc0"

Page 7
Correct:
 def slip(data):
    out = bytearray()
    for b in data:
        if b == 0xC0:
            out.extend(b"\xdb\xdc")
        elif b == 0xDB:
            out.extend(b"\xdb\xdd")
        else:
            out.append(b)
    out.append(0xC0)
    return bytes(out)
def unslip(frame):
    out = bytearray()
    i = 0
    while i < len(frame) and frame[i] != 0xC0:
        if frame[i] == 0xDB:
            i += 1
            out.append(0xC0 if frame[i] == 0xDC else 0xDB)
        else:
            out.append(frame[i])
        i += 1
    return bytes(out)

A Timer repeats only in PERIODIC mode; the default one-shot mode fires once
py-emb-tim-periodic   lens: creation   level: L1   family: py-emb-tim-creation
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: py-emb-tim-oneshot. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Timer(period=100, callback=f) calls f every 100 ms.
A machine.Timer has two modes. ONE_SHOT calls the callback once after the period, PERIODIC repeats it. Pass
mode=Timer.PERIODIC explicitly, because the default differs between ports and a missing mode is a silent bug. The
callback receives the timer object and runs in interrupt context on many ports, so keep it short.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):

ticks_bad = []
def cb_bad(t):
    ticks_bad.append(1)
tim_bad = Timer(mode=Timer.ONE_SHOT, period=100, callback=cb_bad)
Correct:
 import time
from machine import Timer
ticks = []
def cb(t):
    ticks.append(1)
tim = Timer(mode=Timer.PERIODIC, period=100, callback=cb)
freq is in hertz and period is in milliseconds, so do not mix them
py-emb-tim-freq   lens: transformation   level: L2   family: py-emb-tim-transformation
Prerequisites: py-emb-tim-oneshot. Follow-up: py-emb-tim-deinit. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Timer(freq=10) and Timer(period=10) mean the same.
freq=10 means 10 times per second, a period of 100 ms. period=10 means every 10 ms, which is 100 times per
second. Mixing them changes the rate by a factor of ten. Convert explicitly with period_ms = 1000 // hz so the unit is
visible in the code.

Call deinit() to stop a timer, otherwise it keeps firing and keeps its resources
py-emb-tim-deinit   lens: edge-cases   level: L2   family: py-emb-tim-edge-cases
Prerequisites: py-emb-tim-freq. Follow-up: py-emb-tim-deadline. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Dropping the variable stops the timer.
A hardware timer is not stopped when the Python name goes away on every port, and a periodic callback keeps
running. Call deinit() when you no longer need it, for example before entering a different mode of operation or before
a soft reset, and create the timer again when needed.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 import time
from machine import Timer
seen_bad = []
def cb_seen_bad(t):
    seen_bad.append(1)
t_bad = Timer(mode=Timer.PERIODIC, period=50, callback=cb_seen_bad)
t_bad = None
Correct:
 import time
from machine import Timer
seen = []
def cb_seen(t):
    seen.append(1)
t_ok = Timer(mode=Timer.PERIODIC, period=50, callback=cb_seen)
def stop():
    t_ok.deinit()

Use a one-shot timer for a delayed action instead of blocking with sleep
py-emb-tim-oneshot   lens: insertion-and-deletion   level: L2   family: py-emb-tim-insertion-and-deletion
Prerequisites: py-emb-tim-periodic. Follow-up: py-emb-tim-freq. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. time.sleep_ms(200) before turning the LED off is the simplest way to delay.
Sleeping blocks the program, so buttons and sensors are ignored for the whole delay. A one-shot timer lets the main
loop carry on and runs the action once when the time is up. Re-arming the timer on every new event restarts the
delay, which is how a light stays on for 200 ms after the last motion.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 import time
from machine import Pin
lamp_bad = Pin(40, Pin.OUT)
def pulse_bad():
    lamp_bad.on()
    time.sleep_ms(200)
    lamp_bad.off()
Correct:
 import time
from machine import Pin, Timer
lamp = Pin(41, Pin.OUT)
off_timer = Timer()
def lamp_off(t):
    lamp.off()
def pulse():
    lamp.on()
    off_timer.init(mode=Timer.ONE_SHOT, period=200, callback=lamp_off)

Compare ticks with ticks_diff, since the millisecond counter wraps around
py-emb-tim-deadline   lens: ordering   level: L3   family: py-emb-tim-ordering
Prerequisites: py-emb-tim-deinit. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. now >= deadline tells you that a deadline has passed.
ticks_ms() counts up to a limit and then wraps to zero, so a deadline computed near the end can be a small number.
Plain comparison then says the deadline has already passed. ticks_add computes the deadline with wrapping and
ticks_diff(now, deadline) >= 0 compares correctly as long as the interval is under half the range.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def due_bad(now, deadline):
    return now >= deadline
Correct:
 import time
def due(now, deadline):
    return time.ticks_diff(now, deadline) >= 0

py-emb-tim-oneshot-ex2   format: explain-why   level: L2   grading: rubric   modes: practice, interview
Prompt. Why is a one-shot timer better than sleep for turning an output off after a delay?
Answer key (mentor only, never embedded). sleep blocks the whole program, so inputs, sensors and other outputs
are ignored during the delay. A one-shot timer schedules the action and returns immediately, so the main loop keeps
running and the action happens when the time is up. Restarting the timer also gives a simple retriggerable delay.

Use a one-shot timer for a delayed action instead of blocking with sleep
py-emb-tim-oneshot   lens: insertion-and-deletion   level: L2   family: py-emb-tim-insertion-and-deletion
Prerequisites: py-emb-tim-periodic. Follow-up: py-emb-tim-freq. Complexity: O(1).
Common misconception. time.sleep_ms(200) before turning the LED off is the simplest way to delay.

Python on hardware, Hardware timers · 4. Hardware timers strategies (continued)
Sleeping blocks the program, so buttons and sensors are ignored for the whole delay. A one-shot timer lets the main
loop carry on and runs the action once when the time is up. Re-arming the timer on every new event restarts the
delay, which is how a light stays on for 200 ms after the last motion.

from machine import Pin
lamp_bad = Pin(40, Pin.OUT)
def pulse_bad():
lamp_bad.on()
time.sleep_ms(200)
lamp_bad.off()
Correct:
import time
from machine import Pin, Timer
lamp = Pin(41, Pin.OUT)
off_timer = Timer()
def lamp_off(t):
lamp.off()
def pulse():
lamp.on()
off_timer.init(mode=Timer.ONE_SHOT, period=200, callback=lamp_off)
Compare ticks with ticks_diff, since the millisecond counter wraps around
py-emb-tim-deadline   lens: ordering   level: L3   family: py-emb-tim-ordering
Prerequisites: py-emb-tim-deinit. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(1).
Common misconception. now >= deadline tells you that a deadline has passed.
ticks_ms() counts up to a limit and then wraps to zero, so a deadline computed near the end can be a small number.
Plain comparison then says the deadline has already passed. ticks_add computes the deadline with wrapping and
ticks_diff(now, deadline) >= 0 compares correctly as long as the interval is under half the range.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
def due_bad(now, deadline):
return now >= deadline
Correct:
import time
def due(now, deadline):
return time.ticks_diff(now, deadline) >= 0

A moving average keeps a fixed window and divides by the window size
py-emb-flt-window   lens: iteration   level: L1   family: py-emb-flt-iteration
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: py-emb-flt-ema. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. Averaging every reading since start-up smooths the signal best.
An average over all readings reacts more and more slowly and its sum grows without limit. A moving average keeps
only the last n values. Add the new value, drop the oldest when the window is full and divide by the number of values
held. Dividing by the window size before it fills gives values that are too low.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 class AvgBad:
    def __init__(self):
        self.vals = []
    def add(self, v):
        self.vals.append(v)
        return sum(self.vals) // len(self.vals)
Correct:
 class MovingAvg:
    def __init__(self, n):
        self.n = n
        self.vals = []
    def add(self, v):
        self.vals.append(v)
        if len(self.vals) > self.n:
            self.vals.pop(0)
        return sum(self.vals) // len(self.vals)
An exponential filter needs no history, but it must start from the first sample
py-emb-flt-ema   lens: transformation   level: L2   family: py-emb-flt-transformation
Prerequisites: py-emb-flt-window. Follow-up: py-emb-flt-windup. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Starting the filter at 0 is harmless.
The filter y = y + (x - y) / 4 stores one number. Started at 0 it takes many samples to climb to the real level, so the first
readings are far too low. Initialise it with the first sample. Use a shift or integer division by a power of two to avoid
floats on small chips.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 class EmaBad:
    def __init__(self):
        self.y = 0
    def add(self, x):
        self.y += (x - self.y) // 4
        return self.y

    def __init__(self):

    def add(self, x):
        if self.y is None:
            self.y = x
        else:
            self.y += (x - self.y) // 4
        return self.y
Take the derivative of the measurement so a setpoint change does not kick the output
py-emb-flt-kick   lens: edge-cases   level: L3   family: py-emb-flt-edge-cases
Prerequisites: py-emb-flt-windup. Follow-up: py-emb-flt-dt. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. The derivative of the error is the right input for the D term.
When the setpoint jumps, the error jumps with it and the derivative of the error is a huge one-sample spike (derivative
kick). Differentiate the measurement instead: since the setpoint is constant between jumps, the result is the same
during normal operation and has no spike at a jump.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def d_bad(setpoint, meas, prev_setpoint, prev_meas):
    return (setpoint - meas) - (prev_setpoint - prev_meas)
Correct:
 def d_term(meas, prev_meas):
    return -(meas - prev_meas)

Clamp the PID integral term so it cannot wind up while the output is saturated
py-emb-flt-windup   lens: mutation   level: L3   family: py-emb-flt-mutation
Prerequisites: py-emb-flt-ema. Follow-up: py-emb-flt-kick. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. The integral term can grow without limit and the controller still behaves.
If the output is at its maximum and the error stays positive, the integral keeps growing. When the error finally changes
sign the integral is huge and the output stays saturated for a long time (windup). Clamp the integral to the range that
can still matter, or stop integrating while the output is saturated.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 class PidBad:
    def __init__(self, kp, ki):
        self.kp, self.ki, self.integral = kp, ki, 0
    def update(self, error):
        self.integral += error
        return self.kp * error + self.ki * self.integral
Correct:
 class Pid:
    def __init__(self, kp, ki, imax=100):
        self.kp, self.ki, self.imax, self.integral = kp, ki, imax, 0
    def update(self, error):
        self.integral = max(-self.imax, min(self.imax, self.integral + error))
        return self.kp * error + self.ki * self.integral

Scale the integral and the derivative by the measured time step
py-emb-flt-dt   lens: complexity   level: L3   family: py-emb-flt-complexity
Prerequisites: py-emb-flt-kick. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Loops run at exactly the same interval every time.
An integral accumulates error times time, and a derivative is a change per unit time. A loop that sometimes takes 10
ms and sometimes 30 ms gives wrong results if the code assumes a constant step. Measure dt with ticks_diff and
scale: integral += error * dt, derivative = delta / dt.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def integrate_bad(integral, error, dt_ms):
    return integral + error
Correct:
 def integrate(integral, error, dt_ms):
    return integral + error * dt_ms // 1000

Prompt. The error is 10 and the loop step is 20 ms, then 500 ms, from an integral of 0. What does print("RESULT:%d
%d") print for (integrate(0, 10, 20), integrate(0, 10, 500)), written as print("RESULT:%d %d" % (integrate(0, 10, 20),
integrate(0, 10, 500)))?

py-emb-flt-windup-ex2   format: explain-why   level: L3   grading: rubric   modes: practice, interview
Prompt. What is integral windup and how does clamping the integral prevent it?
Answer key (mentor only, never embedded). When the actuator is saturated the error stays large, and the integral
term keeps accumulating it. After the error changes sign the huge integral has to unwind first, so the output stays at its
limit for a long time and the process overshoots. Limiting the integral to a useful range keeps it small enough for the
controller to respond quickly when the error reverses.

3. Core concepts (tested chunks)
3 concept chunks, ordered by level. Read the misconception first and try to predict why it fails before reading the
explanation.
Choose the edge that matches the wiring: a pull-up button presses on the falling edge
py-emb-irq-edge   lens: access   level: L1   family: py-emb-irq-access
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: py-emb-irq-counter. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. IRQ_RISING detects a button press.
With the internal pull-up a button reads 1 when released and 0 when pressed, so the press is a falling edge and the
release is a rising edge. Register the handler with Pin.IRQ_FALLING to count presses. Using IRQ_RISING counts
the releases, and using both edges counts every press twice.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 from machine import Pin
presses_bad = []
btn_bad = Pin(10, Pin.IN, Pin.PULL_UP)
btn_bad.irq(lambda p: presses_bad.append(1), Pin.IRQ_RISING)
Correct:
 from machine import Pin
presses = []
btn = Pin(11, Pin.IN, Pin.PULL_UP)
btn.irq(lambda p: presses.append(1), Pin.IRQ_FALLING)
Bind the loop variable with a default argument when you create handlers in a loop
py-emb-irq-closure   lens: creation   level: L2   family: py-emb-irq-creation
Prerequisites: py-emb-irq-counter. Follow-up: py-emb-irq-atomic. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. A lambda created in a loop remembers the value the variable had at that moment.
A closure captures the variable and not its value, so after the loop every handler sees the last value. A default
argument is evaluated when the lambda is created, so lambda p, i=i: freezes the current index. The same applies to
callbacks given to Timer and to asyncio tasks.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 from machine import Pin
hits_bad = []
pins_bad = [Pin(20 + i, Pin.IN) for i in range(3)]
for i in range(3):
    pins_bad[i].irq(lambda p: hits_bad.append(i), Pin.IRQ_RISING)
Correct:
 from machine import Pin
hits = []
pins = [Pin(30 + i, Pin.IN) for i in range(3)]
for i in range(3):
    pins[i].irq(lambda p, i=i: hits.append(i), Pin.IRQ_RISING)

Read and clear a shared counter with interrupts disabled, or an event can arrive between the
two steps
py-emb-irq-atomic   lens: edge-cases   level: L3   family: py-emb-irq-edge-cases
Prerequisites: py-emb-irq-closure. Follow-up: py-emb-irq-gate. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Reading the counter and then setting it to zero is safe.
An interrupt can fire between reading n = count and writing count = 0. The event it counted is then erased and never
processed. Wrap the pair in machine.disable_irq() and enable_irq(state) so it cannot be interrupted, and keep the
protected section as short as possible.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 count_bad = [0]
def take_bad(between=None):
    n = count_bad[0]
    if between:
        between()
    count_bad[0] = 0
    return n
Correct:
 from machine import disable_irq, enable_irq
count_ok = [0]
def take_ok():
    state = disable_irq()
    n = count_ok[0]
    count_ok[0] = 0
    enable_irq(state)
    return n

4.4 Algorithm chunks
Count events in the handler and consume the count in the main loop, so no event is lost
py-emb-irq-counter   lens: mutation   level: L2   family: py-emb-irq-mutation
Prerequisites: py-emb-irq-edge. Follow-up: py-emb-irq-closure. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. A boolean flag set by the handler records every event.
A flag only says that something happened since it was last cleared. Two events before the main loop looks give one
flag and one handled event. A counter that the handler increments keeps the number of events, and the main loop
subtracts what it processed. Keep the handler short: no printing, no allocation, no waiting.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 from machine import Pin
flag_bad = [False]
src_bad = Pin(12, Pin.IN)
def on_flag(pin):
    flag_bad[0] = True
src_bad.irq(on_flag, Pin.IRQ_RISING)
Correct:
 from machine import Pin
count = [0]
src = Pin(13, Pin.IN)
def on_edge(pin):
    count[0] += 1
src.irq(on_edge, Pin.IRQ_RISING)
def take():
    n = count[0]
    count[0] -= n
    return n

Measure frequency by counting rising edges in a fixed gate time
py-emb-irq-gate   lens: complexity   level: L3   family: py-emb-irq-complexity
Prerequisites: py-emb-irq-atomic. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Counting both edges gives the frequency of the signal.
A signal at f Hz has f rising edges and f falling edges per second. Counting both doubles the result. Count one edge
type for a gate time of gate_ms milliseconds and compute freq = edges * 1000 // gate_ms. A longer gate improves
resolution to 1000 / gate_ms Hz but delays the answer.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def freq_bad(edges, gate_ms):
    return edges * 1000 // gate_ms
Correct:
 def freq_hz(rising_edges, gate_ms):
    return rising_edges * 1000 // gate_ms

Prompt. Pin 13 rises three times before the main loop calls take(). What does print("RESULT:%d %d" % (take(),
take())) print?
Answer key (mentor only, never embedded). 3 0
py-emb-irq-gate-ex1   format: predict-output   level: L3   grading: exact   modes: practice, quiz
Prompt. A 50 Hz signal is observed for 500 ms. Counting both edges gives 50 edges and counting rising edges gives
25. What does print("RESULT:%d %d") print for (freq_hz(25, 500), freq_bad(50, 500)), written as print("RESULT:%d
%d" % (freq_hz(25, 500), freq_bad(50, 500)))?
Answer key (mentor only, never embedded). 50 100
py-emb-irq-counter-ex2   format: explain-why   level: L2   grading: rubric   modes: practice, interview
Prompt. Why should an interrupt handler be short and only update a counter or flag, with the real work done in the
main loop?
Answer key (mentor only, never embedded). While a handler runs, other interrupts may be delayed and the main
program is stopped, so long handlers add latency and lose events. Printing, allocating memory or waiting inside a
handler can also fail or block, because the runtime may be in the middle of its own work. A counter or flag is a tiny
update, and the main loop can then process the events at a safe time.

## 1 Scope and how to use this guide
Learn HTML by understanding what an element means, what its attributes configure, and which browser objects and algorithms consume those settings. This reference covers all 113 HTML-namespace element names in the observed WHATWG element index, every attribute definition in its attribute index, the indexed HTML event-handler attributes, all input type states, and worked connections to Web APIs. HTML5 is the familiar name for modern HTML; the maintained authority is the HTML Living Standard rather than a frozen HTML5 tag list.
The element catalogue explains each tag separately, including h1 through h6. Every element inherits the shared attribute families described in Part 3, subject to their applicability rules. Element-specific attributes are mapped to the numbered dictionary in Part 4, where each attribute has its meaning, permitted-value summary, contextual limits and a mistake to avoid. Read an element entry together with those dictionary entries. This avoids teaching the same attribute inconsistently across several tags.

Element-specific attributes are mapped to the numbered dictionary in Part 4, where each attribute has its meaning, permitted-value summary, contextual limits and a mistake to avoid. Read an element entry together with those dictionary entries. This avoids teaching the same attribute inconsistently across several tags.

Coverage is tied to the public specification pages retrieved on October 16 2026. The specification is living text, so the included inventory and source hashes record what was used. Some current features are newer than the original HTML5 snapshot and some browser implementations lag behind the standard. Specification coverage is not a browser compatibility certification. Newer features are called out where they need particular care.

SVG and MathML can be embedded in an HTML document but have their own element and attribute vocabularies. They are explained as integration boundaries rather than counted among the 113 HTML elements. Obsolete elements are listed in a migration appendix and are not presented as current authoring choices. Arbitrary data-* attributes and custom-element attributes are open-ended families; no finite list could exhaust every application's additions. ARIA, CSS Shadow Parts and media extension attributes are separately identified so their rules are not confused with core HTML.

This is tutor reference material with original examples and expected reasoning, not a package of admitted graded workouts. Illustrations that refer to images, servers or scripts need those resources before execution. The practice tasks state what should be observed; no browser run, screen-reader result or cross-browser pass is implied by the presence of example code. A browser runner and independent review remain necessary before these tasks can establish a verified solve in the application.

### Reading routes

- New learner: read Part 2, document and text elements, shared attributes, then forms and resource elements. Work through the API examples after understanding the markup.
- Language switcher: focus on parsed DOM versus source, string attributes versus live properties, input applicability, native behavior, and browser security boundaries.
- Interview or DSA learner: use HTML as the interface layer for an algorithm visualizer or practice tool. HTML describes the interface; JavaScript or another executable language implements the algorithm. Do not invent a time complexity for a tag.
- Mentor or content author: retrieve the element entry, its attribute records, the relevant API case study and the misconception together. A fluent answer is not execution evidence.

## 2 Fourteen teaching lenses

The supplied curriculum blueprints organize a topic through reusable lenses. For HTML, apply the following questions to every lesson rather than importing data-structure complexity claims into markup.

1. Mental model: What meaning does the element communicate and what native behavior exists?
2. Creation: Which parent, children and serialization rules make the markup valid?
3. Access: How do a learner, browser and script locate the element and its relationships?
4. Mutation: Which operation changes source attributes, live state or rendered output?
5. Adding and removing: What happens to focus, labels, form ownership and references when a node changes?
6. Traversal: What is the DOM order, reading order and keyboard path?
7. Identity: Which ID, name, object identity or URL is being compared?
8. Ordering: Does source order express meaning, and is CSS only changing the visual order?
9. Transformation: Which browser algorithm parses or normalizes the authored strings?
10. Performance: What resource, decoding or rendering work is requested, and what needs measurement?
11. Edge cases: What if an attribute is absent, empty, invalid, repeated or inapplicable?
12. Fit and alternatives: Is there a native element that better expresses the task?
13. Patterns: Which navigation, input, disclosure, media or component workflow uses the feature?
14. Testing and debugging: Which source, DOM, accessibility, network and interaction observations establish the claim?

### From source to behavior

HTML bytes are decoded, tokenized and parsed into a DOM tree. The tree is not a literal copy of tag indentation. The parser may close a paragraph before a div, insert a tbody, or otherwise recover from malformed source. Conformance and recovery are different: a browser displaying something does not prove the source is valid.

DOM nodes expose interfaces such as HTMLInputElement and HTMLDialogElement. Attributes are serialized settings, while interface properties can reflect settings, resolve URLs, expose live state or hold a value with no content-attribute counterpart. CSS uses the tree for styling and layout; accessibility mappings use its semantics and state; resource loaders and Web APIs use element-specific algorithms. A single change can affect several of these consumers.

A tag is syntax in the source. An element is the resulting structured object. A void element, such as img or input, has no HTML end tag. A slash on a void start tag does not switch the document to XML. A comment and a doctype are markup constructs rather than element tags. For a normal HTML document use <!doctype html> so the browser can select standards mode.

### Attribute value models

A boolean attribute is true by presence: disabled="false" still supplies disabled. Remove the attribute or set the corresponding boolean property to false when the intended state is off. Enumerated attributes, such as contenteditable and draggable, interpret defined keywords; their missing and invalid states can differ. Do not transfer a boolean rule to an enumerated attribute.

Token-list attributes such as class and rel contain separate tokens rather than arbitrary prose. URL attributes are resolved against the document base and may expose a normalized absolute URL through a property. Numeric attributes can clamp, default or reject invalid values according to their own rules. ID references connect nodes, so duplicates and incorrect tree scope can break a relationship even when the text looks right.

In text content, escape an actual markup less-than sign as < and an ampersand beginning a character reference as appropriate. Attribute quoting, URL validation, CSS strings and JavaScript strings are distinct contexts. Escaping a text node is not a universal sanitizer for a URL, script or iframe document.

### Evidence and accessible behavior

Begin with a semantic choice: a navigates, button acts, table expresses data relationships, and label names a control. Native HTML can provide useful keyboard and state behavior with no script. ARIA supplements permitted semantics; it cannot make a div behave like a button or stop interaction merely by declaring aria-disabled.

Inspect authored source, parsed DOM, computed accessibility names, keyboard behavior and actual network requests as different kinds of evidence. For example, a form can look correct but omit a field from submission because name is missing or the control is disabled. An image can load while its alternative is misleading. A dialog can look modal while background interaction remains available because it was opened nonmodally.

References: WHATWG syntax, DOM, common DOM interfaces and interaction chapters; W3C ARIA in HTML. Exact topic links appear in the element and attribute records.

## 3 Shared attributes and their families

These attributes apply across HTML elements, subject to defined context and behavior. An attribute can be syntactically available while having no useful effect on a particular element. Event handlers are in Part 7; ARIA and other specifications are distinguished in Part 11. The same dictionary IDs are used throughout this document.

### A004 accesskey

`accesskey`. Suggest keyboard shortcuts using space-separated single-character tokens. The browser chooses the actual modifier combination.

Watch for: Shortcuts can conflict with browser or assistive-technology commands; never make them the only path.

### A010 aria-family

`aria-*`. Provide defined ARIA states, relationships and properties where allowed for the element or role.

Watch for: This is a separate finite vocabulary, not permission to invent arbitrary aria names or duplicate native state.

### A013 autocapitalize

`autocapitalize`. Recommend capitalization behavior for supported text-entry methods, with values such as sentences, words, characters, none or off.

Watch for: This is an input-method hint, not a transformation or validation rule.

### A015 autocorrect

`autocorrect`. Recommend whether supported entry methods correct user text, using on or off.

Watch for: Do not assume every browser or keyboard honors the preference.

### A016 autofocus

`autofocus`. Request focus during the applicable document or dialog focus process. It is a boolean attribute.

Watch for: Choose focus deliberately; unexpected focus can skip context or open an on-screen keyboard.

### A022 class

`class`. Assign space-separated class tokens used by selectors and application conventions. classList provides token operations.

Watch for: A class name has no native HTML meaning and does not grant a role.

### A031 contenteditable

`contenteditable`. Enable editing using true, false or plaintext-only; an empty value enables editing. Behavior can inherit from an ancestor.

Watch for: This is enumerated, not boolean; editable content still needs sanitization and storage logic.

### A036 data-family

`data-*`. Carry application-defined string data through valid custom data attribute names, such as data-route-id. dataset maps hyphenated names to DOMStringMap keys.

Watch for: The family is open-ended; it has no finite attribute list, and data is neither hidden nor trusted.

### A041 dir

`dir`. Specify ltr, rtl or auto text direction. bdo specifically needs an explicit ltr or rtl override.

Watch for: Direction is not the language, and right alignment is not a substitute for directionality.

### A045 draggable

`draggable`. Request drag behavior with true or false. Native auto behavior differs by element.

Watch for: It is enumerated; draggable="false" actually means false, unlike disabled="false".

### A047 enterkeyhint

`enterkeyhint`. Suggest an enter-key label or action such as search, send, next or done on supported virtual keyboards.

Watch for: It does not implement the action or change submission semantics.

### A057 headingoffset

`headingoffset`. Apply a numeric offset to descendant heading levels under the current heading-level rules; allowed values are 0 through 8.

Watch for: This is a newer standard feature; keep explicit meaningful heading ranks and test accessibility mappings before relying on it.

### A058 headingreset

`headingreset`. Stop heading-offset computation from continuing beyond the marked element. It is a boolean boundary.

Watch for: This does not rewrite heading tag names or establish tested browser support.

### A060 hidden

`hidden`. Mark content as currently irrelevant to presentation. hidden or empty represents the ordinary hidden state; until-found supports a distinct reveal workflow.

Watch for: hidden="false" is still hidden. CSS can affect rendering, and hidden content is not secret.

### A065 id

`id`. Give an element a unique nonempty identifier without ASCII whitespace in its tree. IDs support fragments, labels, scripts and ID references.

Watch for: Duplicates can silently redirect associations; window named properties are not a safe lookup strategy.

### A068 inert

`inert`. Make a subtree inert for applicable user interaction and focus behavior. It is boolean.

Watch for: It does not authorize access or remove source data; consider modal and flat-tree behavior.

### A069 inputmode

`inputmode`. Hint the entry modality using text, tel, email, url, numeric, decimal, search or none.

Watch for: A numeric keyboard hint accepts no validation responsibility and does not turn text into a number.

### A071 is

`is`. Request a defined customized built-in element at creation, using its registered custom-element name.

Watch for: Changing is later does not upgrade an ordinary element into the requested built-in; support needs checking.

### A073 itemid

`itemid`. Provide a global identifier for a microdata item where the vocabulary and item context allow it.

Watch for: An item ID is metadata, not the DOM id attribute or a security credential.

### A074 itemprop

`itemprop`. Attach one or more microdata property names to an element. The value is derived from the element-specific microdata rules.

Watch for: Do not assume every property takes its value from textContent.

### A075 itemref

`itemref`. Reference additional elements by ID for a microdata item's properties.

Watch for: Resolve IDs in the intended scope and avoid cycles or accidental unrelated properties.

### A076 itemscope

`itemscope`. Start a microdata item. This boolean changes the metadata grouping of descendant properties.

Watch for: It does not instantiate a JavaScript object or validate a vocabulary.

### A077 itemtype

`itemtype`. Declare microdata type URLs on an item.

Watch for: The vocabulary is separate from HTML; a declared type does not guarantee a rich search result.

### A080 lang

`lang`. Declare the human language using a BCP 47 language tag, with inheritance where applicable.

Watch for: It can help pronunciation and processing; it does not translate content.

### A095 nonce

`nonce`. Carry a server-generated cryptographic nonce authorized by an actual Content Security Policy.

Watch for: A nonce without a matching policy does nothing; do not reuse predictable values as a security design.

### A103 popover

`popover`. Create a popover state using auto, manual or hint, with empty meaning auto under current rules.

Watch for: Popover does not automatically supply menu semantics, a modal focus boundary or tooltip usability.

### A113 role

`role`. Declare permitted accessibility semantics from the applicable ARIA role vocabulary.

Watch for: A role does not implement keyboard behavior, and HTML restricts which overrides are allowed.

### A128 slot

`slot`. Assign a light-DOM node to a named slot in a shadow host; an empty name targets the default slot.

Watch for: This attribute and the slot element's name connect different sides of projection.

### A130 spellcheck

`spellcheck`. Recommend spelling and grammar checking using true or false, with an empty value treated under its enumerated rules.

Watch for: It does not enforce language correctness or reliably prevent remote processing by all input tools.

### A137 style

`style`. Supply CSS declarations on the element. The style DOM property exposes a declaration object.

Watch for: It changes presentation; it does not change the content model or sanitize a CSS string.

### A138 tabindex

`tabindex`. Control focusability and sequential focus ordering through an integer. Zero follows normal ordering; negative values remove ordinary sequential entry while permitting relevant focus behavior.

Watch for: Avoid positive ordering as a routine layout repair, and do not make hidden controls focusable.

### A140 title

`title`. Provide advisory text, or a context-specific expansion or stylesheet title. Some elements specialize its meaning.

Watch for: It is not a dependable substitute for a label, visible instructions or image alternatives.

### A141 translate

`translate`. Specify whether text and applicable attribute values should be translated, using yes or no; empty means yes.

Watch for: It is guidance for localization tooling, not an access or privacy control.

### A147 writingsuggestions

`writingsuggestions`. Recommend whether writing suggestions are offered using true or false and the defined empty-value behavior.

Watch for: It is separate from spellcheck, autocorrect and application-generated completions.

## 4 Complete attribute dictionary

Each entry identifies the attribute spelling, its consumers, value model and practical limit. The contexts and value grammar summaries come from the observed WHATWG attribute index; the explanations are teaching prose. A list of elements does not remove a type-specific or contextual restriction. Shared attributes are repeated here as lookup records so the dictionary is complete in one place.

### A001 abbr definition

`abbr`. On th, offer a concise header label for contexts that reference the header.

Watch for: It is not the abbr element and does not replace the full visible header.

Context: th. Value grammar: Text*.

Source: https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/tables.html#attr-th-abbr

`accept`. On file input, suggest file types using MIME types, wildcards and valid extension tokens such as .pdf.

Watch for: It is a chooser hint; inspect type, size and content on the server.

`accept-charset`. On form, declare UTF-8 for submission using the currently permitted encoding value.

Source: https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/forms.html#attr-form-accept-charset

Watch for: Disabled form controls are excluded from normal entry construction; disabled is not supported on anchors.

Source: https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/form-control-infrastructure.html#attr-fe-disabled

Context: fieldset. Value grammar: Boolean attribute.

Source: https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/form-elements.html#attr-fieldset-disabled

Context: link. Value grammar: Boolean attribute.

Source: https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/semantics.html#attr-link-disabled

### A044 download definition

`download`. Request download behavior on a or area and optionally suggest a filename.

Watch for: Origin, response headers and browser policy affect the result; it cannot force every resource to download.

Context: a; area. Value grammar: Text.

Source: https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/links.html#attr-hyperlink-download

### A045 draggable definition

`draggable`. Request drag behavior with true or false. Native auto behavior differs by element.

Watch for: It is enumerated; draggable="false" actually means false, unlike disabled="false".

Context: HTML elements. Value grammar: "true"; "false".

Source: https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/dnd.html#attr-draggable

### A046 enctype definition

`enctype`. Choose a form's entry encoding: application/x-www-form-urlencoded, multipart/form-data or text/plain.

Watch for: Use multipart for file uploads; the server must parse the actual payload safely.

Context: form. Value grammar: "application/x-www-form-urlencoded"; "multipart/form-data"; "text/plain".

Source: https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/form-control-infrastructure.html#attr-fs-enctype

### A047 enterkeyhint definition

`enterkeyhint`. Suggest an enter-key label or action such as search, send, next or done on supported virtual keyboards.

Watch for: It does not implement the action or change submission semantics.

Context: HTML elements. Value grammar: "enter"; "done"; "go"; "next"; "previous"; "search"; "send".

Source: https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/interaction.html#attr-enterkeyhint

### A048 fetchpriority definition

`fetchpriority`. Hint high, low or auto priority for eligible image, link or script fetches.

Watch for: It is a scheduling hint, not a guarantee of faster loading or a substitute for measurement.

Context: img; link; script. Value grammar: "auto"; "high"; "low".

Source: https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/embedded-content.html#attr-img-fetchpriority

### A049 for definition

`for`. On label, reference one labelable control ID. On output, list contributing control IDs. On current template update mechanisms, identify a same-tree marker or start ProcessingInstruction by its name.

Watch for: These meanings are distinct; do not copy the same ID-list grammar between contexts.

Context: label. Value grammar: ID*.

Source: https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/forms.html#attr-label-for

Context: output. Value grammar: Unordered set of unique space-separated tokens consisting of IDs*.

Source: https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/form-elements.html#attr-output-for

Context: template. Value grammar: Text.

Source: https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/scripting.html#attr-template-for

### A050 form definition

`form`. Associate an eligible element with a form by the form's ID.

Watch for: Visual containment is not the same as form ownership, and shadow-root boundaries affect associations.

Context: button; fieldset; input; object; output; select; textarea; form-associated custom elements. Value grammar: ID*.

Source: https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/form-control-infrastructure.html#attr-fae-form

### A051 formaction definition

`formaction`. Override the form's destination for the activated submit button or applicable input submitter.

Watch for: It applies to the submitter context, not arbitrary buttons or input types.
