all nodes
ruby-trie-insert   lens: creation   level: L1   family: ruby-trie-creation
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: ruby-trie-search. Complexity: O(L).
Common misconception. Hash.new({}) is a convenient way to give every node an empty children Hash that fills itself
in.

Ruby Trie · 4. Trie strategies (continued)
The default value of Hash.new({}) is a single shared Hash object, and reading a missing key returns it without storing
anything, so children[ch] ||= is never true and the code walks into a bare Hash that has no node methods. Writes
through the default would be visible from every node. Use a plain {} per node and create children with ||=. Insert costs
O(L) for a word of length L.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
BadNode = Struct.new(:children, :terminal)
def new_bad_node
BadNode.new(Hash.new({}), false)
end
def insert_bad(root, word)
node = root
word.each_char { |ch| node = (node.children[ch] ||= new_bad_node) }
node.terminal = true
end
Correct:
class TrieNode
attr_reader :children
attr_accessor :terminal, :pass
def initialize
@children = {}
@terminal = false
@pass = 0
end
end
class Trie
attr_reader :root, :size
def initialize
@root = TrieNode.new
@size = 0
end
def insert(word)
existing = find(word)
return false if existing && existing.terminal
node = @root
word.each_char do |ch|
node = (node.children[ch] ||= TrieNode.new)
node.pass += 1
end
node.terminal = true
@size += 1
end
private
def find(str)
node = @root
str.each_char do |ch|
node = node.children[ch]
return nil unless node
end
node
end
end
A word exists only if its last node is terminal; a prefix exists if the path exists
ruby-trie-search   lens: access   level: L2   family: ruby-trie-access
Prerequisites: ruby-trie-insert. Follow-up: ruby-trie-autocomplete. Complexity: O(L).
Common misconception. A word is in the trie when its path of characters exists.

Ruby Trie · 4. Trie strategies (continued)
The path for "app" exists as soon as "apple" is inserted, but "app" was never added as a word. Words need a terminal
flag on the last node, while a prefix check only needs the path. Both walk L nodes, O(L), independent of how many
words are stored.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
def search_bad(trie, word)
!trie.send(:find, word).nil?
end
Correct:
class Trie
def include?(word)
node = find(word)
!node.nil? && node.terminal
end
def prefix?(prefix)
!find(prefix).nil?
end
end
Autocomplete walks the subtree and builds each word with prefix + ch, never by mutating a
shared string
ruby-trie-autocomplete   lens: iteration   level: L2   family: ruby-trie-iteration
Prerequisites: ruby-trie-search. Follow-up: ruby-trie-delete. Complexity: O(L+k).
Common misconception. Appending the character with << to the prefix as the recursion descends builds the words.
The same String object is passed to every recursive call, so << keeps lengthening it and siblings see the leftovers of
earlier branches, producing words like "abc" for "ac". Build a new string with prefix + ch for each child. Sort the results
for a deterministic order. Cost is O(L + size of the subtree).
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
def collect_bad(node, prefix, out)
out << prefix.dup if node.terminal
node.children.each { |ch, child| collect_bad(child, prefix << ch, out) }
out
end
Correct:
class Trie
def words_with_prefix(prefix)
node = find(prefix)
return [] unless node
out = []
collect(node, prefix, out)
out.sort
end
private
def collect(node, prefix, out)

Ruby Trie · 4. Trie strategies (continued)
out << prefix if node.terminal
node.children.each { |ch, child| collect(child, prefix + ch, out) }
end
end
Counting words with a prefix reads one pass counter instead of traversing the subtree
ruby-trie-count   lens: patterns   level: L2   family: ruby-trie-patterns
Prerequisites: ruby-trie-delete. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(L).
Common misconception. The number of words with a prefix is 1 if the prefix node is terminal, otherwise 0.
That only counts the prefix itself. Every node stores how many inserted words pass through it, so the count for a
prefix is the pass counter of its node, or 0 when the path is missing. Duplicate inserts must be ignored or the counters
inflate. The query is O(L), independent of the number of matches.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
def count_bad(trie, prefix)
node = trie.send(:find, prefix)
node && node.terminal ? 1 : 0
end
Correct:
class Trie
def count_prefix(prefix)
node = find(prefix)
node ? node.pass : 0
end
end
Deleting a word must not remove longer words that share its path
ruby-trie-delete   lens: insertion-and-deletion   level: L3   family: ruby-trie-insertion-and-deletion
Prerequisites: ruby-trie-autocomplete. Follow-up: ruby-trie-count. Complexity: O(L).
Common misconception. Deleting a word means removing the last character's node from its parent.
Removing that node also removes every longer word below it, so deleting "app" would delete "apple". Keep a pass
count on each node (how many words go through it). Decrement along the path, delete the first child whose count
reaches zero, and otherwise just clear the terminal flag. Delete costs O(L).
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
def delete_bad(trie, word)

Ruby Trie · 4. Trie strategies (continued)
node = trie.root
parent = nil
word.each_char do |ch|
parent = node
node = node.children[ch]
return false unless node
end
parent.children.delete(word[-1])
end
Correct:
class Trie
def delete(word)
existing = find(word)
return false unless existing && existing.terminal
node = @root
word.each_char do |ch|
child = node.children[ch]
child.pass -= 1
if child.pass.zero?
node.children.delete(ch)
@size -= 1
return true
end
node = child
end
node.terminal = false
@size -= 1
end
end

Every element starts as its own parent: parent[i] = i, not a repeated default
ruby-disjointset-create   lens: creation   level: L1   family: ruby-disjointset-creation
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: ruby-disjointset-compress. Complexity: O(h).
 Common misconception. Array.new(n, 0) is a fine initial parent array.
With every parent set to 0, all elements start in the set of element 0, so every pair looks connected before any union.
A root is defined by parent[x] == x, so the initial array must be the identity: Array.new(n) { |i| i }. Then n elements form
n sets, find walks parents up to the root, and union links one root to the other. The count of sets starts at n and drops
by one per successful union.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def find_bad(parent, x)
  x = parent[x] while parent[x] != x
  x
end
Correct:
 class DisjointSet
  attr_reader :parent, :rank, :count
  def initialize(n)
    @parent = Array.new(n) { |i| i }
    @rank = Array.new(n, 0)
    @count = n
  end
  def find(x)
    x = @parent[x] while @parent[x] != x
    x
  end
  def union(a, b)
    ra = find(a)
    rb = find(b)
    return false if ra == rb
    @parent[ra] = rb
    @count -= 1
    true
  end
  def connected?(a, b)
    find(a) == find(b)
  end
end

For arbitrary keys use a Hash whose default block stores the key as its own parent
ruby-disjointset-named   lens: creation   level: L2   family: ruby-disjointset-creation
Prerequisites: ruby-disjointset-kruskal. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(α(n)).
 Common misconception. A plain Hash of parents works for strings and symbols, since missing keys can be added
later.
find on an unseen key returns nil with a plain Hash, so union of two new keys compares nil with nil, decides they are
already connected and merges nothing. A Hash.new { |h, k| h[k] = k } default block stores each new key as its own
root on first access. Keep sizes in a Hash.new(1) for union by size. Group the keys by their root to list the sets.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):

  def initialize
    @parent = {}
  end
  def find(x)
    x = @parent[x] while @parent[x] != x
    x

  def union(a, b)

    rb = find(b)

    true

end
Correct:
 class NamedSets
  def initialize
    @parent = Hash.new { |h, k| h[k] = k }
    @size = Hash.new(1)
  end
  def find(x)
    root = x
    root = @parent[root] while @parent[root] != root
    while @parent[x] != root
      nxt = @parent[x]
      @parent[x] = root
      x = nxt
    end
    root
  end
  def union(a, b)
    ra = find(a)
    rb = find(b)
    return false if ra == rb
    ra, rb = rb, ra if @size[ra] < @size[rb]
    @parent[rb] = ra
    @size[ra] += @size[rb]
    true
  end
  def groups
    @parent.keys.group_by { |k| find(k) }.values.map(&:sort).sort
  end
  def sets_count
    groups.size
  end
end

Path compression must repoint every node on the path, saving the next node before
changing the link
ruby-disjointset-compress   lens: access   level: L2   family: ruby-disjointset-access
Prerequisites: ruby-disjointset-create. Follow-up: ruby-disjointset-rank. Complexity: O(α(n)).
 Common misconception. After finding the root, setting parent[x] = root for the starting node is enough.
Only the first node would then skip ahead; the nodes in the middle of the path keep long chains, so repeated finds
stay slow. Walk the path again from the start and set each node to the root, reading the old parent before overwriting
it. With compression, find is nearly constant on average (inverse Ackermann amortised with union by rank).
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def compress_bad(parent, x)
  root = x
  root = parent[root] while parent[root] != root
  parent[x] = root
  root
end
Correct:
 class DisjointSet
  def find(x)
    root = x
    root = @parent[root] while @parent[root] != root
    while @parent[x] != root
      nxt = @parent[x]
      @parent[x] = root
      x = nxt
    end
    root
  end
end
Union by rank attaches the shorter tree under the taller one to keep trees shallow
ruby-disjointset-rank   lens: insertion-and-deletion   level: L2   family: ruby-disjointset-insertion-and-deletion
Prerequisites: ruby-disjointset-compress. Follow-up: ruby-disjointset-kruskal. Complexity: O(log n).
 Common misconception. Always attach the first root under the second root.
Sequential unions such as (0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 3) then build a single long chain, and find becomes O(n). Attach the root
with the smaller rank (an upper bound of the height) under the other, and increase the rank only when both ranks are
equal. Trees then have height O(log n); with path compression the amortised cost per operation is nearly constant.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def union_bad(parent, a, b)
  ra = a
  ra = parent[ra] while parent[ra] != ra
  rb = b
  rb = parent[rb] while parent[rb] != rb
  parent[ra] = rb unless ra == rb
end
def depth_of(parent, x)
  d = 0
  while parent[x] != x
    x = parent[x]
    d += 1
  end
  d
end

  def union(a, b)
    ra = find(a)
    rb = find(b)

Union returns false for an edge inside one set, which is how cycles are detected and Kruskal
skips edges
ruby-disjointset-kruskal   lens: patterns   level: L3   family: ruby-disjointset-patterns
Prerequisites: ruby-disjointset-rank. Follow-up: ruby-disjointset-named. Complexity: O(E log E).
 Common misconception. Kruskal can union every sorted edge and add its weight.
An edge whose endpoints are already connected would close a cycle and must be skipped, so the weight is added
only when union reports that it merged two different sets. Sort the edges by weight, take the cheapest edges that do
not form a cycle, and stop when the forest is connected. Sorting dominates: O(E log E). The same test finds cycles in
an undirected graph.

    ds.union(u, v)
    w
  end
end

  ds = DisjointSet.new(n)
  edges.sort_by { |e| e[2] }.sum { |u, v, w| ds.union(u, v) ? w : 0 }
end
def has_cycle?(n, edges)
  ds = DisjointSet.new(n)
  edges.any? { |u, v| !ds.union(u, v) }
end

ruby-disjointset-create   lens: creation   level: L1   family: ruby-disjointset-creation
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: ruby-disjointset-compress. Complexity: O(h).
Common misconception. Array.new(n, 0) is a fine initial parent array.

Ruby Disjoint set · 4. Disjoint set strategies (continued)
With every parent set to 0, all elements start in the set of element 0, so every pair looks connected before any union.
A root is defined by parent[x] == x, so the initial array must be the identity: Array.new(n) { |i| i }. Then n elements form
n sets, find walks parents up to the root, and union links one root to the other. The count of sets starts at n and drops
by one per successful union.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):

Correct:
class DisjointSet
attr_reader :parent, :rank, :count
def initialize(n)
@parent = Array.new(n) { |i| i }
@rank = Array.new(n, 0)
@count = n
end
def find(x)
x = @parent[x] while @parent[x] != x
x
end
def union(a, b)
ra = find(a)
rb = find(b)
return false if ra == rb
@parent[ra] = rb
@count -= 1
end
def connected?(a, b)
find(a) == find(b)
end
end
For arbitrary keys use a Hash whose default block stores the key as its own parent

Prerequisites: ruby-disjointset-kruskal. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(α(n)).

later.
find on an unseen key returns nil with a plain Hash, so union of two new keys compares nil with nil, decides they are
already connected and merges nothing. A Hash.new { |h, k| h[k] = k } default block stores each new key as its own
root on first access. Keep sizes in a Hash.new(1) for union by size. Group the keys by their root to list the sets.

class NamedSets
def initialize
@parent = Hash.new { |h, k| h[k] = k }
@size = Hash.new(1)

def find(x)
root = x
root = @parent[root] while @parent[root] != root
while @parent[x] != root
nxt = @parent[x]
@parent[x] = root
x = nxt
end
root

def union(a, b)
ra = find(a)
rb = find(b)
return false if ra == rb
ra, rb = rb, ra if @size[ra] < @size[rb]
@parent[rb] = ra
@size[ra] += @size[rb]
end
def groups
@parent.keys.group_by { |k| find(k) }.values.map(&:sort).sort
end
def sets_count
groups.size
end
end

changing the link

Prerequisites: ruby-disjointset-create. Follow-up: ruby-disjointset-rank. Complexity: O(α(n)).
Common misconception. After finding the root, setting parent[x] = root for the starting node is enough.
Only the first node would then skip ahead; the nodes in the middle of the path keep long chains, so repeated finds
stay slow. Walk the path again from the start and set each node to the root, reading the old parent before overwriting
it. With compression, find is nearly constant on average (inverse Ackermann amortised with union by rank).

Union by rank attaches the shorter tree under the taller one to keep trees shallow
ruby-disjointset-rank   lens: insertion-and-deletion   level: L2   family: ruby-disjointset-insertion-and-deletion
Prerequisites: ruby-disjointset-compress. Follow-up: ruby-disjointset-kruskal. Complexity: O(log n).
Common misconception. Always attach the first root under the second root.
Sequential unions such as (0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 3) then build a single long chain, and find becomes O(n). Attach the root
with the smaller rank (an upper bound of the height) under the other, and increase the rank only when both ranks are
equal. Trees then have height O(log n); with path compression the amortised cost per operation is nearly constant.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
def union_bad(parent, a, b)
ra = a
ra = parent[ra] while parent[ra] != ra
rb = b
rb = parent[rb] while parent[rb] != rb

end
def depth_of(parent, x)

while parent[x] != x
x = parent[x]
d += 1
end
d

Correct:
class DisjointSet
def union(a, b)
ra = find(a)
rb = find(b)
return false if ra == rb
ra, rb = rb, ra if @rank[ra] < @rank[rb]
@parent[rb] = ra
@rank[ra] += 1 if @rank[ra] == @rank[rb]
@count -= 1
end
end
Union returns false for an edge inside one set, which is how cycles are detected and Kruskal
skips edges
ruby-disjointset-kruskal   lens: patterns   level: L3   family: ruby-disjointset-patterns
Prerequisites: ruby-disjointset-rank. Follow-up: ruby-disjointset-named. Complexity: O(E log E).
Common misconception. Kruskal can union every sorted edge and add its weight.

Ruby Disjoint set · 4. Disjoint set strategies (continued)
An edge whose endpoints are already connected would close a cycle and must be skipped, so the weight is added
only when union reports that it merged two different sets. Sort the edges by weight, take the cheapest edges that do
not form a cycle, and stop when the forest is connected. Sorting dominates: O(E log E). The same test finds cycles in
an undirected graph.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
def mst_bad(n, edges)

edges.sort_by { |e| e[2] }.sum do |u, v, w|
ds.union(u, v)
w
end
end
Correct:
def mst_weight(n, edges)
ds = DisjointSet.new(n)
edges.sort_by { |e| e[2] }.sum { |u, v, w| ds.union(u, v) ? w : 0 }
end
def has_cycle?(n, edges)
ds = DisjointSet.new(n)
edges.any? { |u, v| !ds.union(u, v) }
end

A stack pops from the same end it pushes to, and popping an empty stack must be handled
ruby-stack-pushpop   lens: insertion-and-deletion   level: L1   family: ruby-stack-insertion-and-deletion
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: ruby-stack-balanced. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Array#pop on an empty array is a safe way to read the top of a stack.
Array#pop and Array#last return nil on an empty array instead of raising, so a missing element travels onward until a
later call such as nil + nil fails far from the cause. A Stack class can raise a clear error on pop and peek of an empty
stack. push, pop and peek are O(1). Iterating from the top gives last-in, first-out order.

 def add_top_bad(items)

Correct:
 class EmptyStackError < StandardError; end
class Stack
  include Enumerable
  def initialize
    @items = []
  end
  def push(v)
    @items.push(v)
    self
  end
  def pop
    raise EmptyStackError, "pop from empty stack" if @items.empty?
    @items.pop
  end
  def peek
    raise EmptyStackError, "peek at empty stack" if @items.empty?
    @items.last
  end
  def empty?
    @items.empty?
  end
  def size
    @items.size
  end
  def each(&block)
    return to_enum(:each) unless block
    @items.reverse_each(&block)
    self
  end
end

Balanced brackets need a stack because a counter cannot check the order of different kinds
ruby-stack-balanced   lens: patterns   level: L2   family: ruby-stack-patterns
Prerequisites: ruby-stack-pushpop. Follow-up: ruby-stack-minstack. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. Counting opening and closing brackets of each kind is enough to validate a string.
Equal counts do not mean proper nesting: "([)]" has one of each kind and ")(" has equal counts but closes before it
opens. Push each opener, and on a closer pop and compare with the matching opener. The string is balanced only if
no mismatch occurs and the stack ends empty. One pass, O(n).
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):

  s.count("([{") == s.count(")]}")
end
Correct:
 PAIRS = { ")" => "(", "]" => "[", "}" => "{" }
def balanced?(s)
  stack = Stack.new
  s.each_char do |ch|
    if PAIRS.value?(ch)
      stack.push(ch)
    elsif PAIRS.key?(ch)
      return false if stack.empty? || stack.pop != PAIRS[ch]
    end
  end
  stack.empty?
end

left one. Swapping them is harmless for + and * but reverses - and /. Pop b, pop a, then compute a op b. Evaluation is
O(n).

Array#pop and Array#last return nil on an empty array instead of raising, so a missing element travels onward until a

end

@items.pop

@items.last
end

@items.empty?
end

return to_enum(:each) unless block
@items.reverse_each(&block)
self

stack.push(ch)

2. Overview and mental model: AVL tree
An AVL tree is a binary search tree that keeps the heights of every node's two subtrees within one. Rotations restore

number of links, so it is O(1), and it preserves the in-order sequence of keys.

class AVL
  include Enumerable
  attr_reader :root, :size
  def initialize
    @root = nil
    @size = 0
  end
  def insert(key)
    @root = insert_at(@root, key)
    self
  end
  def height
    height_of(@root)
  end
  def each(&block)
    return to_enum(:each) unless block
    walk(@root, &block)
    self
  end
  private
  def height_of(node)
    node ? node.height : 0

2. Overview and mental model: Heap
A binary min-heap stores a complete binary tree in an Array: node i has children 2i + 1 and 2i + 2 and parent (i - 1) / 2.
The smallest element is always at index 0.
push and pop are O(log n), peek is O(1) and bottom-up build is O(n). Ruby has no built-in heap; a small class or an
array with min and delete is the usual choice.
Ruby division and negative array indexes hide off-by-one bugs: (0 - 1) / 2 is -1 and @a[-1] is the last element, so
guard the loop with i > 0.

negative-index trap, sift-down, O(n) heapify, kth largest and a max-heap from negation. Examples are run
with Ruby 3.3.6.

failures. Concept chunks carry verified: true in the export.

2. Overview and mental model: Heap
A binary min-heap stores a complete binary tree in an Array: node i has children 2i + 1 and 2i + 2 and parent (i - 1) / 2.
The smallest element is always at index 0.
push and pop are O(log n), peek is O(1) and bottom-up build is O(n). Ruby has no built-in heap; a small class or an
array with min and delete is the usual choice.
Ruby division and negative array indexes hide off-by-one bugs: (0 - 1) / 2 is -1 and @a[-1] is the last element, so
guard the loop with i > 0.

4.4 Algorithm chunks
Sift-up must stop at index 0, because in Ruby (0 - 1) / 2 is -1 and -1 indexes the last element
ruby-heap-pushsift   lens: insertion-and-deletion   level: L1   family: ruby-heap-insertion-and-deletion
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: ruby-heap-pop. Complexity: O(log n).
 Common misconception. The loop can end naturally when the parent is not larger than the value.
A binary heap stores node i's parent at (i - 1) / 2. Ruby integer division rounds toward negative infinity, so for i = 0 the
parent index is -1, and @a[-1] is the last element of the array, not an error. Without an i > 0 guard the root is
compared with the last element and the two can be swapped, corrupting the heap. push is O(log n).
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def sift_up_bad(a, i)
  parent = (i - 1) / 2
  while a[parent] > a[i]
    a[parent], a[i] = a[i], a[parent]
    i = parent
    parent = (i - 1) / 2
  end
  a
end

Correct:
 class MinHeap
  attr_reader :size
  def initialize
    @a = []
  end
  def size
    @a.size
  end
  def empty?
    @a.empty?
  end
  def peek
    @a.first
  end
  def push(v)
    @a.push(v)
    sift_up(@a.size - 1)
    self
  end
  def pop
    return nil if @a.empty?
    top = @a[0]
    last = @a.pop
    unless @a.empty?
      @a[0] = last
      sift_down(0)
    end
    top
  end
  private
  def sift_up(i)
    while i > 0
      parent = (i - 1) / 2
      break if @a[parent] <= @a[i]
      @a[parent], @a[i] = @a[i], @a[parent]
      i = parent
    end
  end
  def sift_down(i)
    n = @a.size
    loop do
      l = 2 * i + 1
      r = l + 1
      small = i
      small = l if l < n && @a[l] < @a[small]
      small = r if r < n && @a[r] < @a[small]
      break if small == i
      @a[small], @a[i] = @a[i], @a[small]
      i = small
    end
  end
end

Build a heap in O(n) by sifting down from the last parent to the root
ruby-heap-heapify   lens: creation   level: L2   family: ruby-heap-creation
Prerequisites: ruby-heap-pop. Follow-up: ruby-heap-kth. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. Sifting down from index 0 upward to the last parent builds the heap.
Sift-down assumes both child subtrees are already heaps, so the work must start at the bottom: from index n / 2 - 1
down to 0. Going from the root downwards fixes the root before its subtrees are ordered and leaves violations behind.
Most nodes are near the leaves and move little, so the total is O(n), better than n pushes at O(n log n).
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def build_bad(items)
  a = items.dup
  n = a.size
  (0...(n / 2)).each do |start|
    i = start
    while 2 * i + 1 < n
      l = 2 * i + 1
      r = l + 1
      s = i
      s = l if a[l] < a[s]
      s = r if r < n && a[r] < a[s]
      break if s == i
      a[s], a[i] = a[i], a[s]
      i = s
    end
  end
  a
end
Correct:
 class MinHeap
  def build(items)
    @a = items.dup
    (@a.size / 2 - 1).downto(0) { |i| sift_down(i) }
    self
  end
end
Sift-down swaps with the smaller of the two children, not always the left one
ruby-heap-pop   lens: insertion-and-deletion   level: L2   family: ruby-heap-insertion-and-deletion
Prerequisites: ruby-heap-pushsift. Follow-up: ruby-heap-heapify. Complexity: O(log n).
 Common misconception. After moving the last element to the root, swapping it with the left child when it is larger is
enough.
If the right child is smaller than the left one, swapping with the left child leaves the right child smaller than its new
parent, which breaks the heap order. Compare with both children and swap with the smallest. Children of i are 2i + 1
and 2i + 2, and each must be checked against the array size. pop is O(log n).
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def sift_down_bad(a, i)
  n = a.size
  while 2 * i + 1 < n
    l = 2 * i + 1
    break if a[l] >= a[i]
    a[l], a[i] = a[i], a[l]
    i = l
  end
  a
end

Correct:
 def sift_down_ok(a, i)
  n = a.size
  loop do
    l = 2 * i + 1
    r = l + 1
    small = i
    small = l if l < n && a[l] < a[small]
    small = r if r < n && a[r] < a[small]
    break if small == i
    a[small], a[i] = a[i], a[small]
    i = small
  end
  a
end
A max-heap can reuse a min-heap by negating keys, and must negate again on the way out
ruby-heap-maxheap   lens: ordering   level: L2   family: ruby-heap-ordering
Prerequisites: ruby-heap-kth. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(log n).
 Common misconception. Pushing negated values is enough; pop and peek already return the right numbers.
The negation trick turns the smallest negated value into the largest original one, but the heap stores and returns
negated numbers. Negate on push and negate again on pop and peek. It works for numeric keys only; for other types
pass a comparator or store an ordering key. Operations stay O(log n).
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 class MaxHeapBad
  def initialize
    @h = MinHeap.new
  end
  def push(v)
    @h.push(-v)
    self
  end
  def pop
    @h.pop
  end
end
Correct:
 class MaxHeap
  def initialize
    @h = MinHeap.new
  end
  def push(v)
    @h.push(-v)
    self
  end
  def pop
    v = @h.pop
    v && -v
  end
  def peek
    v = @h.peek
    v && -v
  end
  def size
    @h.size
  end
end

The kth largest element comes from a min-heap capped at k items, trimmed after each push
ruby-heap-kth   lens: patterns   level: L3   family: ruby-heap-patterns
Prerequisites: ruby-heap-heapify. Follow-up: ruby-heap-maxheap. Complexity: O(n log k).
 Common misconception. Trim the heap before adding the new value to keep it at k items.
Trimming before the push evicts the smallest stored value even when the new value is smaller still, so a small
newcomer displaces a larger value that belongs in the top k. Push first, then pop while the size exceeds k; the root is
then the smallest of the k largest values, which is the kth largest. Time O(n log k) and O(k) space, better than sorting
when k is small.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def kth_largest_bad(nums, k)
  h = MinHeap.new
  nums.each do |x|
    h.pop if h.size >= k
    h.push(x)
  end
  h.peek
end
Correct:
 def kth_largest(nums, k)
  h = MinHeap.new
  nums.each do |x|
    h.push(x)
    h.pop if h.size > k
  end
  h.peek
end

Prompt. Why is building a heap bottom-up with sift-down O(n) although each sift-down can cost O(log n)?
Answer key (mentor only, never embedded). Sift-down from a node costs at most the height of its subtree. Half of the
nodes are leaves and need no work, a quarter have height 1, an eighth have height 2, and so on. The total work is the
sum of height times the number of nodes at that height, which converges to a constant times n. Only the few nodes near
the root pay the full logarithmic cost.

A max-heap can reuse a min-heap by negating keys, and must negate again on the way out
ruby-heap-maxheap   lens: ordering   level: L2   family: ruby-heap-ordering
Prerequisites: ruby-heap-kth. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(log n).
Common misconception. Pushing negated values is enough; pop and peek already return the right numbers.
The negation trick turns the smallest negated value into the largest original one, but the heap stores and returns
negated numbers. Negate on push and negate again on pop and peek. It works for numeric keys only; for other types
pass a comparator or store an ordering key. Operations stay O(log n).

@h = MinHeap.new
end
def push(v)

self
end
def pop

end
end
Correct:
class MaxHeap
def initialize
@h = MinHeap.new
end
def push(v)
@h.push(-v)
self
end
def pop
v = @h.pop
v && -v
end
def peek
v = @h.peek
v && -v
end
def size
@h.size
end
end
The kth largest element comes from a min-heap capped at k items, trimmed after each push
ruby-heap-kth   lens: patterns   level: L3   family: ruby-heap-patterns
Prerequisites: ruby-heap-heapify. Follow-up: ruby-heap-maxheap. Complexity: O(n log k).
Common misconception. Trim the heap before adding the new value to keep it at k items.

Trimming before the push evicts the smallest stored value even when the new value is smaller still, so a small
newcomer displaces a larger value that belongs in the top k. Push first, then pop while the size exceeds k; the root is
then the smallest of the k largest values, which is the kth largest. Time O(n log k) and O(k) space, better than sorting
when k is small.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
def kth_largest_bad(nums, k)
h = MinHeap.new
nums.each do |x|
h.pop if h.size >= k
h.push(x)
end
h.peek
end
Correct:
def kth_largest(nums, k)
h = MinHeap.new
nums.each do |x|
h.push(x)
h.pop if h.size > k
end
h.peek
end

4.4 Algorithm chunks
Enumerator#next raises StopIteration at the end; loop rescues it, while and until do not
ruby-enumerator-next   lens: iteration   level: L2   family: ruby-enumerator-iteration
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: ruby-enumerator-lazy. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. e.next returns nil when the enumerator is exhausted.
External iteration with next hands out one element per call and raises StopIteration when the sequence is over.
Kernel#loop rescues StopIteration and ends quietly, so loop { out << e.next } is the idiom. A while true loop lets the
exception escape. peek looks ahead without consuming, and rewind starts again.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def drain_bad(arr)
  e = arr.each
  out = []
  while true
    out << e.next
  end
  out
end
Correct:
 def drain(arr)
  e = arr.each
  out = []
  loop { out << e.next }
  out
end

Page 5
map.with_index(1) numbers from 1; each_with_index starts at 0
ruby-enumerator-index   lens: transformation   level: L2   family: ruby-enumerator-transformation
Prerequisites: ruby-enumerator-generator. Follow-up: ruby-enumerator-window. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. each_with_index numbers the elements from 1.
each_with_index and with_index default to a zero-based offset. Pass an argument to start elsewhere:
map.with_index(1). The enumerator returned by map without a block carries the method with it, so with_index
decides the offset and map decides what is collected.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def numbered_bad(items)
  items.each_with_index.map { |x, i| "#{i}. #{x}" }
end
Correct:
 def numbered(items)
  items.map.with_index(1) { |x, i| "#{i}. #{x}" }
end
Enumerator.new generates values with yielder << x; a generator without loop is finite
ruby-enumerator-generator   lens: creation   level: L3   family: ruby-enumerator-creation
Prerequisites: ruby-enumerator-lazy. Follow-up: ruby-enumerator-index. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. An Enumerator.new block keeps producing values by itself.
The block runs once and ends when it returns. To produce an infinite stream, wrap the yielding in loop { y << value }.
The stream is consumed on demand: take(8), first(8) or lazy chains stop it. Without loop the block yields its single
value and finishes, so take(8) returns one element.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def fib_bad
  Enumerator.new do |y|
    a, b = 0, 1
    y << a
  end
end
Correct:
 def fib
  Enumerator.new do |y|
    a, b = 0, 1
    loop do
      y << a
      a, b = b, a + b
    end
  end
end

lazy evaluates elements one at a time and stops early; eager map and select process the
whole collection first
ruby-enumerator-lazy   lens: iteration   level: L3   family: ruby-enumerator-iteration
Prerequisites: ruby-enumerator-next. Follow-up: ruby-enumerator-generator. Complexity: O(k).
 Common misconception. map.select.first(n) only processes as many elements as it needs.
Eager methods build a full intermediate array at every step, so (1..1000).map { }.select { }.first(2) calls the map block
1000 times. enum.lazy passes each element through the whole chain before taking the next, and first(n) stops once n
results exist. Lazy chains also work on infinite sources such as (1..).
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def eager(n)
  calls = 0
  r = (1..1000).map { |x| calls += 1; x * 2 }.select { |x| (x % 3).zero? }.first(n)
  [r, calls]
end
Correct:
 def lazily(n)
  calls = 0
  r = (1..1000).lazy.map { |x| calls += 1; x * 2 }.select { |x| (x % 3).zero? }.first(n)
  [r, calls]
end
each_cons gives overlapping windows; each_slice gives disjoint chunks
ruby-enumerator-window   lens: patterns   level: L3   family: ruby-enumerator-patterns
Prerequisites: ruby-enumerator-index. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(n * k).
 Common misconception. each_slice(k) visits every window of size k.
each_slice(k) cuts the collection into non-overlapping groups, so a sliding-window maximum sees only n / k windows.
each_cons(k) yields every consecutive window of size k: n - k + 1 of them. Summing each window is O(n * k), or O(n)
with a running sum.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def best_window_bad(nums, k)
  nums.each_slice(k).map(&:sum).max
end
Correct:
 def best_window(nums, k)
  nums.each_cons(k).map(&:sum).max
end

Prompt. Why does lazy make map and select over a large range cheaper when you only need the first few results?
Answer key (mentor only, never embedded). An eager chain finishes each step for the whole collection before the
next step starts, so map runs on every element and builds an array even though only a few results are used. A lazy chain
sends one element at a time through map and select and stops as soon as first(n) has n results, so only the elements up
to that point are ever processed, and no full intermediate arrays are created.

ruby-enumerator-generator   lens: creation   level: L3   family: ruby-enumerator-creation
Prerequisites: ruby-enumerator-lazy. Follow-up: ruby-enumerator-index. Complexity: O(n).
Common misconception. An Enumerator.new block keeps producing values by itself.
The block runs once and ends when it returns. To produce an infinite stream, wrap the yielding in loop { y << value }.
The stream is consumed on demand: take(8), first(8) or lazy chains stop it. Without loop the block yields its single
value and finishes, so take(8) returns one element.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
def fib_bad
Enumerator.new do |y|
a, b = 0, 1
y << a
end
end
Correct:
def fib
Enumerator.new do |y|
a, b = 0, 1
loop do
y << a
a, b = b, a + b
end
end
end
lazy evaluates elements one at a time and stops early; eager map and select process the
whole collection first
ruby-enumerator-lazy   lens: iteration   level: L3   family: ruby-enumerator-iteration
Prerequisites: ruby-enumerator-next. Follow-up: ruby-enumerator-generator. Complexity: O(k).
Common misconception. map.select.first(n) only processes as many elements as it needs.
Eager methods build a full intermediate array at every step, so (1..1000).map { }.select { }.first(2) calls the map block
1000 times. enum.lazy passes each element through the whole chain before taking the next, and first(n) stops once n
results exist. Lazy chains also work on infinite sources such as (1..).
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
def eager(n)
calls = 0
r = (1..1000).map { |x| calls += 1; x * 2 }.select { |x| (x % 3).zero? }.first(n)
[r, calls]
end
Correct:
def lazily(n)

Ruby Enumerator · 4. Enumerator strategies (continued)
calls = 0
r = (1..1000).lazy.map { |x| calls += 1; x * 2 }.select { |x| (x % 3).zero? }.first(n)
[r, calls]
end
each_cons gives overlapping windows; each_slice gives disjoint chunks
ruby-enumerator-window   lens: patterns   level: L3   family: ruby-enumerator-patterns
Prerequisites: ruby-enumerator-index. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(n * k).
Common misconception. each_slice(k) visits every window of size k.
each_slice(k) cuts the collection into non-overlapping groups, so a sliding-window maximum sees only n / k windows.
each_cons(k) yields every consecutive window of size k: n - k + 1 of them. Summing each window is O(n * k), or O(n)
with a running sum.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
def best_window_bad(nums, k)
nums.each_slice(k).map(&:sum).max
end
Correct:
def best_window(nums, k)
nums.each_cons(k).map(&:sum).max
end

4.4 Algorithm chunks
Split a segment into [l, mid] and [mid + 1, r] so the halves never overlap
ruby-segmenttree-build   lens: creation   level: L2   family: ruby-segmenttree-creation
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: ruby-segmenttree-query. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. Splitting a range at mid into [l, mid] and [mid, r] is the natural way to divide it.
The two halves share the element at mid, so it is counted twice, and a range of two elements recurses on itself
forever (SystemStackError). Use [l, mid] and [mid + 1, r]. Store node i's children at 2i and 2i + 1 and allocate 4n slots,
which always suffices for the recursive layout. Building is O(n).
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def build_bad(arr, l, r)
  return arr[l] if l == r
  mid = (l + r) / 2
  build_bad(arr, l, mid) + build_bad(arr, mid, r)
end
Correct:
 class SegTree
  attr_reader :tree, :size
  def initialize(arr)
    @size = arr.size
    @tree = Array.new(4 * [@size, 1].max, 0)
    build(arr, 1, 0, @size - 1) if @size > 0
  end
  def total
    @tree[1]
  end
  private
  def build(arr, node, l, r)
    if l == r
      @tree[node] = arr[l]
      return
    end
    mid = (l + r) / 2
    build(arr, 2 * node, l, mid)
    build(arr, 2 * node + 1, mid + 1, r)
    @tree[node] = @tree[2 * node] + @tree[2 * node + 1]
  end
end

A point update must recompute every ancestor on the path from the leaf to the root
ruby-segmenttree-update   lens: mutation   level: L2   family: ruby-segmenttree-mutation
Prerequisites: ruby-segmenttree-query. Follow-up: ruby-segmenttree-min. Complexity: O(log n).
 Common misconception. Changing the leaf value is enough, because queries read from the leaves.
Queries use the stored sums of inner nodes, so an ancestor that is not recomputed keeps answering with the old
value. After changing the leaf, recompute each ancestor as the sum of its children while the recursion unwinds. Only
one root-to-leaf path changes, so an update is O(log n).
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def update_bad(t, node, l, r, i, v)
  if l == r
    t[node] = v
    return
  end
  mid = (l + r) / 2
  if i <= mid
    update_bad(t, 2 * node, l, mid, i, v)
  else
    update_bad(t, 2 * node + 1, mid + 1, r, i, v)
  end
end
Correct:
 class SegTree
  def update(i, v)
    update_at(1, 0, @size - 1, i, v)
    self
  end
  private
  def update_at(node, l, r, i, v)
    if l == r
      @tree[node] = v
      return
    end
    mid = (l + r) / 2
    if i <= mid
      update_at(2 * node, l, mid, i, v)
    else
      update_at(2 * node + 1, mid + 1, r, i, v)
    end
    @tree[node] = @tree[2 * node] + @tree[2 * node + 1]
  end
end

A range query returns the identity for disjoint segments, the stored value for covered ones,
and combines otherwise
ruby-segmenttree-query   lens: access   level: L3   family: ruby-segmenttree-access
Prerequisites: ruby-segmenttree-build. Follow-up: ruby-segmenttree-update. Complexity: O(log n).
 Common misconception. A query can return the stored value whenever the segment is covered, and recurse
otherwise, without a disjoint case.
Without the disjoint check the recursion reaches leaves that lie outside the query and adds their values. For a sum
the identity is 0: return 0 when the node range does not intersect the query, return the stored sum when it is fully
inside, and otherwise add the answers from both children. At most about 2 log n nodes are expanded, so a query is
O(log n).
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def query_bad(t, node, l, r, ql, qr)
  return t[node] if l == r || (ql <= l && r <= qr)
  mid = (l + r) / 2
  query_bad(t, 2 * node, l, mid, ql, qr) +
    query_bad(t, 2 * node + 1, mid + 1, r, ql, qr)
end
Correct:
 class SegTree
  def query(ql, qr)
    query_at(1, 0, @size - 1, ql, qr)
  end
  private
  def query_at(node, l, r, ql, qr)
    return 0 if qr < l || r < ql
    return @tree[node] if ql <= l && r <= qr
    mid = (l + r) / 2
    query_at(2 * node, l, mid, ql, qr) + query_at(2 * node + 1, mid + 1, r, ql, qr)
  end
end
Lazy propagation must push pending additions to the children before descending into them
ruby-segmenttree-lazy   lens: mutation   level: L3   family: ruby-segmenttree-mutation
Prerequisites: ruby-segmenttree-min. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(log n).
 Common misconception. A pending range addition stored on a node can stay there until the whole node is queried.
A partial query or update descends into the children, which do not yet know about the addition stored on their parent,
so they return stale values. Push the pending value down (apply it to both children and clear it) before recursing.
Then range add and range sum are both O(log n) instead of O(n) per update.

 class LazySeg
  def initialize(arr)
    @n = arr.size
    @sum = Array.new(4 * @n, 0)
    @lazy = Array.new(4 * @n, 0)
    build(1, 0, @n - 1, arr)
  end
  def add(l, r, v)
    range_add(1, 0, @n - 1, l, r, v)
  end
  def sum(l, r)
    range_sum(1, 0, @n - 1, l, r)
  end
  private
  def build(node, l, r, arr)
    if l == r
      @sum[node] = arr[l]
      return
    end
    mid = (l + r) / 2
    build(2 * node, l, mid, arr)
    build(2 * node + 1, mid + 1, r, arr)
    @sum[node] = @sum[2 * node] + @sum[2 * node + 1]
  end
  def apply(node, l, r, v)
    @sum[node] += v * (r - l + 1)
    @lazy[node] += v
  end
  def push(node, l, r)
    return if @lazy[node].zero?
    mid = (l + r) / 2
    apply(2 * node, l, mid, @lazy[node])
    apply(2 * node + 1, mid + 1, r, @lazy[node])
    @lazy[node] = 0
  end
  def range_add(node, l, r, ql, qr, v)
    return if qr < l || r < ql
    if ql <= l && r <= qr
      apply(node, l, r, v)
      return
    end
    push(node, l, r)
    mid = (l + r) / 2
    range_add(2 * node, l, mid, ql, qr, v)
    range_add(2 * node + 1, mid + 1, r, ql, qr, v)
    @sum[node] = @sum[2 * node] + @sum[2 * node + 1]
  end
  def range_sum(node, l, r, ql, qr)
    return 0 if qr < l || r < ql
    return @sum[node] if ql <= l && r <= qr
    push(node, l, r)
    mid = (l + r) / 2
    range_sum(2 * node, l, mid, ql, qr) + range_sum(2 * node + 1, mid + 1, r, ql, qr)
  end
end

The identity element must match the operation: Float::INFINITY for minimum, not 0
ruby-segmenttree-min   lens: patterns   level: L3   family: ruby-segmenttree-patterns
Prerequisites: ruby-segmenttree-update. Follow-up: ruby-segmenttree-lazy. Complexity: O(log n).
 Common misconception. Starting the running result at 0 works for any combine operation.
Zero is the identity for sum, but for minimum any positive value is larger than 0, so every query returns 0. The identity
of min is Float::INFINITY and of max is -Float::INFINITY. This bottom-up version stores the leaves at n..2n-1 and
answers half-open ranges [l, r) by climbing; build is O(n) and query O(log n).
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 class MinSegBad
  def initialize(arr)
    @n = arr.size
    @t = Array.new(2 * @n, 0)
    arr.each_with_index { |v, i| @t[@n + i] = v }
    (@n - 1).downto(1) { |i| @t[i] = [@t[2 * i], @t[2 * i + 1]].min }
  end
  def query(l, r)
    res = 0
    l += @n
    r += @n
    while l < r
      if l.odd?
        res = [res, @t[l]].min
        l += 1
      end
      if r.odd?
        r -= 1
        res = [res, @t[r]].min
      end
      l /= 2
      r /= 2
    end
    res
  end
end
Correct:
 class MinSegTree
  def initialize(arr)
    @n = arr.size
    @t = Array.new(2 * @n, Float::INFINITY)
    arr.each_with_index { |v, i| @t[@n + i] = v }
    (@n - 1).downto(1) { |i| @t[i] = [@t[2 * i], @t[2 * i + 1]].min }
  end
  def query(l, r)
    res = Float::INFINITY
    l += @n
    r += @n
    while l < r
      if l.odd?
        res = [res, @t[l]].min
        l += 1
      end
      if r.odd?
        r -= 1
        res = [res, @t[r]].min
      end
      l /= 2
      r /= 2
    end
    res
  end
end

Prompt. Why is a recursive segment tree usually stored in an array of 4n slots?
Answer key (mentor only, never embedded). The recursive layout puts the children of node i at 2i and 2i + 1 and splits
ranges in the middle, so for sizes that are not powers of two the tree is not complete and some indexes are skipped. The
deepest level can reach an index of almost 4n, so 4n slots are a simple safe upper bound. A power-of-two padded size of
2 * 2^ceil(log2 n) would also work.

Split a segment into [l, mid] and [mid + 1, r] so the halves never overlap
ruby-segmenttree-build   lens: creation   level: L2   family: ruby-segmenttree-creation
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: ruby-segmenttree-query. Complexity: O(n).
Common misconception. Splitting a range at mid into [l, mid] and [mid, r] is the natural way to divide it.

Ruby Segment tree · 4. Segment tree strategies (continued)
The two halves share the element at mid, so it is counted twice, and a range of two elements recurses on itself
forever (SystemStackError). Use [l, mid] and [mid + 1, r]. Store node i's children at 2i and 2i + 1 and allocate 4n slots,
which always suffices for the recursive layout. Building is O(n).
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
def build_bad(arr, l, r)
return arr[l] if l == r
mid = (l + r) / 2
build_bad(arr, l, mid) + build_bad(arr, mid, r)
end

class SegTree
attr_reader :tree, :size
def initialize(arr)
@size = arr.size
@tree = Array.new(4 * [@size, 1].max, 0)
build(arr, 1, 0, @size - 1) if @size > 0
end
def total
@tree[1]
end
private
def build(arr, node, l, r)
if l == r
@tree[node] = arr[l]
return
end
mid = (l + r) / 2
build(arr, 2 * node, l, mid)
build(arr, 2 * node + 1, mid + 1, r)
@tree[node] = @tree[2 * node] + @tree[2 * node + 1]
end
end
A point update must recompute every ancestor on the path from the leaf to the root
ruby-segmenttree-update   lens: mutation   level: L2   family: ruby-segmenttree-mutation
Prerequisites: ruby-segmenttree-query. Follow-up: ruby-segmenttree-min. Complexity: O(log n).
Common misconception. Changing the leaf value is enough, because queries read from the leaves.
Queries use the stored sums of inner nodes, so an ancestor that is not recomputed keeps answering with the old
value. After changing the leaf, recompute each ancestor as the sum of its children while the recursion unwinds. Only
one root-to-leaf path changes, so an update is O(log n).

t[node] = v
return
end
mid = (l + r) / 2

update_bad(t, 2 * node, l, mid, i, v)
else
update_bad(t, 2 * node + 1, mid + 1, r, i, v)
end
end

A range query returns the identity for disjoint segments, the stored value for covered ones,
and combines otherwise
ruby-segmenttree-query   lens: access   level: L3   family: ruby-segmenttree-access
Prerequisites: ruby-segmenttree-build. Follow-up: ruby-segmenttree-update. Complexity: O(log n).
Common misconception. A query can return the stored value whenever the segment is covered, and recurse
otherwise, without a disjoint case.
Without the disjoint check the recursion reaches leaves that lie outside the query and adds their values. For a sum
the identity is 0: return 0 when the node range does not intersect the query, return the stored sum when it is fully
inside, and otherwise add the answers from both children. At most about 2 log n nodes are expanded, so a query is
O(log n).

mid = (l + r) / 2

query_bad(t, 2 * node + 1, mid + 1, r, ql, qr)

return 0 if qr < l || r < ql
return @tree[node] if ql <= l && r <= qr
mid = (l + r) / 2
query_at(2 * node, l, mid, ql, qr) + query_at(2 * node + 1, mid + 1, r, ql, qr)

Lazy propagation must push pending additions to the children before descending into them
ruby-segmenttree-lazy   lens: mutation   level: L3   family: ruby-segmenttree-mutation
Prerequisites: ruby-segmenttree-min. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(log n).
Common misconception. A pending range addition stored on a node can stay there until the whole node is queried.
A partial query or update descends into the children, which do not yet know about the addition stored on their parent,
so they return stale values. Push the pending value down (apply it to both children and clear it) before recursing.
Then range add and range sum are both O(log n) instead of O(n) per update.

The identity element must match the operation: Float::INFINITY for minimum, not 0
ruby-segmenttree-min   lens: patterns   level: L3   family: ruby-segmenttree-patterns
Prerequisites: ruby-segmenttree-update. Follow-up: ruby-segmenttree-lazy. Complexity: O(log n).
Common misconception. Starting the running result at 0 works for any combine operation.

Ruby Segment tree · 4. Segment tree strategies (continued)
Zero is the identity for sum, but for minimum any positive value is larger than 0, so every query returns 0. The identity
of min is Float::INFINITY and of max is -Float::INFINITY. This bottom-up version stores the leaves at n..2n-1 and
answers half-open ranges [l, r) by climbing; build is O(n) and query O(log n).

String#hash
ruby-bloomfilter-hash   lens: creation   level: L2   family: ruby-bloomfilter-creation
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: ruby-bloomfilter-bits. Complexity: O(k).
 Common misconception. item.hash is a quick way to get the hash value for a Bloom filter.
String#hash is seeded randomly for every Ruby process, so the same string hashes differently after a restart. A filter
that was saved, shared or rebuilt elsewhere then answers wrongly. Use deterministic hashes: Zlib.crc32 and
Digest::MD5 give two independent values h1 and h2, and double hashing derives all k positions as (h1 + i * h2) % m.
Keep h2 non-zero so positions differ. Each add or lookup costs O(k).

Correct:
 require "digest"
require "zlib"
class BloomFilter
  attr_reader :m, :k, :bits
  def initialize(m, k)
    @m = m
    @k = k
    @bits = 0
  end
  def positions(item)
    s = item.to_s
    h1 = Zlib.crc32(s)
    h2 = Digest::MD5.hexdigest(s).to_i(16) % (@m - 1) + 1
    Array.new(@k) { |i| (h1 + i * h2) % @m }
  end
  def add(item)
    positions(item).each { |i| @bits |= 1 << i }
    self
  end
  def include?(item)
    positions(item).all? { |i| @bits[i] == 1 }
  end
end

Date#+ adds days, so Jan 31 + 30 is Mar 1 in a leap year. Date#>> adds months and clamps the day to the last day
of the target month: Jan 31 >> 1 is Feb 29 (2024). Use >> for calendar months and + for exact day counts. Both
return new objects and are O(1).

end
Correct:

end

ruby-datetime-diff   lens: transformation   level: L2   family: ruby-datetime-transformation
Prerequisites: ruby-datetime-month. Follow-up: ruby-datetime-weekday. Complexity: O(1).

Date#- returns a Rational, so (Date.new(2024,3,10) - Date.new(2024,3,5)) is (5/1). It prints as "5/1" in strings and
compares equal to 5, but arithmetic with it stays Rational. Convert with to_i when you want a plain count of days.

Ruby Date, Time and DateTime · 4. Date, Time and DateTime strategies (continued)
Date.new validates its arguments and raises Date::Error (invalid date) for February 30. Date.valid_date?(y, m, d)
returns false instead of raising, which suits user input. Leap years are handled by the calendar: 2024 has February
29, 2100 does not.

Date.new(y, m, d)

ruby-datetime-month   lens: mutation   level: L2   family: ruby-datetime-mutation
Prerequisites: ruby-datetime-invalid. Follow-up: ruby-datetime-diff. Complexity: O(1).
Common misconception. Adding 30 days is the same as adding one month.
Date#+ adds days, so Jan 31 + 30 is Mar 1 in a leap year. Date#>> adds months and clamps the day to the last day
of the target month: Jan 31 >> 1 is Feb 29 (2024). Use >> for calendar months and + for exact day counts. Both
return new objects and are O(1).

Date#- returns a Rational, so (Date.new(2024,3,10) - Date.new(2024,3,5)) is (5/1). It prints as "5/1" in strings and
compares equal to 5, but arithmetic with it stays Rational. Convert with to_i when you want a plain count of days.

4.4 Algorithm chunks
Matrix rows must have equal length; a ragged literal raises ErrDimensionMismatch
ruby-matrix-ragged   lens: creation   level: L1   family: ruby-matrix-creation
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: ruby-matrix-multiply. Complexity: O(r * c).
 Common misconception. Matrix[[1, 2], [3]] pads the short row with zeros.
Every row of a Matrix must have the same number of columns. A ragged row list raises
ExceptionForMatrix::ErrDimensionMismatch. Build matrices with Matrix[[...]], Matrix.build(rows, cols) { |r, c| ... },
Matrix.identity(n) or Matrix.zero(r, c). Matrix needs require "matrix" (a bundled gem since Ruby 3.1).
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 require "matrix"
def ragged_bad
  Matrix[[1, 2], [3]]
end
Correct:
 require "matrix"
def built
  Matrix.build(2, 2) { |r, c| r * 2 + c + 1 }
end

Page 5
* is the matrix product; use hadamard_product for element-wise multiplication
ruby-matrix-multiply   lens: transformation   level: L2   family: ruby-matrix-transformation
Prerequisites: ruby-matrix-ragged. Follow-up: ruby-matrix-shape. Complexity: O(n^3).
 Common misconception. Multiplying two matrices with * multiplies matching elements.
* computes the row-by-column matrix product, so [[1, 2], [3, 4]] squared is [[7, 10], [15, 22]]. Element-wise
multiplication is hadamard_product (also called entrywise_product). The product of an r x k and a k x c matrix takes
O(r * k * c) operations.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 require "matrix"
def square_bad(m)
  Matrix.build(m.row_count, m.column_count) { |r, c| m[r, c] * m[r, c] }
end
Correct:
 require "matrix"
def square(m)
  m * m
end
def entrywise(m)
  m.hadamard_product(m)
end
Multiplying needs left columns equal to right rows; otherwise ErrDimensionMismatch is
raised
ruby-matrix-shape   lens: edge-cases   level: L2   family: ruby-matrix-edge-cases
Prerequisites: ruby-matrix-multiply. Follow-up: ruby-matrix-inverse. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Any two matrices can be multiplied.
The product A * B requires A.column_count == B.row_count. A 1 x 2 matrix times a 1 x 2 matrix raises
ExceptionForMatrix::ErrDimensionMismatch. Check the shapes before multiplying, or transpose one operand: A *
B.transpose is 1 x 1 here.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 require "matrix"
def product_bad(a, b)
  a * b
end
Correct:
 require "matrix"
def product(a, b)
  return nil unless a.column_count == b.row_count
  a * b
end

Page 6
inverse of an integer matrix has Rational entries and a singular matrix raises ErrNotRegular
ruby-matrix-inverse   lens: edge-cases   level: L3   family: ruby-matrix-edge-cases
Prerequisites: ruby-matrix-shape. Follow-up: ruby-matrix-fib. Complexity: O(n^3).
 Common misconception. The inverse of an integer matrix is made of floats, and every square matrix has one.
Matrix#inverse uses exact arithmetic: integer input gives Rational entries such as (3/2). A matrix with determinant 0
has no inverse and raises ExceptionForMatrix::ErrNotRegular. Test determinant.zero? first, or use rescue.
Determinant and inverse are O(n^3).
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 require "matrix"
def invert_bad(m)
  m.inverse
end
Correct:
 require "matrix"
def invert(m)
  return nil if m.determinant.zero?
  m.inverse
end
Use inner_product for the dot product; Vector * Vector is not defined
ruby-matrix-vector   lens: patterns   level: L3   family: ruby-matrix-patterns
Prerequisites: ruby-matrix-fib. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. v * w computes the dot product of two vectors.
Vector * Vector raises ExceptionForMatrix::ErrOperationNotDefined; * with a number scales the vector and * with a
Matrix multiplies. The dot product is v.inner_product(w) (also dot), the length is v.norm (also magnitude). Both are
O(n).
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 require "matrix"
def dot_bad(v, w)
  v * w
end
Correct:
 require "matrix"
def dot(v, w)
  v.inner_product(w)
end

Raise [[1, 1], [1, 0]] to the n-th power to get Fibonacci numbers in O(log n) multiplications
ruby-matrix-fib   lens: patterns   level: L4   family: ruby-matrix-patterns
Prerequisites: ruby-matrix-inverse. Follow-up: ruby-matrix-vector. Complexity: O(log n).
 Common misconception. Any 2x2 matrix of ones gives Fibonacci numbers.

Common misconception. Matrix[[1, 2], [3]] pads the short row with zeros.
Every row of a Matrix must have the same number of columns. A ragged row list raises
ExceptionForMatrix::ErrDimensionMismatch. Build matrices with Matrix[[...]], Matrix.build(rows, cols) { |r, c| ... },

def ragged_bad

end

Matrix.build(2, 2) { |r, c| r * 2 + c + 1 }

* is the matrix product; use hadamard_product for element-wise multiplication

Prerequisites: ruby-matrix-ragged. Follow-up: ruby-matrix-shape. Complexity: O(n^3).
Common misconception. Multiplying two matrices with * multiplies matching elements.
* computes the row-by-column matrix product, so [[1, 2], [3, 4]] squared is [[7, 10], [15, 22]]. Element-wise
multiplication is hadamard_product (also called entrywise_product). The product of an r x k and a k x c matrix takes
O(r * k * c) operations.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):

def square_bad(m)
Matrix.build(m.row_count, m.column_count) { |r, c| m[r, c] * m[r, c] }
end
Correct:
require "matrix"
def square(m)
m * m
end
def entrywise(m)
m.hadamard_product(m)

B.transpose is 1 x 1 here.

4.4 Algorithm chunks
a..b includes b and a...b excludes it; index loops over an array need the exclusive form
ruby-range-exclusive   lens: creation   level: L1   family: ruby-range-creation
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: ruby-range-endless. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. (0..a.size) is the right range for visiting every index of an array.
The two-dot range includes its end, the three-dot range stops before it. The valid indexes of an array are 0...a.size, so
(0..a.size) visits one extra index, where a[i] is nil. (1..5).size is 5 and (1...5).size is 4. For simple loops prefer
each_index or each_with_index.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def doubled_bad(a)
  (0..a.size).map { |i| a[i] * 2 }
end
Correct:
 def doubled(a)
  (0...a.size).map { |i| a[i] * 2 }
end
An endless range cannot be turned into an array; take from it or use lazy
ruby-range-endless   lens: iteration   level: L2   family: ruby-range-iteration
Prerequisites: ruby-range-exclusive. Follow-up: ruby-range-member. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. (1..).to_a returns the numbers from 1 upwards.
An endless range (1..) has no last element, so to_a raises RangeError (cannot convert endless range to an array).
Use first(n), take_while, find, or lazy to consume only what you need. The same range works as a slice end: a[1..] is
the array without its first element.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def first_squares_bad(n)
  (1..).to_a.first(n).map { |x| x * x }
end
Correct:
 def first_squares(n)
  (1..).lazy.map { |x| x * x }.first(n)
end

A Float range cannot be iterated with each; use step
ruby-range-float   lens: iteration   level: L3   family: ruby-range-iteration
Prerequisites: ruby-range-member. Follow-up: ruby-range-bsearch. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. (0.0..1.0).each walks the values with a step of 0.1.
Iteration needs a successor, and Float has none, so each on a Float range raises TypeError (can't iterate from Float).
Use (0.0..1.0).step(0.25) for evenly spaced values, or iterate over integers and scale. step is O(number of values).
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def samples_bad
  out = []
  (0.0..1.0).each { |x| out << x }
  out
end
Correct:
 def samples
  (0.0..1.0).step(0.25).to_a
end

Prompt. Why must a Range#bsearch block in find-minimum mode be monotone?
Answer key (mentor only, never embedded). Binary search discards half of the range after each probe, assuming that
if the block is true at some x it stays true for every larger x, and false for every smaller one. A block such as x * x == n is
true at one point only, so a probe on the wrong side of it throws away the part that contains the answer. A condition like x
* x > n is false then true, so each probe is safe.

 class RBNode

class RBTree
  include Enumerable
  attr_reader :root, :size
  def initialize
    @root = nil
    @size = 0
  end
  def insert(key)
    @root = insert_at(@root, key)
    @root.red = false
    self
  end
  def height(node = @root)
    node ? 1 + [height(node.left), height(node.right)].max : 0
  end
  def each(&block)
    return to_enum(:each) unless block
    walk(@root, &block)
    self
  end
  private
  def red?(node)
    !node.nil? && node.red
  end
  def rotate_left(h)
    x = h.right
    h.right = x.left
    x.left = h
    x.red = h.red
    h.red = true
    x
  end
  def rotate_right(h)
    x = h.left
    h.left = x.right
    x.right = h
    x.red = h.red
    h.red = true
    x
  end
  def flip_colors(h)
    h.red = true
    h.left.red = false
    h.right.red = false
  end
  def insert_at(h, key)
    if h.nil?
      @size += 1
      return RBNode.new(key)

    if key < h.key
      h.left = insert_at(h.left, key)
    elsif key > h.key
      h.right = insert_at(h.right, key)

    h = rotate_left(h) if red?(h.right) && !red?(h.left)
    h = rotate_right(h) if red?(h.left) && red?(h.left.left)
    flip_colors(h) if red?(h.left) && red?(h.right)
    h
  end
  def walk(node, &block)
    return unless node
    walk(node.left, &block)
    block.call(node.key)
    walk(node.right, &block)

end

A linked queue must reset its tail when the last node is dequeued
ruby-queue-linked   lens: insertion-and-deletion   level: L1   family: ruby-queue-insertion-and-deletion
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: ruby-queue-twostack. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. dequeue only needs to move the head pointer.
When the last node is removed the head becomes nil but the tail still points to the removed node. The next enqueue
then links the new node behind the dead node, and the queue looks empty or loses elements. Reset the tail to nil
whenever the head becomes nil. enqueue and dequeue are O(1).

      @head = node
    end
    @tail = node
  end
  def dequeue
    return nil unless @head
    v = @head[0]
    @head = @head[1]
    v
  end

    node = @head

      out << node[0]
      node = node[1]

    out

class LinkedQueue
  include Enumerable
  attr_reader :size
  def initialize
    @head = @tail = nil
    @size = 0
  end
  def enqueue(v)
    node = QNode.new(v)
    if @tail
      @tail.next = node
    else
      @head = node
    end
    @tail = node
    @size += 1
    self
  end
  def dequeue
    return nil unless @head
    v = @head.value
    @head = @head.next
    @tail = nil unless @head
    @size -= 1
    v
  end
  def front
    @head && @head.value
  end
  def empty?
    @size.zero?
  end
  def each
    return to_enum(:each) unless block_given?
    node = @head
    while node
      yield node.value
      node = node.next
    end

end

Breadth-first search marks a node as seen when it is enqueued, not when it is dequeued
ruby-queue-bfs   lens: patterns   level: L2   family: ruby-queue-patterns
Prerequisites: ruby-queue-ring. Follow-up: ruby-queue-movingavg. Complexity: O(V+E).
 Common misconception. Marking a node visited when it is dequeued avoids repeats.
A node reachable by two paths is enqueued twice if it is only marked on dequeue, producing duplicates in the visiting
order and wasted work. Mark on enqueue so each node enters the queue once. An Array works as the queue
because shift is O(1) amortised in CRuby. BFS is O(V + E).
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def bfs_bad(graph, start)
  order = []
  seen = {}
  queue = [start]
  until queue.empty?
    node = queue.shift
    seen[node] = true
    order << node
    graph[node].each { |n| queue.push(n) unless seen[n] }
  end
  order
end
Correct:
 def bfs(graph, start)
  order = []
  seen = { start => true }
  queue = [start]
  until queue.empty?
    node = queue.shift
    order << node
    graph[node].each do |n|
      next if seen[n]
      seen[n] = true
      queue.push(n)
    end
  end
  order
end
A moving average keeps a queue of the window and divides by its current length
ruby-queue-movingavg   lens: patterns   level: L2   family: ruby-queue-patterns
Prerequisites: ruby-queue-bfs. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Dividing the running sum by the window size is right from the first value.
Until the window fills, the queue holds fewer values than the window size, so dividing by the size understates the
average. Add the new value, subtract the value that leaves the queue, and divide by the queue length. fdiv avoids
integer division. Each update is O(1).

A ring buffer queue wraps its indexes with modulo so storage stays fixed
ruby-queue-ring   lens: mutation   level: L3   family: ruby-queue-mutation
Prerequisites: ruby-queue-twostack. Follow-up: ruby-queue-bfs. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Advancing head and tail with += 1 is enough for a fixed-size queue.
Without modulo the indexes grow forever, and assigning past the end of a Ruby Array silently extends it, so the
supposedly fixed buffer keeps growing. Wrap with (i + 1) % capacity. Track size separately to tell full from empty.
enqueue and dequeue are O(1) with constant memory.

 class RingQueue
  def initialize(cap)
    @buf = Array.new(cap)
    @head = @tail = @size = 0
  end
  def slots
    @buf.size
  end
  def enqueue(v)
    return false if @size == @buf.size
    @buf[@tail] = v
    @tail = (@tail + 1) % @buf.size
    @size += 1
    true
  end
  def dequeue
    return nil if @size.zero?
    v = @buf[@head]
    @buf[@head] = nil
    @head = (@head + 1) % @buf.size
    @size -= 1
    v
  end
  def to_a
    Array.new(@size) { |i| @buf[(@head + i) % @buf.size] }
  end
end

A queue from two stacks moves items across only when the output stack is empty
ruby-queue-twostack   lens: patterns   level: L3   family: ruby-queue-patterns
Prerequisites: ruby-queue-linked. Follow-up: ruby-queue-ring. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. dequeue can always move everything from the input stack to the output stack first.
Moving every time puts newer items on top of older ones that are still waiting in the output stack, so the order is
wrong. Transfer only when the output stack is empty. Each element moves at most once, so dequeue is O(1)
amortised.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):

  def initialize
    @in = []
    @out = []
  end
  def enqueue(v)
    @in.push(v)
    self
  end
  def dequeue
    @out.push(@in.pop) until @in.empty?
    @out.pop
  end
end
Correct:
 class TwoStackQueue
  def initialize
    @in = []
    @out = []
  end
  def enqueue(v)
    @in.push(v)
    self
  end
  def dequeue
    @out.push(@in.pop) until @in.empty? if @out.empty?
    @out.pop
  end
  def size
    @in.size + @out.size
  end
end

Prompt. Why is dequeue O(1) amortised in a queue built from two stacks even though one call can move many
elements?
Answer key (mentor only, never embedded). Each element is pushed onto the input stack once, moved to the output
stack at most once, and popped once. A single dequeue may transfer many elements, but the transfer only happens
when the output stack is empty, so across n operations the total number of moves is at most n. The cost spread over all
operations is constant per operation.

Inserting between two nodes rewires four pointers, and sentinels remove the edge cases
ruby-doublylinkedlist-insert   lens: insertion-and-deletion   level: L1   family: ruby-doublylinkedlist-insertion-and-deletion
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: ruby-doublylinkedlist-remove. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Inserting after a node only needs node.next and the new node's prev.
A doubly linked list has two links per edge. Inserting between a and b must set the new node's prev and next and also
a.next and b.prev. Forgetting b.prev leaves the backward chain skipping the new node, so forward and backward
traversal disagree. Head and tail sentinel nodes mean every real node has both neighbours, so push_front,
push_back and middle inserts share one code path in O(1).

class DList
  include Enumerable
  attr_reader :head, :tail, :size
  def initialize
    @head = DNode.new
    @tail = DNode.new
    @head.next = @tail
    @tail.prev = @head
    @size = 0
  end
  def link_after(node, fresh)
    fresh.prev = node
    fresh.next = node.next
    node.next.prev = fresh
    node.next = fresh
    @size += 1
    fresh
  end
  def insert_after(node, v)
    link_after(node, DNode.new(v))
  end
  def push_front(v)
    insert_after(@head, v)
  end
  def push_back(v)
    insert_after(@tail.prev, v)
  end
  def each
    return to_enum(:each) unless block_given?
    node = @head.next
    until node.equal?(@tail)
      yield node.value
      node = node.next
    end
  end
  def reverse_each
    return to_enum(:reverse_each) unless block_given?
    node = @tail.prev
    until node.equal?(@head)
      yield node.value
      node = node.prev
    end

Index from the nearer end, and normalise negative indexes before walking
ruby-doublylinkedlist-at   lens: access   level: L2   family: ruby-doublylinkedlist-access
Prerequisites: ruby-doublylinkedlist-reverse. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. Walking i times from the head also handles negative indexes.
Integer#times does nothing for a negative count, so a negative index silently returns the first element. Normalise it by
adding the size, reject out-of-range values with nil, then walk from whichever end is closer, at most size/2 steps.
Access by position is still O(n); a list is not a replacement for an Array when you index a lot.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def at_bad(list, i)
  node = list.head.next
  i.times { node = node.next }
  node.value
end
Correct:
 class DList
  def at(i)
    i += @size if i < 0
    return nil unless i >= 0 && i < @size
    if i < @size / 2
      node = @head.next
      i.times { node = node.next }
    else
      node = @tail.prev
      (@size - 1 - i).times { node = node.prev }
    end
    node.value
  end
end
Removing a node you already hold is O(1) because it knows both neighbours
ruby-doublylinkedlist-remove   lens: insertion-and-deletion   level: L2   family: ruby-doublylinkedlist-insertion-and-deletion
Prerequisites: ruby-doublylinkedlist-insert. Follow-up: ruby-doublylinkedlist-lru. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Unlinking a node only needs prev.next = node.next.
The node after the removed one still points back to it through prev unless node.next.prev is updated too. Backward
traversal then visits a node that forward traversal no longer sees. With both links fixed, removal given a node
reference is O(1); a singly linked list must first find the previous node in O(n).
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):

  node.prev.next = node.next
  node.value
end
Correct:

  def remove(node)
    node.prev.next = node.next
    node.next.prev = node.prev
    @size -= 1
    node.value
  end
end

Reverse a doubly linked list by swapping prev and next in every node, sentinels included
ruby-doublylinkedlist-reverse   lens: mutation   level: L3   family: ruby-doublylinkedlist-mutation
Prerequisites: ruby-doublylinkedlist-lru. Follow-up: ruby-doublylinkedlist-at. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. After swapping a node's links, node.next still leads to the next node to visit.
Once node.next and node.prev are swapped, node.next points to the old previous node, so advancing with it walks
backwards and stops at once. Save the old next first, swap, then move on. Swap the two sentinels too, then
exchange the head and tail references. O(n) time, O(1) extra space.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def reverse_bad(list)
  node = list.head
  while node
    node.next, node.prev = node.prev, node.next
    node = node.next
  end
  list
end
Correct:
 class DList
  def reverse!
    node = @head
    while node
      nxt = node.next
      node.next, node.prev = node.prev, node.next
      node = nxt
    end
    @head, @tail = @tail, @head
    self
  end
end
An LRU cache pairs a Hash for lookup with a doubly linked list for recency order
ruby-doublylinkedlist-lru   lens: patterns   level: L3   family: ruby-doublylinkedlist-patterns
Prerequisites: ruby-doublylinkedlist-remove. Follow-up: ruby-doublylinkedlist-reverse. Complexity: O(1).

unlink and relink, and the Hash maps each key to its node, so get and put are both O(1). Evict the node before the tail
sentinel and delete its key from the Hash as well.

 class LRU
  def initialize(cap)
    @cap = cap
    @map = {}
    @list = DList.new
  end
  def get(k)
    node = @map[k]
    return nil unless node
    @list.remove(node)
    @list.link_after(@list.head, node)
    node.value[1]
  end
  def put(k, v)
    if (node = @map[k])
      @list.remove(node)
      @list.link_after(@list.head, node)
      node.value = [k, v]
      return v
    end
    if @map.size >= @cap
      old = @list.tail.prev
      @list.remove(old)
      @map.delete(old.value[0])
    end
    @map[k] = @list.push_front([k, v])
    v
  end
end

Prompt. Why do head and tail sentinel nodes simplify a doubly linked list?

so insert and remove never have to test for the first or last node or update separate head and tail references. push_front,
push_back and middle inserts all use the same four pointer updates, and an empty list is just two linked sentinels, which
removes a whole class of nil bugs.

2. Overview and mental model: Data
Data.define(:x, :y) (Ruby 3.2+) creates an immutable value class. Instances are frozen, have readers but no setters,
compare by value and have a stable hash. with(x: 5) returns a modified copy.
Construction is strict: every member is required (positionally or by keyword) and extra arguments raise
ArgumentError. Defaults come from overriding initialize with keyword defaults and calling super.
Immutability is shallow: mutable members such as arrays can still change unless you copy and freeze them. Use
Data for keys, set elements and values passed between layers; use Struct when you need mutation.

2. Overview and mental model: Data
Data.define(:x, :y) (Ruby 3.2+) creates an immutable value class. Instances are frozen, have readers but no setters,
compare by value and have a stable hash. with(x: 5) returns a modified copy.
Construction is strict: every member is required (positionally or by keyword) and extra arguments raise
ArgumentError. Defaults come from overriding initialize with keyword defaults and calling super.
Immutability is shallow: mutable members such as arrays can still change unless you copy and freeze them. Use
Data for keys, set elements and values passed between layers; use Struct when you need mutation.
Toolbox

p = Point.new(x: 1, y: 2)
p.with(x: 5)
p.to_h
p == Point.new(1, 2)
p.frozen?

4.4 Algorithm chunks
Data instances have no setters; use with to get a changed copy
ruby-data-immutable   lens: mutation   level: L1   family: ruby-data-mutation
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: ruby-data-args. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. A Data object can be changed with a setter like a Struct.
Data.define(:x, :y) creates readers only, and instances are frozen. Assigning pt.x = 5 raises NoMethodError, and
instance_variable_set raises FrozenError. with(x: 5) returns a new object with the changed field and leaves the
original untouched.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 Pt = Data.define(:x, :y)
def move_bad(pt)
  pt.x = 5
  pt
end
Correct:
 Vec = Data.define(:x, :y)
def move(vec, dx)
  vec.with(x: vec.x + dx)
end
Data requires every member; supply defaults by overriding initialize with keyword defaults

 Common misconception. Data.new(1) fills the missing member with nil, like Struct.
Data is strict: a missing member raises ArgumentError (missing keyword: :y) and an extra one raises too. Both
positional and keyword construction are accepted. To give a member a default, override initialize with keyword
parameters and call super.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):

ruby-data-equality   lens: equality   level: L2   family: ruby-data-equality
Prerequisites: ruby-data-args. Follow-up: ruby-data-shallow. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. Two plain objects with the same fields are equal.
Data defines ==, eql? and hash from its members, and instances cannot change, so their hash code stays valid in a
Set or as a Hash key. A plain class compares by identity, so a Set keeps duplicates. This makes Data a good fit for
visited-set coordinates in a grid search.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):

  attr_reader :row, :col
  def initialize(row, col)

    @col = col
  end
end
def visited_bad(moves)

Correct:

def visited(moves)
  moves.map { |r, c| Cell.new(row: r, col: c) }.to_set.size

with returns a new Data; ignoring its result leaves the original unchanged
ruby-data-with   lens: transformation   level: L2   family: ruby-data-transformation
Prerequisites: ruby-data-shallow. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. pt.with(x: 1) updates pt.
Because Data is immutable, with builds and returns a new instance. Calling it as a statement and then using the
original gives the old values. Assign the result or return it. Chained updates (a.with(x: 1).with(y: 2)) create one object
per step.

end
Correct:

end

ruby-data-shallow   lens: mutation   level: L3   family: ruby-data-mutation
Prerequisites: ruby-data-equality. Follow-up: ruby-data-with. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. A frozen Data object cannot change at all.
Freezing applies to the Data object, not to the objects it refers to. A Data with an array member lets callers push into
that array, and the same array may also be shared with the caller. Copy and freeze mutable members in initialize or
at construction, for example items.dup.freeze.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 Box = Data.define(:items)
def box_bad(items)
  Box.new(items: items)
end
Correct:
 Box2 = Data.define(:items) do
  def initialize(items:)
    super(items: items.dup.freeze)
  end
end
def box(items)
  Box2.new(items: items)
end

ruby-data-immutable-ex2   format: explain-why   level: L2   grading: rubric   modes: practice, interview
Prompt. Why is Data a better fit than Struct for a value used as a Hash key?
Answer key (mentor only, never embedded). A Hash stores each key under its hash code at insertion time. A Struct
can be changed after it was stored, which changes its hash code and makes the entry unreachable. A Data instance is
frozen, so its members cannot change and its hash code stays valid. Data also defines equality by value, so equal
instances find the same entry.

Safe Rust
Beginner
O(N^2) Time, O(1) Space
Purpose and mental model
Bubble sort as an adjacent-swap teaching algorithm, with early-exit optimization.
Why Rust changes this topic
The algorithmic idea is language-independent, but the implementation must make ownership, aliasing, mutation, failure, and allocation explicit. Prefer borrowing slices and references for read-only work, narrowly scoped &mut borrows for mutation, owned values when ownership transfer is the cleanest API, and smart pointers/interior mutability only when the data model genuinely requires shared topology.
